item.content:encoded:
Ranger Suarez is back to having fun after clinching the playoffs. Despite losing on Sunday, the Boston Red Sox clinched their spot in the postseason due to other teams' losses. The Sox took a team picture on the field at Tropicana Field before heading into the clubhouse for the usual champagne showers and beer.
In the team photo, Suarez clearly sticks out. Standing right in the middle, the lefty starter had bright red shorts pulled up well above his waist, and his celebratory shirt tucked in. He was also the only player in the picture with his goggles already covering his eyes. Suarez was known as a fun celebration guy with the Philadelphia Phillies, and it was something the fans there loved about him; Red Sox Nation was just waiting to see in Boston.
While Suarez is all fun and games with good spirits during a celebration, he does a complete 180 once the playoffs start. He's been one of the best playoff pitchers ever. His 1.48 ERA is the sixth-lowest of all time among pitchers with at least 40 innings pitched in the playoffs.
The 31-year-old has pitched in each of the last four postseasons. In 2023, he allowed just two earned runs in 14 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed four earned runs in 18 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed no runs in 4 1/3 innings. In 2025, he allowed one earned run in five innings. In the regular season, the lefty has a career 8.4 K/9; in the playoffs, it's 9.3
Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree should excite fans after last season's playoff rotation
His playoff excellence was part of the reason the Red Sox signed him. While Suarez has been a very solid regular-season pitcher, it was his success in the playoffs that really made him stand out in last season's free-agent pool. After Garrett Crochet, the Red Sox ended up relying on Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. The Sox knew they needed another playoff-tested arm for the postseason and made the splash signing of the lefty to do so.
The Red Sox now head into the 2026 playoffs with a projected Wild Card round rotation that will consist of Suarez, Sonny Gray, and Payton Tolle. While the exact order is yet to be determined, those three arms will instill much more confidence than the three who started the games last year.
Suarez likes to have his fun. He did so in Philly and is doing so again here in Boston. That doesn't mean that opponents should take him lightly. Come playoff time, Suarez turns it on and shuts down the other teams.

item.title: [nesn.com] Chad Tracy Delivers Powerful Message After Red Sox Clinch Playoff Spot | NESN
item.dc:creator: Rodney Knuppel
item.description: The Boston Red Sox did not clinch their postseason berth with a dramatic walk-off hit or a dominant performance from their pitching staff. They clinched after losing 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays and receiving help from Mike Yastrzemski and the Atlanta Braves. Interim manager Chad Tracy did not care how the ticket was punched. “When you work as hard as we have worked, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” Tracy told reporters. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.” That message per
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox did not clinch their postseason berth with a dramatic walk-off hit or a dominant performance from their pitching staff. They clinched after losing 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays and receiving help from Mike Yastrzemski and the Atlanta Braves.
Interim manager Chad Tracy did not care how the ticket was punched.
“When you work as hard as we have worked, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” Tracy told reporters. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.”
That message perfectly captured Boston’s remarkable season. The Red Sox were 32-46 and appeared destined to spend the summer discussing trades, organizational changes and another disappointing finish. Instead, they became the first team in MLB history to finish above .500 and reach the playoffs after losing at least 46 of its first 78 games.
“They didn’t take no for an answer,” Tracy said.
Where It Started
Tracy inherited a 10-17 team when the Red Sox moved on from Alex Cora in April. There was no immediate transformation, and Boston’s season continued to drift for several weeks.
Eventually, everything changed. Boston swept four games from the New York Yankees at Fenway Park in late June and began one of the most impressive turnarounds in franchise history. Young players developed into meaningful contributors, the clubhouse remained together and the Red Sox kept finding ways to survive injuries.
The result is a second consecutive postseason appearance and another likely Wild Card Series against the Yankees. That matchup did not work out for Boston last October. The Red Sox won the opener behind Garrett Crochet but dropped the next two games in New York.
This year’s roster has traveled a much different road.
The Red Sox have played meaningful baseball for months because almost every loss threatened to undo the progress they had made. Players such as Roman Anthony, Payton Tolle and Connelly Early have grown up in that environment, while veterans including Trevor Story and Willson Contreras helped keep the clubhouse steady.
Getting Things Set Up
Now Boston has an opportunity to set its rotation, protect tired relievers and enter the postseason with more than a week to prepare. The final regular-season games still matter, especially with the Cleveland Guardians visiting Fenway Park. Boston can use the series to evaluate potential postseason matchups and determine which pitchers are best equipped for important October innings.
The celebration also strengthens Tracy’s case to remain manager beyond this season. Boston did not merely improve after he took control. The Red Sox completed a turnaround that had never been accomplished in major league history.
Tracy did not want credit Sunday. His message remained focused on the players who refused to allow a terrible start to define them. That approach may be one of the biggest reasons the Red Sox are still playing.

When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultim
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

item.content:encoded:
レッドソックスの吉田正尚外野手（３３）が厳しい状況を迎えている。現在も左足ハムストリングの負傷で故障者リスト入りしており、ポストシーズンのロースター入りも望み薄。ＭＬＢ４年目の今季もケガに悩まされて８７試合で打率２割７分４厘、５本塁打、２８打点にとどまり、結果を出せなかった。吉田をめぐっては何度となく放出の噂があったが、そのたびに５年９０００万ドル（約１４２億円）の高額契約が足かせとなって移籍には至らなかったとされる。
しかし、今シーズンも期待を裏切り、契約期間が来年まで続くことを思えば球団の我慢も限界。米メディア「アルバット」は「吉田はまさに時限爆弾だ。かつてフロントの最も大胆な賭けの１つと見られたこの日本人スターは度重なるケガとその真の実力に対する疑問に悩まされてきた。彼は現在も故障者リスト入りし、プレーオフのロースター入りも疑問符だ」と切り捨てている。
さらに「２０２７年まで年俸１８００万ドル（約２８億円）を受け取る彼は、長打力も守備力もない指名打者だ。特に外野争いが激化している現状では正当化しがたいぜいたく品だ。フロントは彼を放出するために契約のかなりの部分を負担しなければならないだろうが、忍耐も限界に近づいている」と見ている。状態さえよければ非凡な打撃力を発揮できるが、今や球団の信頼を取り戻すのは難しい。
地元メディア「ボソックス・インジェクション」も「レッドソックスのユニホームを着て最後の時を過ごす選手」として紹介し「彼がプレーオフのロースター入りに値しない理由はあまりに多い。どうフィットするのか想像しにくい」と報じている。

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Risky business: In 2026, Craig Breslow and the Red Sox defied expectations with bold in-season risks - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Alex Speier
item.description: Even with the Red Sox having secured their second straight postseason berth, the magnitude of Craig Breslow’s gamble five months ago remains startling. There have been times when teams reacted to slow starts with a managerial or coaching staff change. item.content:encoded:
Even with the Red Sox having secured their second straight postseason berth, the magnitude of Craig Breslow’s gamble five months ago remains startling.
There have been times when teams reacted to slow starts with a managerial or coaching staff change. But longtime members of the industry could not recall anything like the shakeup enacted by Breslow in April, when he fired manager Alex Cora and replaced six other members of the coaching staff.
It was a move that departed from convention both for when it happened (barely a month into the season) and the extent of the change. It also pointed to an emerging theme of Breslow’s time as chief baseball officer: The willingness of the Sox to take significant in-season risks.
The firing of Cora and the staff members (with replacements plucked from the minors with little big league clubhouse experience), the mid-June trade of Rafael Devers in 2025, and the acquisition of catcher Adley Rutschman in exchange for a package of young talent (four of the Sox’ top 10 prospects, as well as catcher Carlos Narváez) that exceeded any in-season move by the Sox this century all pointed to an organization making massive bets on in-season changes.
“I always try to be guided by what I believe to be right and best for the organization,” Breslow said of his in-season risk tolerance. “Oftentimes, most people in these jobs would say their initial read or inclination of a situation was largely a correct one, but friction and inertia and emotion prevented you from acting on that. Then, you look back and say I wish I would have done whatever it was you were thinking at the time more often than you say that was probably not the right decision, and I wish I hadn’t.
“When you evaluate decisions through that lens, I think I default to, when you reach a certain level of conviction, you have to act.”
That sounds straightforward, but given baseball’s 162-game schedule, there’s often a willingness by heads of baseball operations to let situations play out over larger samples rather than intervene quickly. On both a personal and organizational level, a major in-season shakeup is uncomfortable.
“I certainly don’t sleep well [after a major change] for a few reasons, mostly because these are people that you have relationships with, and it’s not the outcome that you were looking for,” said Breslow. “These decisions are incredibly difficult. We’re talking about people’s lives, their families, children … there are a lot of implications to making these changes. So, it is wildly uncomfortable.”
Still, in a view perhaps informed by his playing career, Breslow has learned to remain open to uncomfortable in-season change — not for its own sake, but instead as a course correction when he sees a path to improving the club.
“I try to balance my [playing] experiences with what more information is telling me,” Breslow said. “I don’t think if I were only looking through things as I had experienced them that that would necessarily position us to make better decisions. But I think ignoring them would be ignoring valuable insights that I’ve learned.
“I was a lefthanded reliever that bounced around, who didn’t find success early on, pretty consistently evaluated the information that my performance was telling me, and tried to make adjustments as quickly as possible. I didn’t have the luxury of infinite runway in front of me to figure things out over time. If that’s an attitude or approach that I take to this job, then I think that’s OK.”
Breslow’s playing career may also inform his approach to in-season risks in another way: The way he values the chance to contend for a title.
It certainly would have been understandable if the Sox had decided by mid-June — around their 32-46 nadir — that they were open for business in a sell-off. Indeed, the Sox were at least starting to prepare for such an eventuality, with some of their pro scouts assigned to organizations who might be interested in short-term veterans, particularly Sonny Gray (who will be a free agent after 2026).
That said, Breslow had experience as a player of a long-shot team emerging as a champion. And so, even though there were few precedents for a team such as the Sox to overcome their long odds, based on his belief in the talent of the group, Breslow wanted to give the team as much time as possible to compete, respecting what he referred to as “the sanctity of a season.”
“Maybe that is born out of my playing career and the fact that the Red Sox won the World Series in 2013 as an improbable group going into the season,” he said. “Fundamentally, my confidence and belief in the players that we had on our roster [in 2026] had not changed. Players didn’t become meaningfully less talented. My belief in the roster was consistent.”
“But it’s interesting. Everybody who sits in my seat is going to talk about sustainability and the ability to compete for championships every single year. I think it’s very important to balance that with acknowledging the importance of every individual season. Otherwise, you talk about windows and about how maybe this isn’t the year, but that’s OK because next year we’ll still have the core of a really good team.
“I have learned that sometimes really good teams don’t have the seasons that they want. Sometimes teams that you don’t have maybe the highest expectations far outperform them for a season’s length. So you don’t want to dismiss what is immediately in front of you in exchange for this idea of lumping seasons together and just kind of thinking about being in the midst of a window.”
And so, the Sox ended up doing the opposite of what everyone forecast. A team for whom a veteran sell-off seemed almost inevitable instead ended up — thanks to one of the great runs in franchise history from late June to mid-August — taking big swings for deadline upgrades with moves to add infielder Curtis Mead and Rutschman.
In different ways, both moves stunned the industry given what the Sox gave up (Connelly Early for Mead; prospects Anthony Eyanson, Kyson Witherspoon, Enddy Azocar, and Harold Rivas, as well as Narváez for Rutschman). But from afar, Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young — like Breslow, a former player — could appreciate what his colleague did.
“In general, careers are short, and I want every player that puts on our uniform to have a chance to compete for a World Series. That should be our goal as an organization,” said Young. “When you have a team that’s in a win cycle, you need to be bold at times to go for it.
“It doesn’t mean necessarily you’re going to sustain success, but the goal is not to just make the playoffs. The goal is to win championships. And for me, especially in 2023 when we made very bold moves, it led to [a championship]. It easily could not have, but I know that if we didn’t make those moves, we wouldn’t have won. [And] there’s no doubt the player in me is influenced by the opportunity to win.”
Breslow’s deadline deals were motivated by a similar hunger. Now that the Red Sox have qualified for the playoffs, the ultimate impact of the bets made by Breslow in what he repeatedly described as a “difficult” season will gain greater definition in the postseason tournament.
But regardless of what happens, the path to get to the playoffs represented a fascinating shift in how the Red Sox conducted business, in a fashion that defied expectations at numerous turns on and off the field.
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.dc:creator: Justice delos Santos

item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO — First, the good news: outfielder Bo Davidson and infielder Marcelo Mayer will make their long-awaited Giants debuts on Monday night at Oracle Park against the Minnesota Twins. Now, the bad: Bryce Eldridge and Jung Hoo Lee became the latest players to hit the injured list.
Mayer, acquired at the trade deadline from the Boston Red Sox, was reinstated from the injured list, while Davidson was called up from Triple-A Sacramento. Davidson will play right field and bat third in his major-league debut, while Mayer will bat fourth and be the team’s designated hitter.
“Just showing them what I can do and giving them the best I can every game until the season’s over,” Davidson said when asked what he could provide. “Just showing them what Bo is.”
What is Bo?
“You’ll see,” Davidson said with a smile.
Meanwhile, Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion list after bumping his head at the team’s hotel in Los Angeles, while Lee landed on the 10-day injured list with a groin contusion after fouling a ball off himself on Sunday. Lee’s season is over, and manager Tony Vitello said he doesn’t anticipate Eldridge will play again this season, which ends Sunday.
With Lee landing on the injured list, every member of the Opening Day lineup is either on the injured list (Lee, Willy Adames, Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman, Logan Webb, Casey Schmitt, Harrison Bader) or has been traded (Patrick Bailey, Heliot Ramos, Luis Arraez). The only players from the Opening Day roster still on the roster are infielder Christian Koss and right-hander Landen Roupp.
Adames (left elbow sprain) took grounders and batting practice on Monday afternoon, but he’s very unlikely to return before the end of the season.
Eldridge, who will turn 22 next month, exceeded expectations as a rookie and should be a foundational piece of the Giants’ lineup alongside Devers. Over 107 games, Eldridge hit .269/.364/.461 with 17 home runs, 23 doubles and 57 RBIs. Among rookies, Eldridge’s 130 wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) was the third-highest in the majors.
“Incredibly impressive,” Vitello said of Eldridge’s season. “We summarized that a little bit with him this morning in there. Maturity is the word that gets thrown around a bunch, but it got thrown around in there, too. I think consistency is the other word. He attached that to himself in a good way, not in a braggadocious way.
“If I could speak for him through his own words, a big difference between last year and this year is understanding the ups and downs and how to maintain consistency, which is a lot easier to formulate or plan out than it is to put into act.”
Along with the offense, Vitello also highlighted Eldridge’s defense, which was his biggest question as a prospect. After committing 18 errors in 2024 and 9 in 2025, Eldridge only had two errors this season in the majors and minors. Eldridge also graded out well by Baseball Savant’s new first baseman receiving metric.
Going into next season, one area where Vitello believes Eldridge can improve is baserunning.
“He’s got good instincts, but there’s so many things that he’s seeing for the first time in his life, literally,” Vitello said. “Safety bunts, stuff like that. And then on the base running … he didn’t do anything that would cause us to jump here in the dugout or cost us big, but for a guy that’s going to be on base as often as he is — and he’s not a burner — he’s got to be good on those little separators of reads, preparation before a pitch.”
Davidson, 24, is the Giants’ No. 5 prospect, per Baseball America. Over 125 games this season with Double-A Richmond and Triple-A Sacramento, Davidson hit .290 with 29 home runs, 20 steals and 94 RBIs. He was a candidate to get called up earlier this month but missed a week after fouling a ball off his foot on Sept. 9.
For all of Davidson’s production on the field, he believes the biggest area he’s grown has been “being a better man off the field.”
Davidson is one of many intriguing prospects in a farm system that has climbed the rankings. Along with Davidson, the Giants’ farm system is headlined by shortstops Josuar Gonzalez and Luis Hernandez, as well as right-handed pitcher Jackson Flora.
“We’ve got a very special group of guys that’s coming through,” said Davidson, whose mother, brother, girlfriend and daughter will be in attendance. “The farm itself, the numbers this year just showed. Us being really good brothers off the field, it just shows on the field with the chemistry.”
“I’m excited to see Bo again,” Vitello said. “Just kind of knowing who he was in high school and junior college. … We were able to get him some action in spring training, and then you’re following along, following along. We knew [his promotion] would happen at some point.”
Mayer, 23, was traded to the Giants on Aug. 3 from the Boston Red Sox in exchange for lefty reliever Erik Miller and minor-league outfielder Carlos Gutierrez. The infielder had been recovering from a bone stress reaction to the left ulna, as well as a bone bruise on his right foot.
Vitello anticipates Mayer will primarily be the team’s designated hitter over the final six games, but he could also see some time in the infield.

item.content:encoded:
As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies

item.title: [eldia.com.do] Sistema de firmas MLB convierte prestamistas en un “mal necesario”
item.dc:creator: Juan Mercado
item.description: Santo Domingo.-El actual sistema de firmas de prospectos de Major League Baseball (MLB), que arranca con niños de 12 años de edad para oficializarlos a los 16 y medio, trajo consigo la aparición de los prestamistas, que según varios entrenadores se “benefician más que ellos” de su trabajo. Los prestamistas más conocidos son Jaime Ramos, Carlos Mejía, Santo Caraballo, quien es sindicado como socio del inmortal David Ortiz; Paulino Sports, Ernesto Segura (Mamá Celia) y el cubano Isbel Medina. Todo
item.content:encoded:
Santo Domingo.-El actual sistema de firmas de prospectos de Major League Baseball (MLB), que arranca con niños de 12 años de edad para oficializarlos a los 16 y medio, trajo consigo la aparición de los prestamistas, que según varios entrenadores se “benefician más que ellos” de su trabajo.
Los prestamistas más conocidos son Jaime Ramos, Carlos Mejía, Santo Caraballo, quien es sindicado como socio del inmortal David Ortiz; Paulino Sports, Ernesto Segura (Mamá Celia) y el cubano Isbel Medina. Todos, excepto Caraballo, son propietarios de academias para formar prospectos.
La brecha de los años para los entrenadores recibir los pagos de los bonos de los equipos de Grandes Ligas, que pueden extenderse hasta cinco años, son aprovechados por los prestamistas, cediendo tasas entre un 5% y un 2% del bono acordado por el prospecto. “Los prestamistas son los más beneficiados de este negocio, con eso no te digo que estoy en contra de ellos, porque me han respondido cuando los he necesitado”, aseguró el entrenador Raúl Valera (Banana).
Los prestamistas solo hacen inversiones, luego de investigar con algún personal de las organizaciones de Grandes Ligas, que ese prospecto acordado pasó las pruebas físicas, dopaje y de edad.
“Los prestamos son de varias formas, pero las más conocidas son las que te compran un porcentaje de beneficio que tiene el entrenador del bono y la otra es mediante un pagaré notarial”, explicó Banana.
Prestamistas, necesarios
El entrenador Cristian Batista (Niche) considera a los prestamistas la salvación del sistema de firmas de prospectos. “Sin ellos la mayoría de academias independientes tendrían que cerrar. Ningún entrenador soporta la presión que trae el gasto diario de una academia”, sostuvo Niche.
En tanto que Ramón- Papiro -Genao asegura que los prestamistas son los salvavidas de los programas pequeños. “Ningún entrenador de programa pequeño sobrevive esperando el beneficio del bono de un pelotero que firmó por tres años o más”, dijo Papiro. Mientras que Basilio Vizcaíno (Cachaza) dice que los entrenadores incurren en demasiados gastos y el negocio se ha hecho insostenible, razón por la que tienen que recurrir a los prestamistas. “Esta industria no puede sostenerse con este sistema de esperar tantos años para recibir el beneficio de tu trabajo. De ahí la importancia de los prestamistas”, aseveró Cachaza.
Prestamos a padres
Los prestamistas negocian con los padres de los prospectos, a quienes les prestan en base al porcentaje que les corresponde del preacuerdo con el equipo de Grandes Ligas. “En este tipo de negocios los prestamistas se corren el riesgo que si el negocio se cae pierden su inversión”, sostuvo Cachaza.
Empuje a prestamos
— Exigencias de MLB
Niche destaca que las presiones que hacen los equipos de GL luego de tener un preacuerdo, los hace más dependientes de los prestamistas. “Quieren que los prospectos se muden a mejores lugares, que no anden en motores ni en guagua”.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

22 Sep 2026, 08:10 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Jeff Curry)
The San Francisco Giants are down to two members of their Opening Day roster still active with the club after placing first baseman Bryce Eldridge and right fielder Jung Hoo Lee on the injured list Monday.
Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion injured list after getting hurt in the team's Los Angeles hotel on Friday, according to the team. He didn't play in the series as the Dodgers swept three games.
His IL move is retroactive to Friday, leaving open the possibility he could return to action before the season ends this weekend, but manager Tony Vitello told reporters that Eldridge likely will be shut down for the rest of the campaign.
Lee was placed on the 10-day IL due to a groin contusion, so his season is over. He exited San Francisco's 3-1 loss to the Dodgers on Sunday in the seventh inning, an inning after fouling a pitch off his groin.
Right-hander Landen Roupp and shortstop Christian Koss are the last players on the Giants' active roster who were with the team when the season started, though neither was in the lineup on March 25 against the New York Yankees. Many of the other players from the season-opening roster were either part of the team's sell-off at the trade deadline or are on the IL.
Eldridge, 21, has a .269 batting average, a .364 on-base percentage and a .461 slugging percentage with 17 homers and 57 RBIs in 107 games this year. He began his major league career with San Francisco in 2025, hitting .107 with no homers in 10 games.
Lee, 28, batting .276/.320/.404 with 10 home runs and 57 RBIs in 143 games this season. Through three years with the Giants, he has a .270/.322/.397 batting line with 20 homers and 120 RBIs over 330 games.
The Giants filled the two roster vacancies by activating infielder Marcelo Mayer from the injured list and promoting outfielder Bo Davidson from Triple-A Sacramento.
Mayer, 23, hasn't played a major league game since late June due to left arm and right foot injuries. The Giants acquired him from the Boston Red Sox on Aug. 3 in exchange for left-hander Erik Miller, and Mayer played four games for Sacramento in mid-August before he was shut down again.
Davidson, 24, split the minor league season between Double-A Richmond and Sacramento, batting a combined .290/.361/.527 with 29 homers, 94 RBIs and 20 stolen bases in 125 games.
Both newcomers immediately joined San Francisco's starting lineup Monday night against the visiting Minnesota Twins. Davidson, playing right field and batting third, hit a first-inning single in his initial major league at-bat. Mayer served as the designated hitter and was slotted into the cleanup spot.
Left-hander Philip Abner was for assignment to clear a spot for Davidson on the 40-man roster. Abner, 24, had no decisions and a 9.64 ERA in five appearances for the Giants this year before he was optioned to Sacramento on Sunday. He pitched for the Los Angeles Angels earlier this season.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [foxsports.com.mx] Alex Bregman sufre múltiples fracturas tras ser golpeado por bola, pero descartan cirugía
item.content:encoded:
El fin de semana, el jugador de los Chicago Cubs, Alex Bregman, tuvo que abandonar el juego ante los Cincinnati Reds, luego de que recibió un fuerte pelotazo en el rostro mientras estaba esperando su turno al bat.
La situación parece ser más grave de lo que se esperaba, luego de que se dio a conocer un diagnóstico sobre el tercera base de los Cachorros, quien mostró las huellas de la batalla en sus redes sociales.
RECOMENDAMOS: Selección Mexicana jugaría en estadio de Rayados la Nations League; volverían a Monterrey tras 8 años
¿Qué tan grave es la lesión de Alex Bregman?
De acuerdo con información de Jeff Passan de ESPN, la lesión sí es complicada, pues se dice que Alex Bregman sufrió múltiples fracturas en la cara, algo que será complicado para el equipo de los Chicago Cubs.
A pesar de que la lesión es mucho más importante de lo que se esperaba, también hay buenas noticias, puesto que no se espera que el jugador vaya a ser sometido a una cirugía.
¿Cuándo podría regresar Alex Bregman a los campos?
Aunque no está conformado por la gente de los Chicago Cubs, la misma fuente dio a conocer que se espera que Alex Bregman pueda regresar esta misma temporada para el momento más importante, la postemporada.
Hay que recordar que el jugador que ocupa la tercera base de los Cubs tuvo que ser enviado al hospital para evaluar la situación del golpe que recibió en el juego del domingo.
Por otra parte, el propio Alex Bregman se ha encargado de compartir algunas fotos de cómo le quedó la cara después del bolazo que lo dejará fuera en la recta final de la temporada regular de la MLB.
PUEDE INTERESAR: ¡Terrible accidente! Alex Bregman recibe un pelotazo de foul durante el Cubs vs Reds (Video)
¿Cuándo comienza la postemporada en las Grandes Ligas?
Por otra parte, la postemporada de Grandes Ligas arranca con los comodines que comenzarán el próximo martes 29 de septiembre, que se definirán en los siguientes días.

item.title: [El ExtraBase] Willson Contreras: "Nunca dejamos de trabajar por ese cupo a los playoffs" - El ExtraBase
item.dc:creator: Elextrabase
item.description: Jesús David Castellano / @_JDCastellano Willson Contreras se convirtió en el líder espiritual de los Medias Rojas de Boston en lo que fue un camino transformador que pasó de una virtual catástrofe a la clasificación a postemporada por segundo año consecutivo. Y es que tras finalizar la jornada del 17 de junio con récord de 29-42, los Medias Rojas ganaron 55 de sus siguientes 85 juegos —la mayor cantidad de todo el béisbol— para mejorar su foja a 84 victorias y 72 derrotas y sellar su boleto a pl
item.content:encoded:
Jesús David Castellano / @_JDCastellano
Willson Contreras se convirtió en el líder espiritual de los Medias Rojas de Boston en lo que fue un camino transformador que pasó de una virtual catástrofe a la clasificación a postemporada por segundo año consecutivo.
Y es que tras finalizar la jornada del 17 de junio con récord de 29-42, los Medias Rojas ganaron 55 de sus siguientes 85 juegos —la mayor cantidad de todo el béisbol— para mejorar su foja a 84 victorias y 72 derrotas y sellar su boleto a playoffs el pasado domingo, luego de que los Bravos de Atlanta ayudaran venciendo a los Astros de Houston.
Los Medias Rojas no pudieron celebrar con un triunfo en el bolsillo. Cayeron ante Tampa Bay en el último de la serie en Tropicana Field, pero eso poco importó, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta todo el camino recorrido para anotar su nombre en la fiesta de octubre luego de estar destinados al desastre en los primeros tres meses de zafra. Sencillamente nunca se rindieron, y eso lo reconoce Willson y se lo hace ver a sus compañeros.
«Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido»
«Primeramente, darle las gracias a Dios por todo lo vivido este año. Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido», dijo Willson a El Extrabase durante la celebración en el clubhouse visitante del Tropicana Field. «También hay que agradecer por el equipo que tenemos alrededor, los muchachos, la clase de personas que tenemos. Y de verdad que nunca dejamos de trabajar, ni de perseguir ese cupo a los playoffs».
En un buen tramo de la campaña, el primera base carabobeño comandó a la ofensiva patirroja. Primeramente, despuntó bateando por encima de .300 en abril y luego mantuvo la constancia suficiente como para terminar encabezando al equipo —con seis compromisos por disputar en el calendario regular— en cuadrangulares (27), carreras impulsadas (81), porcentaje de embasado (.387), slugging (.518) y OPS (.905).
Su escolta en el renglón de vuelacercas fue Wilyer Abreu (24), que no solo aportó con el bate, sino con su prodigiosa defensa en los jardines que lo tiene como firme candidato a obtener su tercer guante de oro consecutivo.
Elogios para Abreu y Monasterio
«Estoy orgulloso de todos mis compañeros, especialmente de Wilyer; por todo lo que ha hecho este año y lo que ha logrado, ha sido bastante importante, igual que (Andruw) Monasterio, que lo trajeron para acá a hacer un trabajo. Se amoldó muy bien a su rol y mira, esto es lo que hace un equipo unido, clasificar», añadió.
«Estoy verdaderamente orgulloso del equipo que formamos y que tenemos ahora mismo», acotó Wilyer, que comanda a los jardineros derechos de la Liga Americana en Carreras Salvadas a la Defensiva con 26. «Le dimos la vuelta a la temporada de una forma increíble. Me siento orgulloso de haber sido parte de esto, de poder ayudar y contribuir al equipo en este momento y durante toda la temporada».
Wilyer también destaca entre los jugadores de su posición en el nuevo circuito siendo segundo en Outs Por Encima del Promedio (3) y primero en valor en carreras de fildeo (5). Igualmente, despunta en asistencias desde los jardines (12) y en el apartado ofensivo, lidera a los Medias Rojas en carreras anotadas (81), dobles (36, con lo que comanda la Liga Americana) y bases por bolas (70). El zuliano estableció topes personales en las categorías ofensivas antes mencionadas, además de traídas al plato (74), imparables (144) y, por supuesto, bambinazos (24).
Monasterio ha entendido su rol
Por su parte, Andruw Monasterio supo adaptarse a su rol de pelotero de reemplazo, con tramos destacados a la ofensiva. Un ejemplo de ello fue julio. En ese entonces asumió la titularidad de las paradas cortas en ausencia del lesionado Trevor Story, lo que coincidió con la racha de 15 triunfos seguidos que le dio vida a Boston. Exhibió un promedio de .338 (de 65-22), OBP de .413, slugging de .631 y OPS de 1.044, con tres cuadrangulares, 11 producidas y nueve anotadas.
Pero no se limitó al campo corto; Monasterio también vio acción en segunda, en primera, e incluso en tercera.
«Para mí, todo fue amoldarme a mi rol», comentó Monasterio a El Extrabase. «Fui al Spring Training y me gané el puesto. Súper contento porque son cuatro años en el show y cuatro años clasificando, es una bendición. Es muy satisfactorio, porque tú trabajas mucho para esto, para este momento del año, el béisbol en octubre».
Suárez ha sido clave en el tramo final
En el renglón del pitcheo, Ranger Suárez ha sido clave en este tramo final de la zafra, luego de presentar altibajos durante gran parte del año e incluso estar en lista de lesionados después de la pausa del juego de estrellas.
En sus últimas cinco aperturas exhibe foja de 3-1 y una efectividad de 2.70 en 30 innings de labor, con 22 ponches, 12 pasaportes y un WHIP de 1.27. Todo eso ha confluido en una actuación general en su primera contienda en la Liga Americana, en la que posee un promedio de carreras limpias de 3.27 en 143.1 capítulos de trabajo a lo largo de 27 salidas.
«Contento del sacrificio que hicimos durante la temporada, especialmente por cómo empezamos», expresó el zurdo de Pie de Cuesta. «Entonces, mira lo que nos recompensó Dios, estamos en los playoffs».
A Ranger se lo ha caracterizado por ser un lanzador bastante calmado, casi imperturbable. Y bastante de eso mostró el equipo para lograr revertir su situación de inicio de temporada. «No comenzamos de la manera que queríamos, pero el talento de los muchachos es increíble. Sabíamos que le íbamos a dar vuelta a la situación».
Sigue la cobertura por El Extrabase

item.title: [si.com] Pete Alonso Hits 2 Homers, Including His 40th, As Orioles Stave Off Elimination For Now
item.dc:creator: Jason La Canfora; Unknown
item.description: When you are as bush league an operation as Craig Albernaz’s 2026 Baltimore Orioles, it usually doesn’t take long for your complete lack of fundamentals and remedial-at-best baseball IQ to shine through. item.content:encoded:
When you are as bush league an operation as Craig Albernaz’s 2026 Baltimore Orioles, it usually doesn’t take long for your complete lack of fundamentals and remedial-at-best baseball IQ to shine through.
Monday night, starting pitcher Shane Baz issued a leadoff walk on a pitch timer violation, then gave up three runs on three straight pitchers, continuing his ability to focus and command in the first inning, and these baseball losers were on the cusp of clinching yet another losing season under baseball failure exec Mike Elias. Thanks to Pete Alonso they staved off loss No. 82 – don’t worry, it’s coming – and won game No. 75 (they’re better than last year!) in a 4-3 victory over Toronto at a predictably desolate Camden Yards.
Alonso hit an opposite field homer early in the game and Gunnar Henderson delivered a solo homer and Alonso won it for them by clubbing homer No. 40 to left field, a two-run shot that gave them a rare one-run victory. Problem is they are 4.5 games back in the Wild Card and they have five to play, so you do the math.
“Just really stoked I was able to come through for the team right there,” Alonso said on the MASN post-game show.
Baz – as utterly middling of an MLB starter as you will fine who Elias mortgaged what was left of his middling farm system for at the time – showed guts, getting over his poor first inning (that’s been a constant) – and performed well after taking a liner off his elbow last time out. There is a good chance that this trade haunts this organization with 21-year old catcher Caden Bodine already on the Rays taxi squad, but Elias is a human curse so we’ve come to expect no less
So Close To Finally Being Over
Outside of Alonso, hasn’t been much to come to the park to see, yet again, this season. (Rookie catcher Samuel Basallo was for a while but is clearly beat up and getting checked for a concussion after taking a hard foul tip behind the plate Monday).
And with Elias and Albernaz coming back, you can already smell the stench of their 2027 season before it starts, and the propaganda campaign to whitewash this season and try to grift you into spending on next year’s model is well under way.
Does anyone get excited about a team that can catch or run or throw? Do you enjoy watching AAA players all over the place nine years into a rebuild? Let me guess, Albernaz now pretending that getting tough about mistakes made by guys like Rece Hinds and Jeremiah Jackson – who have no business being in MLB, but Elias is so inexplicably horrible at his job they are – doesn’t do it for you?
No problem, MASN went to great lengths Monday to gaslight you about this lost season, and the bumbling clown running the dugout. They run interference and peddle fake talking points about what Henderson has become, pretending he hasn’t tanked as bad as Adley Rutschman did here, and cover for his constant misstep in all aspects of play … And now all of a sudden they’re championing Albernaz’s pathetic rants, 150 games into a lost year, about guys who don’t belong here and are riffing on what a tone he is setting by castrating career minor leaguers.
You aren’t fooling anybody, just demeaning yourselves. Yuck.
Just when you thought you couldn’t lose any more respect for an absolute joke of a franchise, they go and surprise you again by taking their overt PR campaign to another level. There is no bottom with these people and how low they are willing to sink for their paychecks. They all deserve each other. Baltimore deserves so much more.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are almost guaranteed to face the Boston Red Sox in an upcoming best-of-three Wild Card series, and can lock up homefield advantage with either a singular win in their final seven games or one Boston loss. The time is now for forecasting and getting your ducks in a row, and the Yankees have acknowledged as such; resetting Brent Headrick, for example, is more important than going all out to embarrass the Tampa Bay Rays this week.
That makes every rotation decision or perceived pattern seem magnified, especially after Boston lined up their starters for their upcoming series with the Cleveland Guardians: Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, Ranger Suárez. Is that the chips falling where they may, or is that foreshadowing? Either way, while winking and nodding, it's probably time to read similarly into the way the Yankees are handlng things.
That's why our eyebrows raised on Sunday when the Yanks revealed that Cam Schlittler and Gerrit Cole will stay on turn in the Rays series (for now), with Schlittler closing the four-game set and Cole pitching Game 3, both staying out of the doubleheader. That will leave Cole with an extra day of rest ahead of the WIld Card opener and Schlittler on normal rest. You're not saying ... ?
All the love in the world to Gerrit Cole, who got closer to securing an all-important Wild Card Series start with his strong appearance in the desert on Friday night. But given that his spot in the rotation in general has been rightly questioned, there is no world where he should start Game 1 over Schlittler. That is not even something that should be rolling around in the canals of my addled gray brain. And yet!
Yankees giving Gerrit Cole the rest he needs ahead of Wild Card Series. Will Cam Schlittler even start vs. Rays?
For now, this is all hypothetical, but ... Cole has always seemed like a candidate for a deciding Game 3, but nothing before it. Would the Yankees really dare to use him in a deciding game with three extra days of rest building up on his right arm?
And, if the Rays clinch the AL East this week and the Yankees lock down their positioning, will they use Schlittler at all in this series? Will he make a perfunctory three-inning cameo just to keep his sea legs ahead of the Sox showdown and prevent overthrowing/overcompensating? The Cy Young race between he and Dylan Cease is informally over, and Cease may not even be healthy enough to make another start. If positioning gets more solidified throughout the week, these decisions only become more fascinating.
As of now, though, before any adjustments ... it seems like there's at least a chance the Yankees are lining up Cole for Game 1 - or working him out of the picture entirely.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox's Craig Breslow Sends Message to Doubters Heading Into Postseason originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Many criticized some of the decisions the Boston Red Sox made when they parted ways with Alex Cora and other coaches in the organization.
Instead of those decisions failing to work out as planned, the Red Sox completely defied the odds, making the playoffs after a historic second half.
Many people deserve credit, but ownership and Craig Breslow have to feel they made the right decision.
Speaking to reporters after making the playoffs, Breslow had a lot to say about how he feels. He added that he believed in the players the Red Sox had and that he had to change the environment to put them in a position to succeed.
"I believed in the players that we had," Breslow said, per The Athletic.
"I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive. And they responded. While there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered resoundingly."
It's awesome to hear Breslow say things like this, but it's even better that he was given the opportunity to make some of these changes.
Some ownership groups would want to see out the year, but the Red Sox decision-makers understood that this was one of the better teams in baseball talent-wise, even if it hadn't shown that.
It'll be interesting to see how things look in the playoffs, but regardless, it was a very impressive second half, and everybody should be happy with that.

item.title: [NESN] Red Sox's Willson Contreras Happy With Earlier Coaching Changes | NESN
item.dc:creator: Jon Conahan
item.description: After what once seemed like an impossible outcome, the Boston Red Sox officially clinched a playoff spot, a very exciting moment for a team that has a real chance to win it all. A few months ago, it seemed like the Red Sox didn’t have a chance to come close to accomplishing this feat, but they did exactly that because of some of the decisions ownership made. Ultimately, while those decisions were questioned, the Red Sox decision-makers clearly made the right move by parting ways with Alex Cora.
item.content:encoded:
After what once seemed like an impossible outcome, the Boston Red Sox officially clinched a playoff spot, a very exciting moment for a team that has a real chance to win it all.
A few months ago, it seemed like the Red Sox didn’t have a chance to come close to accomplishing this feat, but they did exactly that because of some of the decisions ownership made. Ultimately, while those decisions were questioned, the Red Sox decision-makers clearly made the right move by parting ways with Alex Cora.
Speaking to reporters, it sounded like players in the clubhouse felt the same way. Willson Contreras, a longtime veteran and a big part of the Red Sox playoff push in the second half, said the staff change affected the chemistry and that all they needed was time.
The Red Sox proved that to be true.
“New staff, same energy, same grinding staff,” Contreras said of the early season changes that rocked the club, per The Athletic. “We created a family here with good chemistry throughout the season. We just needed time. And the time came for us.
“The most important thing to me is that everybody never stopped working. Everyone was finding their way to make an adjustment and play their game the right way. This is what we play for. This is just the first step ahead to get to the postseason. I just wanted everyone to know that I’m proud of every one of you. It’s a long season. We played through injuries, we played through a staff change, but we never stopped believing, and that’s why we’re here.”
Right now, barring something drastic, the Red Sox will play the New York Yankees in the Bronx.
This is going to be a crazy series, as many could argue that these are the two best teams in the American League.
Whoever wins this series has to feel pretty good about making the World Series, though there’s still a lot that has to happen before making any assumptions. The Tampa Bay Rays also seem to be very good.

item.content:encoded:
吉田正尚、今季限りで放出も…オフの“退団候補”にレ軍専門サイトが予想「価値が無いと考えられる理由は、あまりにも多い」
吉田の去就は不透明なままだ(C)Getty Images
吉田正尚が所属するレッドソックスは、現地時間9月20日レイズに1-5で敗れたものの、アストロズがブレーブスに2-4で黒星を喫したため、プレーオフ進出が決定した。その一方で、選手の去就にも関心が向けられるシーズン終盤、来季陣容の話題も現地メディアで報じられている。
球団の情報を専門に扱う『BOSOXINJECTION』が20日、「レッドソックス退団が近づいている可能性がある選手」を予想する特集記事を掲載。現在、左太腿を痛め負傷者リスト（IL）入りとなっている吉田をそのうちの1人として候補に挙げている。
ルーキーイヤーの2023年は140試合に出場し、中軸として活躍が注目されたものの、2年目以降は肩や指の故障に悩まされ、フルシーズンでプレー出来ない状況が続いた。またレッドソックスは常に、外野や指名打者で吉田のライバルとなるプレーヤーが多く在籍。背番号7がベンチに座る大きな理由となっている。
同メディアは5年契約を結んでいる吉田が、球団との間でもう1年契約が残っていることから、「（今オフに）トレードで移籍させる場合でも、球団が契約のかなりの部分を負担する可能性が高い。これは、ジョン・ヘンリー・オーナーが簡単に受け入れそうな話ではない」などと主張。
だがその上で、「しかし、33歳のヨシダにロースターの1枠を使う価値が無いと考えられる理由は、あまりにも多い」と訴えている。

item.content:encoded:
OK, hand up. Amidst the emotional trauma that wrecked Chicago sports fans on Sunday afternoon, as Alex Bregman and Caleb Williams both left their respective games injured, somewhere in my brain, there was a world where the Chicago Cubs and Atlanta Braves could play in the Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field - and that came to life in my piece detailing Ozzie Albies' bid to unseat Eugenio Suarez as Cubs Killer #1.
That's obviously not in the cards (although the two could meet in the first round) - but that doesn't mean there's not a great deal of uncertainty when it comes to how the National League playoff field will ultimately shake out. So much so that it could come down to the final weekend of the regular season, when the Cubs are slated to square off against another playoff-bound team, the Boston Red Sox, at Fenway Park.
There's just one problem here.
The weather forecast looks awful for the Northeast, so much so that playing any baseball feels like a stretch if these forecase models come to life.
Crowded NL playoff picture could be complicated by awful Red Sox weather forecast
Entering Tuesday, the Cubs and Padres are tied for the first spot in the Wild Card standings, with the Philadelphia Phillies just one game back and the Arizona Diamondbacks clinging for deal life with playoff hopes hanging by a thread. It's completely feasible that, given how crowded things are in the NL Wild Card race, those games between the Cubs and Red Sox are critical in determining the pecking order.
I have no idea what happens if the entire weekend gets washed. The playoff schedule is set and, with the expanded field, balancing the national broadcast schedule across multiple networks is no easy feat. In other words, shifting the whole postseason back a day or two feels like a long-shot, at best.
Could we get a neutral site series for the final weekend? That would really be the cherry on top of a season that's been filled with oddities and strange luck for the Cubs. But, hey, as we all remember when 'neutral site games' come to mind, maybe we'll get a Carlos Zambrano v. the Astros at Miller Park-esque performance?
Probably not, so let's just stay tuned to see how the week takes shape.

item.content:encoded:
Every Monday, this column will break down the most popular waiver wire and free agent acquisitions from the weekend. I dig into the top adds on the ever-popular Fantrax and in the NFBC Online Championship (OC), a national mid-stakes contest with 240 total leagues of 12 and a six-figure grand prize. Reviewing player adds between the two should provide us with a well-rounded perspective and barometer of the fantasy baseball marketplace.
Week 26 Overview
Hitters
The San Diego Padres took advantage of their four-game series with the Rockies at Coors Field and a home set with the Marlins, scoring 51 runs, 12 more than any other team. Fernando Tatis Jr. (along with Brandon Lowe and Pete Crow-Armstrong) led the way with a week-high four dingers. Last week’s streamers turned out to be dynamite: Jake Cronenworth (.464-8-2-8-2), Dustin Harris (.379-5-0-7-2) and Samad Taylor (.556-6-1-7-1) really stepped up, particularly Taylor for my competitive Main Event squad that gained two category points in batting average last week. Rake Cronenworth was true to his nickname from several years ago. He led all Major League hitters with 13 hits. The Brewers swiped a league-high 12 bags last week: four each for Jackson Chourio and rookie Cooper Pratt. Tampa’s Chandler Simpson led all runners with five swipes, finally catching Washington’s Nasim Nuñez for the MLB lead with 46. Expect Simpson to finish with 50+ and win the stolen base crown.
Pitchers
Of the 29 two-start pitchers excluding Pirates opener Lake Bachar, three earned two wins: Tarik Skubal, Sean Burke and David Peterson. Houston’s Hunter Brown had an outstanding two-step (10 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 5 K – 20 K) and those 20 punchouts led all pitchers for the week. Gavin Williams punched out 16 in 12 innings and is back atop the AL lead in strikeouts with 244. Dylan Cease (239) may not make his final start of the season and Cam Schlittler (234) is unlikely to catch Williams as both have one start remaining. It’s very possible that Williams catches and passes Jacob Misiorowski (247) for the Major League lead. The Miz pitched three innings in his weekend start and might be limited for his final one.
Tampa’s Bryan Baker was the first reliever to reach 40 saves this season. It’s possible that Cade Smith (39), Riley O’Brien (38) and Mason Miller (37) join Baker. The last time there were three closers with 40 or more saves was in 2019: Edwin Díaz (57), Wade Davis (43), and Craig Kimbrel (42). Shout out to folks who drafted O’Brien late, and/or picked up Baker, Louis Varland or Jacob Latz off waivers and didn’t have to worry about the saves category all season.
Week 27 Most Added Players: NFBC Main Event, NFBC OC, and Fantrax
It’s the last hurrah for managers with FAB dollars left, hoping to get the best bang for the buck and for variance to lean their way and tip them into league titles. As is usually the case in the final week, we hope to optimize our pitching rotations and hitters in hitter-friendly ballparks against bad pitching. It was odd seeing Shohei Ohtani available in several leagues, and perhaps fortuitous as he should be activated this week and start a few games. Ohtani was acquired in 26 OCs for an AWB of $17. In Main Events, there were 12 shares available and they went for a reasonable $12 a pop. I scooped up a rare Ohtani share in an OC for $2, winning a tiebreaker over the team in 1st place in that league. Andy Pages will be activated on Tuesday, which should push Tommy Edman back to second base. Pages had been out since August 21, but was producing at an exciting clip before the injury — .272 – 72 R – 21 HR – 80 RBI – 12 SB in 550 PA. Managers who acquired him are hoping that he dusts the cobwebs back off and gets right into the swing of things, with all the marbles on the line.
| # | Player | Team | Position(s) | % of Lgs Added | AWB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Andy Pages | LAD | OF | 60% | $5 |
| 2 | JR Ritchie | ATL | SP | 57% | $3 |
| 3 | Daniel Lynch IV | KC | SP | 57% | $6 |
| 4 | Samad Taylor | SD | OF | 48% | $5 |
| 5 | Jose Siri | LAA | OF | 45% | $4 |
| 6 | Heliot Ramos | NYY | OF | 35% | $7 |
| 7 | Dansby Swanson | CHC | SS | 35% | $8 |
| 8 | Brayan Bello | BOS | SP | 35% | $11 |
| 9 | Dustin Harris | SD | OF | 32% | $10 |
| 10 | Garrett Whitlock | BOS | RP | 32% | $5 |
| 11 | Pavin Smith | ARI | 1B | 30% | $4 |
| 12 | Anthony Volpe | NYY | SS | 30% | $5 |
AWB = Average Winning Bid (min: $4 AWB)
Pitchers were the most popular targets, specifically two-steppers, as we chase wins and strikeouts, hoping the Ratio Monster doesn’t eat our leads in ERA and WHIP. JR Ritchie and Daniel Lynch IV were the most added starters who we expect two starts from this week. Ritchie’s MLB debut back in April came with great promise, but walks haunted him greatly, which led to trips back to Triple-A to refine his craft and some bulk inning relief work when he returned to Atlanta in July. Ritchie was recently promoted again, and ran into a juggernaut Cubs offense last week, allowing six runs on seven hits in 4.2 innings. The walk rate (13.7%) isn’t pretty, and he has a good opportunity to end his season on a high note with two reasonable matchups — against the Reds at home and the Marlins on the road. Lynch had served the Royals well as their top southpaw out of the bullpen for most of the season. He moved to the rotation in August and slowly worked his pitch counts upward. Lynch has made it to five innings in each of his last three starts. His latest one (at HOU on September 16) went well — 5 IP – 2 H – 0 ER – 1 BB – 3 K. More of that please as he faces the White Sox and Guardians at Kauffman Stadium in the final week. If I could only choose one for the week, it would be Ritchie.
Red Sox pitchers Brayan Bello and Garrett Whitlock were popular buys as the likelihood of roto stars shining bright on them this week is high. Bello is coming off a tremendous outing against the AL-leading Rays on Saturday where he posted an 11:0 K:BB with just one run allowed in eight innings. Those 11 punchies tied his career high. Bello had been the worst starter in the game (6.49 ERA, 1.67 WHIP) through June 4, when he was optioned to Triple-A. Since the All-Star break, mostly out of relief and with two starts, the 27-year-old has been shining. Over those 51.1 innings, he is rocking exemplary ratios (2.28 ERA, 1.01 WHIP) and a 17% K-BB% (22.3% K, 5.3% BB). Bello should make a start against the Cubs next Saturday. The Cubs should be settled into a playoff spot by then, so perhaps they give Pete Crow-Armstrong and some of the other regulars that day off. Boston’s closer Aroldis Chapman has been day-to-day with a lat issue, so perhaps the Red sox have him take it easy and provide Whitlock with some save opportunities. Whitlock has a 7-2 record with a 17.5 ERA, 0.88 WHIP and four saves.
Streaming Diamondbacks is a good idea this week, specifically for their three-game set at Coors Field against the Rockies in the early part of the week. Pavin Smith was a coveted target, coming off a four-day stretch where three of his hits were home runs. Don’t expect Smith to start against lefty Kyle Freeland, but he should be in the lineup for the other two contests against righties. Nolan Arenado was available in one of the 60 Main Event leagues and was acquired for just one dollar.
Better late than never for two punchless Padres who have been quite productive and certainly enjoyed their visit to Coors Field in the first half of last week. Dustin Harris ($10 AWB) and Samad Taylor ($5) have been red hot and playing often over the last 10 days. Though he doesn’t have a home run yet, Harris has been quite productive and helpful to early-bird managers: eight runs, 12 runs batted in and three steals, batting .384 with a 166 wRC+ in 40 plate appearances since September 11. He’s also been batting second against right-handed starters. Taylor has at least one hit in nine of his last 10, including a 3-for-3 effort on Sunday, and has driven in seven in his last seven games.

AWB = Average Winning Bid (min: $4 AWB)
As always, more reliable starting pitcher depth was available in the 12-team OC pool. Cristian Javier, Anthony Kay, Robert Gasser, Lynch, Yusei Kikuchi, and Max Scherzer were the most added pitchers this week. Javier should pitch twice this week and will hope to put his best foot forward (in this case, his right arm) as the Astros fight for the AL West and a playoff spot. Sutter Health Park is not a fun place to pitch, but the A’s lineup is a watered-down version without Brent Rooker, Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, and Jacob Wilson윌슨. Javier’s first start is in Seattle may not be a picnic with gluten-free granola and Pearl Jam on the Discman.
Milwaukee’s Robert Gasser only draws one start (home vs. STL), but is considered a reliable ratios guy who can score a much-needed win for fantasy managers, as the Brewers will certainly be favorites in that matchup. Gasser earned his fifth win on Saturday, throwing seven scoreless innings against the Orioles. White Sox lefty Anthony Kay has good matchups (at KC on Tuesday and vs. COL on Sunday), though that second start could be pulled away from him. The main problems here is that Kay hasn’t made it to the fifth inning in any of his last five starts. I feel much more comfortable with a single start against the Orioles from Max Scherzer than I do a double (at SEA, at ATH) from wily Yusei Kikuchi. Kikuchi has walked 12 batters in his last three starts.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
