| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brewers | 98-58 | 1602 | 1496 | 100.0% | 1637 |
| Rays | 95-60 | 1594 | 1489 | 100.0% | 1631 |
It was a great week for the Brewers. They won their fourth straight NL Central title and sixth in the last nine years, and also set another franchise record for wins in a single season, one year after setting the previous record. They now have a chance to win 100 games for the first time in club history this week and still have the top seed in the NL to play for.
The Rays swept the Athletics and won their series against the Red Sox last week to put some distance between themselves and the Yankees in the AL East race. The gap in the division is now six games, and even though the two rivals play each other four times during the final week of the season, it would take a massive collapse from Tampa Bay to upset the current standings. Because the Rays also currently lead the season series with the Yankees, 6-3, all they need is to win one of the four games in New York to take the division title. With Shane McClanahan still recovering from his forearm injury — his availability for the playoffs is up in the air — Freddy Peralta has stepped up to lead the pitching staff over the last few weeks. Across his last five starts, he’s allowed just three runs in 28 2/3 innings. That’s the kind of production the Rays were hoping to get when they acquired him at the trade deadline.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dodgers | 96-60 | 1580 | 1492 | 100.0% | 1621 |
| Padres | 87-69 | 1578 | 1501 | 97.2% | 1618 |
| Braves | 92-64 | 1565 | 1500 | 100.0% | 1610 |
| Yankees | 89-66 | 1556 | 1497 | 100.0% | 1603 |
The Dodgers are getting all their pieces in place for the postseason. Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki will be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and Shohei Ohtani should follow on Wednesday. There’s a lingering question about Blake Snell’s status after he injured his groin last week, but it sounds like he’ll be able to make a start during the final weekend of the season. And even though the majority of the year has been a slog for Kyle Tucker, his bat seems to have finally woken up at the right time; he collected nine hits and three home runs last week.
Having won 13 of their last 14 games, the Padres are peaking at exactly the right moment. They’ve surged five games ahead of the Diamondbacks and one ahead of the Phillies in the NL Wild Card standings, and are now tied with the Cubs for the top spot. San Diego’s final series of the season against Arizona still looms large, especially if the Friars stumble against the Dodgers in the series beforehand. You’re probably familiar with Fernando Tatis Jr.’s hot streak — he blasted four home runs last week to bring his total in September up to eight — but the biggest contributor to the Padres’ success recently has been Ty France. He had 12 hits and a home run last week and has posted a fantastic 168 wRC+ during the second half of the season.
After a couple of years away from the top, the Braves are NL East champions again — it’s their seventh division title in the last nine years. Atlanta’s dominance this year has been a welcome return to form. Even though his season has been a bit up and down, Ronald Acuña Jr. is looking like the superstar that won the MVP back in 2023 again. Last week, he smacked three home runs, including a go-ahead grand slam on Saturday, and is running a 191 wRC+ in September.
A little more than a week after being activated off the IL, Aaron Judge is back on the shelf, this time with a calf injury sustained on Wednesday. His availability for the playoffs is still up in the air, though he’s confident that he’ll be able to return sooner rather than later. Thankfully, Jazz Chisholm Jr. should be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and there’s some confidence that Trent Grisham will also be ready to return for the postseason. It helps that Ben Rice has bounced back from a rough August to post a 192 wRC+ in September. Still, Judge’s injury is a major blow to the Yankees’ hopes for a deep October run.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Red Sox | 84-72 | 1544 | 1500 | 100.0% | 1594 |
| Phillies | 86-70 | 1546 | 1501 | 97.3% | 1593 |
| Cubs | 87-69 | 1539 | 1501 | 99.9% | 1590 |
Even though the Red Sox lost both of their series last week, they managed to clinch a postseason berth on Sunday. It’s the cap to a remarkable turnaround after the team looked completely lost in mid-June. Boston can officially secure the second Wild Card spot with a couple of wins against the Guardians this week. Then the team can turn its attention to the Yankees and the rematch of last year’s Wild Card matchup between these two historic rivals.
Nothing is going to come easy for the Phillies over the next few weeks. The team placed Jesús Luzardo on the IL last week with a shoulder injury, but thankfully, it sounds like he’ll be ready to pitch in the playoffs. But before they count their chickens, they need to actually clinch a playoff spot. Philadelphia is four games up on the Diamondbacks in the NL Wild Card race, but its upcoming opponents are no cake walk; the Phillies have the Brewers and Rays on the schedule to finish off the regular season. Facing two of the best teams in baseball is quite a test ahead of the postseason, and the Phillies haven’t exactly been playing well lately.
The biggest concern for the Cubs right now is the status of Alex Bregman. He was struck by a foul ball in the face while standing in the on-deck circle during Sunday’s game and was taken to the hospital for further evaluation. Alongside Pete Crow-Armstrong, Bregman has been one of the best hitters in baseball since the All-Star break. It would be a huge blow if the third baseman had to miss any significant amount of time at this point in the season. As for Crow-Armstrong, he’s two stolen bases away from joining the 40/40 club. He put a few finishing touches on his MVP case last week by bopping four more home runs, bringing his season total up to 45.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guardians | 81-75 | 1520 | 1498 | 97.6% | 1572 |
| White Sox | 80-76 | 1494 | 1500 | 96.2% | 1552 |
| Rangers | 78-78 | 1502 | 1496 | 56.5% | 1517 |
| Astros | 77-79 | 1493 | 1493 | 45.8% | 1481 |
There was some upheaval in the two division races represented in this tier. Entering last week one game behind the White Sox in the AL Central standings, the Guardians took two of three games against the South Siders in a dramatic series, which included a walk-off on Tuesday and an improbable go-ahead homer on Wednesday. From there, although Chicago took advantage of playing — and winning — on Thursday while Cleveland was off to pull back into a tie atop the division, the Guardians just kept winning, sweeping the the Athletics over the weekend to bring their winning streak to five. José Ramírez finally broke out of his extended slump, tallying nine hits, a home run, and four stolen bases last week.
As for the White Sox, they won three of their four games against the the Tigers, but that one loss was enough to drop them to a game behind Cleveland in the Central. Still, the Sox have a three-game cushion for the final AL Wild Card spot, and they own the tiebreaker over the Guardians, meaning both first place and a potential first-round bye are still in their sights. Miguel Vargas is carrying most of the load for the lineup right now, hitting three home runs last week, but he needs some support if Chicago wants to make some noise in the postseason.
Over in the AL West, the Astros were swept by the Braves this past weekend, allowing the Rangers to jump into first place with a .500 record. Texas enters this week one game up, but crucially Houston holds the tiebreaker. If the Rangers can manage to hang on, it would be just their second postseason appearance in the last decade. The last time they made the playoffs, they won the World Series.
The Houston bullpen was responsible for the backbreaking losses on Saturday and Sunday, but the lack of offense has been a much bigger problem. Over the Astros’ last 10 games, they’ve scored more than four runs in a game just once. Yordan Alvarez looked fine last week (eight hits, including two home runs) after his ankle scare the previous weekend, and Jeremy Peña has been great too (10 hits, three homers), but the rest of the lineup has been struggling. During this 10-game stretch, Houston hitters not named Alvarez or Peña have combined for an ugly 55 wRC+.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diamondbacks | 82-74 | 1527 | 1505 | 5.6% | 1464 |
| Blue Jays | 77-79 | 1516 | 1504 | 3.6% | 1456 |
The Diamondbacks managed to keep their slim playoff hopes alive with a pair of wins over the Yankees on Saturday and Sunday. The first victory was a walk-off and the second was highlighted by a go-ahead grand slam from Nolan Arenado. Arizona needs to take care of business in Colorado and get some help from the Dodgers to ensure that the final series against the Padres has some stakes. There’s a chance the Phillies could crash out, opening another window for the Snakes, but the direct path is through San Diego.
The Blue Jays’ hopes for a last-minute surge into the playoffs were dashed last week when they lost both of their series to the Tigers and Rangers. They’re three games back and have the Astros to contend with if they want to try and sneak into that final Wild Card spot. It’s probably too little, too late, but the team is activating Trey Yesavage off the IL on Monday as one more reinforcement ahead of a final push.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pirates | 79-77 | 1534 | 1509 | 0.0% | 1465 |
| Mets | 71-85 | 1508 | 1509 | 0.0% | 1446 |
| Orioles | 75-81 | 1493 | 1504 | 0.1% | 1435 |
| Marlins | 76-80 | 1476 | 1503 | 0.0% | 1422 |
| Tigers | 73-83 | 1470 | 1491 | 0.0% | 1417 |
| Reds | 72-84 | 1469 | 1508 | 0.0% | 1416 |
The series between the Orioles and Mets last week in Queens turned out to be more interesting than you’d expect from two teams mired in hugely disappointing seasons. Pete Alonso made his first appearance as a member of the opposing team at Citi Field and wound up hitting his 300th career home run on Tuesday, a game-tying shot in the ninth inning. He received a huge ovation from the hometown crowd, which drew some irksome comments from a few Mets players and staff after the game. Baltimore wound up sweeping New York to cut its deficit in the AL Wild Card race to 2.5 games. Alas, a sweep by the Brewers over the weekend slammed the door shut on any playoff hopes the O’s still had.
Even though the Marlins’ season essentially ended with that 12-game losing streak back in July, they have made some significant progress in their quest to become a contending club. Otto Lopez looks like a star they can build the lineup around, while Eury Pérez and Max Meyer should be strong enough to anchor the pitching staff in the years ahead. There’s also a cohort of young prospects in the upper minors who should be making their debuts soon. The future in Miami is brighter than it’s been in a while.
This is the huge step forward the Reds were hoping to see from Elly De La Cruz. In September, he has blasted seven home runs, including in five straight games earlier this month, and is running a major league-best 236 wRC+. It’s too bad the rest of Cincinnati’s roster is a bit of a mess. Sal Stewart has been excellent as De La Cruz’s sidekick, but the starting rotation has struggled mightily, and the big injury to Hunter Greene has thrown the ceiling of that group up in the air heading into next year. Still, building around a superstar like De La Cruz should make things easier if the resources to improve the rest of the roster are made available.

The AL Central crown runs through Kansas City; both the White Sox and Guardians travel to face the Royals during the final week of the season. Unfortunately, the Royals haven’t been playing well enough recently to act as a spoiler. They ended August with a 13-3 stretch, but they’ve been the worst team in the AL in September, with just five wins in 18 games.
It took a lot longer than expected, but the Twins were finally eliminated from the playoff race last week. It was a drama-filled week, too. They won a wild extra-inning walk-off affair against the Yankees on Wednesday and then were walked-off twice against the Angels between two shutout victories over the weekend. Even though they all made their big league debuts over the last few weeks, Walker Jenkins, Kaelen Culpepper, and Emmanuel Rodriguez never all appeared in a game together. That trio represents the future of the organization, so it’s a little disappointing that that future couldn’t be realized in a small way this year.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Ben Clemens FanGraphs Chat - 9/21/26
item.dc:creator: Ben Clemens
item.description: Ben Clemens Hey everybody, welcome to the chat. We're testing out a new chat interface today, one that we'll hopefully roll out more broadly in the weeks to come. So come on, let's run it through its paces. Kevin In a weekly transactions H2H league, would you risk rolling with Aroldis this week? I don't see why the Bosox would rush him back into action. Ben Clemens Yeah, I would not. For exactly the reason you said. It just feels like you're opening yourself up to some risk without enough upside
item.content:encoded:
Ben Clemens
Hey everybody, welcome to the chat. We're testing out a new chat interface today, one that we'll hopefully roll out more broadly in the weeks to come. So come on, let's run it through its paces.
Kevin
In a weekly transactions H2H league, would you risk rolling with Aroldis this week? I don't see why the Bosox would rush him back into action.
Ben Clemens
Yeah, I would not. For exactly the reason you said. It just feels like you're opening yourself up to some risk without enough upside back for it. You're going to feel REALLY bad if they ease him back in and you're playing him. And on the flip side, what if he's not right immediately? Can't have a 0% chance of that.
SPArn
Any favorite random MLBers as we wind down the stretch, or little hopeful glimpses? I still don't believe Scott Bandura is real, even though Mo'Ne Davis went to his debut, and I nearly shed a tear during Josiah Gray's return
Ben Clemens
I mean, this guy is definitely very real, but David Freese is my all-time favorite good but not great guy who stuck around long enough for me to have fond memories of them.
Ben Clemens
Many of mine are Cardinals themed because that's when I was most strongly a fan of a single team. Pete Kozma. Bo Hart.
Ben Clemens
If we're talking current guys, well, how about Trent Harris, who I've grown inordinately fond of very quickly this year
SPArn
Your piece(s) on Cade Cavalli are excellent, much more thorough and better reasoned than this. But, I think the extension boils down to: 4/47 is low risk enough it doesn't hurt if he regresses or breaks, and if it turns into 5/70, it must have worked out great for the Nats. All reporting seems like he's a truly excellent leader too. We came a long way from "sit down, boy" and we can all be grateful for that
Ben Clemens
Yeah, I think that's basically the risk management part of mine. It's a good bet even if you know he gets hurt some of the time, because on average you get a nice amount of value out of signing him. I leave the leadership stuff aside – I agree with you that it's widely reported that way, I just think that those types of things are extremely subjective and don't hold over long periods of time anyway.
aldrinbatistarocks
A while ago, I remember listening to a BP podcast in which they were talking about christopher morel, the gist of the discussion being "it's okay to acknowledge when a guy is probably having their career year." Are there any candidates in 2026 for guys you think hit their apex production this season?
Ben Clemens
Love this one. Some easy ones for me: Otto Lopez. PCA. Gabriel Moreno. Randy Arozarena. Jake Bauers.
Ben Clemens
I don't mean any of them ill by that. But I just think a ton of stuff broke well for those players in their years, and that it feels hard to have all of that plus more hit right in a future year for them to eclipse it. You can still be a very good player after hitting your apex production
smoothio
Does Tatis have an MVP season in him?
Ben Clemens
Whether he actually wins one? who can say. Whether he has the capability to? Clearly yes. He's played at an MVP level for half of this year, for example. The talent is definitely there. Winning an MVP is tough because you have to have it hit for a whole year when no one else hits their even better outcome.
oaktownblues
Think the A's can hold onto a winning record against every AL west team this season? Just need to not lose series vs Angels and Astros
Ben Clemens
I do. I think that'd be a pretty cool footnote on what was just a real bummer of a season. Kind of a hilarious one, too. The AL is a mess this year.
bosoxforlife
The Red Sox should start Tolle in game 1 in The Bronx. The reality is that the Red Sox look outmatched and his personality fits the occasion perfectly and a few quick K's could change the mood.
Ben Clemens
I like the idea of starting Tolle game one. I feel crazy saying this, but I kind of like the idea of just starting three lefties and daring the Yankees to play their righty platoon bats, kind of gambling on Judge being less than 100%
Anonymous Member #46
Holy crap, I dig the new chat interface so far. No login issues!
Ben Clemens
Great to hear. Sean and team are still working on adding functionality (polls, images, that kinda thing) but I have been liking the clean look and it gives us more flexibility on our end
Ben Clemens
a little more legible and the scroll bars are nicer. Setting up the chat has more options. Basically this just has more options across the board. Oh, and I love the little FanGraphs icon by my name, so fun
oaktownblues
How does the new chat interface differ on your end? Are questions organized differently than before?
Ben Clemens
so, there's something I'm still getting used to, published those two out of order
riceball
where does Yordan rank among unlikely batting title winners? (assuming he holds on)
Ben Clemens
Nowhere near the top. He has a career .300 batting average! Among big league regulars, only Luis Arraez, Chandler Simpson (small-ish sample), and Jose Altuve are better
bosoxforlife
I can't get over the fact that either the Guardians or the White Sox will, most likely, receive a bye in the first round while whoever wins the AL West plays the team that finishes second but gets the home field against a team with a better record. I don't want to pour cold water on the new interface but the submission box is too small to handle more than two lines of copy.
Ben Clemens
Great feedback on the submission box. That sounds like an easy fix to me, I'll let Sean know.
As to the playoff system, yeah, I agree that this is a problem. I really like the bye system we have at current. It gives a reward for teams that have great regular seasons. But I agree that the divisional system interacts awkwardly with it. What if they handed out playoff spots the way they do now but pre-reseeded, ordering teams by record? I'm totally with you that it's a good idea that feels obviuosly unfair in practice.
SPArn
Pitchers having their best year: Nick Martinez, Luzardo, Messick, Louis Varland, Martin Perez some candidates that leap to mind. (Don't say the Miz, don't say the Miz, don't say the Miz)
Ben Clemens
I don't think the Miz counts. Like, yes, he's having an extremely good year. But he could throw more innings. the strikeouts don't look crazy unsustainable. it COULD be a career year but it doesn't feel like a blow-off top (a finance term I love and have been trying to use more of late) in the way that, say, Otto Lopez does
didace
Submission box – The default seems small, but click/hold and drag the little thing in the bottom right corner and you can make it very large.
Sean Dolinar
We are going to fix that once this chat is over. Thanks everyone for the feedback! – Sean
Ben Clemens
Martinez doesn't count because this isn't even his best year! He had his career year in 2024 in Cincy. Luzardo, same kinda deal, he's basically repeating last season. probably not 'career year' territory. I definitely agree with you on Varland, don't think Messick is really fair since he's a rookie, and Martin Perez got a qualifying offer once!
Ben Clemens
My own list would have: Reid Detmers, who I think is good but not this good. Sean Burke, though without much conviction there. And Foster Griffin.
Michael De Vivo
will spencer jones be overmatched by playoff level pitching?
Ben Clemens
If by overwhelmed you mean he'll strike out a lot, absolutely yes. He's a high-strikeout guy and the octane of pitchers ramps up int he playoffs. But it's not like he hasn't faced hard pitches in the regular season or in the minors. His game is tons of strikeouts and sometimes the ball leaves the yard. One playoff homer or so and we'llb e like man, this guy has it. And since homers are pretty rare events, it feels like Jones could be basically the same hitter and based on whether he happens to run into one or not we'll say he just didn't have it or performed as expected.
ado64
Who do you think starts Brewers playoff game 3, and how many innings do they get? 3 innings of Gasser or Drohan, maybe? Does May ever start a game with his recent inconsistency?
Ben Clemens
I think that some kind of piggyback situation is reasonable here. Like, three of Drohan with May backing him up? Or some other lefty/righty switch of that style. I'm extremely curious to see how they deploy Harrison.
Ben Clemens
I really don't know what you do with Harrison. Like, he's been so bad recently! But he has such high highs. The test in relief hasn't gone all that well so far. It's not like they can afford to just not have him pithc, he was a big part of their run prevention this year.
Ben Clemens
Sorry, I missed an answer before messing around iwth the interface. I meant to say that Harrison is the highest-unceratinty question in the entire playoff picture for me. The Brewers were the best team in baseball this year and Kyle Harrison was a ton of that. What are they going to look like with less good pitching? Can they figure out what ails him in time? I have no clue but I'm very excited to find out.
Anon21
Maybe dumb question. When Team A is one game ahead of Team B in the standings and also holds the tiebreaker on Team B, it's often said that they effectively have a two-game lead. But is there a similar way of describing the situations of the Astros and White Sox, who are one game back in the standings but hold the tiebreaker over the team ahead? Like are they effectively 0.8 (or something) games back, rather than one? (I know this is accounted for by magic numbers, just wondering if there's a simple way to describe this situation.)
Ben Clemens
I'd say they're one back with the tiebreaker. Or alternately that they're 'effectively only a half game back' because of the breaker. I agree with you that the wording is kind of tricky, though. You can't say they're 'effectively tied', that's not true. If they hvae the same records they won't make the playoffs
Nomar6666666
No question really. Just a frustrated fan with few places to vent. If the owners lock out the players next season, and we miss one single game, I will not go to a single game next year, nor will I buy the MLB TV package. I Wii continue to support this site
Ben Clemens
Nomar, we appreciate your continued support, of course. That's very kind. And honestly, I feel pretty similar. I think the owners are more to blame than the players for the upcoming fight we're sure to have. I don't feel great about anyone's role in this though. There's so much freaking money in baseball. Work it out between yourselves like adults so that we the fans, who pay a ton of money to enjoy your product, can still get it. No one is on our side in this negotiation, and that makes it feel bad
Braydon Roberts
Thoughts on the NL RoY race? Seems like everyone gave it to Sal Stewart when JJ went on the IL, but Stewart has had a rough September. fWAR is 4.4 to 2.2 in JJ's favor.
Ben Clemens
So, I've had JJ all along. I just don't really buy the arguments that some counting numbers matter so much that they're more important than the overall picture. I'm not saying Stewart's homers don't matter or anything. Obviously they do. But eh, the RBI's, I'm not as convinced by, because a stat like RE24 (which cares about driving in runs, but also cares about how many opportunities you had to drive in runs) says Stewart was about 10 runs better with the bat than Wetherholt this year so far.
Ben Clemens
That's not a ton of runs better. And again, that accounts for the RBI and the homers and all. And if you care about win probability – as in how important those RBIs were – Wetherholt actually has a BETTER bat than Stewart
Ben Clemens
Also he's a plus defender at an important position instead of a first baseman who defensive metrics aren't fond of
Ben Clemens
Like, I get the sentiment. And I get wanting to push back against WAR and be like 'no the old stats we love still matter'
Ben Clemens
There are times where I think that's true! I'd vote for Yordan by a mile for AL MVP, and it's because I think that his offensive value is so high that WAR is overly penalizing him for his defense. no one cares when you hit that well. BUt that's not Sal Stewart's case.
war2d2
Don’t like the new interface, all my questions are still poorly thought out and badly edited. Thought it would have fixed that.
Ben Clemens
That's coming in FanGraphs 2.0 🙂
Greg Simons
Regarding last week's lack of any questions about lunch, I think we all figured someone else would ask. Of course, when that happens, you make a "fig" out of "u" and "re," or something like that. Whatever the case, I hope you have a good lunch planned today.
Ben Clemens
Why thank you. It's like House said once, I think: That's what happens when you make a presumption. You make a pres out of you and some guy named umption.
As for lunch, leftovers from a very nice salmon dish that a friend of ours cooked this weekend.
WonderWall
Piggybacking on Nomar's comments, why do you think that both the owners and the Union seem to pretty much refuse to let the situation continue. Why do both sides feel like something needs to change?
Ben Clemens
Many possible answers to this. I think the most important, for me, is that they'd act this way even if they thought that 'no change' was acceptable, because that's how bargaining well in advance of a deadline works. So I'm hopeful that when the rubber meets the road, both sides will cave simultaneously.
Barbaro Garbey
Thank you for the chat Ben. The Tigers have to feel good about former top prospects Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark thriving in their first big league action this year. Wondering though if you have any thoughts on any of the "other" Tigers rookies who have been getting run down the stretch? Personally, I have loved watching the energy guys like Hao-Yu Lee and Eduardo Valencia have brought; and Ben Malgeri and Brett Callahan have at least looked like quality defensive outfielders (at least compared to some of the butchers the Tigers have put out there). Do you think any of this group could succeed/thrive in closer to a full time role next year?
Ben Clemens
Truthfully I don't think I've seen enough of any of them to be all that sure, but I do think that they did enough that if I'm the Tigers, I'm interested in leaving some space for the minor leaguers to have bigger roles next year. Like, leave an outfield hole perhaps?
Phil
Are we sure the Sox' best option, with Rafaela back, isn't Anthony in right and Gasper/Jones at DH? I'm not really believing in Duran right now.
Ben Clemens
This seems like possibly the best option, but their behavior year to date basically tells me they won't be doing this. Or, well, assuming you mean Anthony in left, I like Abreu in right.
PC1970
Would you even put Harrison on the roster if you were Milwaukee? He looks unplayable at the moment. Maybe overreaction, but, you also can't just punt a playoff game like they can a regular season game.
Ben Clemens
I mean, I would. If I thought playing Harrison was punting a game, I wouldn't put him on there. But I kind of think that you need to give yourself chances to have your best possible team. And c'mon, if he's awful for two innings and you yank him, I think that's short of punting the game. I think that not rostering him would basically be playing too conservative. You should try to hit your high-upside outcomes to win in the playoffs, imo
Anon21
Following up more on the lockout question…I think implicitly I'm assigning the probability of missing any games to be low, definitely less than 10%. Commentators throwing around the possibility of losing the whole season seem nuts to me–isn't that obviously suicidal from a business perspective? Where do you stand on probabilities of losing any games/a significant number of games/the whole season?
Ben Clemens
I'm at least close to you on this one. I think I have the odds of missing games very low and the odds of missing a season at pretty close to zero. I just don't think the owners have the collective will. I don't think the players do either, when push comes to shove.
Robert Stewart
After the Bregman injury, should MLB enforce the rule that on deck hitters should be in the on deck circle? I remember a few years ago when they did that and the batter (I think it was Beltre) moved the actual circle to where he was standing. He may have been ejected.
Ben Clemens
No, because clearly this enforcement wouldn't stick and no one likes feeling either like a nanny or like they're being nanny stated by the umpires. The Beltre thing was a while ago at this point I think? But a specific umpire told him to get back in the circle so he moved it. It wasn't at the same time as an enforcement push or anything, if I'm remembering correctly.
wheelhouse
Boston’s about to sail to the WS, no? Easy opponent after easy opponent ahead of them
Ben Clemens
A jinx? A stealth insult? Who knows, let's hit publish.
Vee
i would be very happy if this is not Pete's peak. I dream of 12 war PCA.
Ben Clemens
Haha right? That one was kind of a gimme just because it's SO hard to imagine a better season.
HappyFunBall
Is Kyle Harrison at risk of not even making the playoff roster?
Ben Clemens
Didn't realize that this was less of a fringe opinion and more of a 'thing people are thinking'. I guess that I underestimated it. I don't really think that it's likely because he's good! Clearly capable of dominance. But the Brewers have a lot more granular data and maybe they really do think he's cooked for the moment. I just…. c'mon, the guy was so good earlier this year, and if you leave him off the playoff roster in the NLDS, you're never bringing him back on, you're accepting that you're just playing without this big important piece. I just hate settling like that.
Tim Tebow's Thunder Thighs
Dider Fuentes is rolling as a mid-reliever, but do you think the Braves should stretch him back out into a starting role next year a la Strider?
Ben Clemens
I think they'll try, realize that he's better in this current role, and move him back. They should try even if they don't think it'll work. The odds of it working are obviously not zero and he'd be more valuable by a lot if it stuck
appayipyip
If you had to sit down and name every baseball player you can think of how many names could you get to?
Ben Clemens
Oh man. Hundreds. Probably a thousand? I think I'd get tired before I ran out of names. Playing OOTP for many years, and Perfect Team in particular (Paul Sporer curates the sets over there and does an incredible job of finding fun old players) has given me a big memory bank of names
Tim Tebow's Thunder Thighs
Holy crap, am I able to submit a question as a logged in FG member? That's the first time in months.
What you do suspect the Braves will do with Profar's contract after two long term suspensions with one year remaining (which isn't far off from a qualifying offer)? I can't imagine AA getting much of anything for him
Ben Clemens
Oh yeah…. I think they'll either cut him or trade him eating all the money for a lottery ticket.
Ben Clemens
Tebow sighting yesterday btw! At the Broncos Jags game. Florida man with Denver connections, makes sense.
Phil
Yes, by right I meant left, sorry, and thanks. Also, Sean, can we bring back the thing where your own question is blue? That was both pleasurable and, particulalry when illicitly following the chat on a phone at work, useful.
Ben Clemens
putting this in the log so Sean can see it too. I didn't even know about that feature. See, this is why it's good to test things.
jonmberra
Do you think the Mariners can fix their defense this offseason? Seems like they hit a little worse than expected, and the team imploded because their defense is terrible.
Ben Clemens
I do think this is fixable. I think it might kind of fix itself, to be honest. Their worst defenders by FRV are Crawford and Arozarena, both FA's. Luke Raley was bad in right before he got hurt, but he was also just not great overall, they're surely looking for better options. TO me, it looks like they're set up to improve on defense without even focusing on it specifically, just from the change in team composition.
draftdingers
Do the Cardinals test the trade market for Herrera this offseason and could they even get a good return? Burleson seems to be the First Basemen for the next few years and I can't see Herrera staying behind the plate with his subpar defense and the glut at catcher coming through the system.
Ben Clemens
I think that they'll test the trade market, and I think they will definitely get a good return if they decide to trade him. I think that zero-ish other teams see him as a catcher, though. I see him as a 1B/DH who can maybe be an emergency catcher, I didn't like the way the Cards kept tring him at catcher even after the writing was on the wall, at least to me.
Ben Clemens
But when I was bouncing players off of my sources this summer and talking about Herrera as a fringy name, probably not top 50 trade value but surely top 100, people didn't have much to say about that eitehr way, which suggests to me that it's roughly right. Good plus bat, might benefit from not having to play catcher so often, cost controlled for a while. Teams would be interested in this for sure. He has a batting line 20% above average for his career and doesnt' cost much; the pitch sells itself.
kingkash7788
how much has nimmala rose post trade deadline
Ben Clemens
This is really more of a question for the prospect guys than for me but his stock is clearly up, impressive performance in Double-A at 20. I am not sure he's their starting shortstop on opening day next year because Neto is awesome and I'm not sold on a move to third base being inevitable. But I think that he's clearly arrow up from what we thought of him at the deadline. Good trade for the Angels. Might be a win-win, I think Soriano is gonna play well in Toronto next year, but the Angels have 100% done well there.
HappyFunBall
re: Dider Fuentes. The question to ask is not whether or not he'll be better as a reliever. MOST pitchers are. That's why they get put there in the first place. The question to ask is will Fuentes be able to thrive in a 5+ innings role or not.
Ben Clemens
Concur with this. And my thinking there is that if you're being honest with yourself, it's not certain whether he'll thrive in a 5+ inning role but he certainly hasn't ruled it out with his performance. Particularly if the Braves feel good about his feel for the splitter, which he's basically been able to mothball in relief but would surely need to add back in as a starter, I think it'd be crazy NOT to try. He's 21 and destroying major league hitting and came up as a starter.
sloejoe
Thanks for the chat! Is Robert Gasser a starter next year? According to Roster Resource he is their 5th starter. Has he shown to have the stuff to move up?
Ben Clemens
Yeah, the Brewers always use a bunch of starters interchangeably throughout the year but I have no reason to think he won't be one of them.
appayipyip
If you were the Jays would you try to extend Soriano?
Ben Clemens
I would. The weird part is the timing – like, if they haven't started on it now, I doubt they're getting it done before the lockout unless both sides really want it. So is it a next year post lockout kinda thing? Maybe. But I am generally a fan of trying to sign contract extensions when it makes even a little sense, and this one clearyl makes some sense.
fincampbell05
What are the Red Sox going to do? They're going to have some money to spend, but there really isn't a clear hole on the roster except for SS, where they surely would not sign someone that blocks Arias, if there were even any good free agent shortstops.
Ben Clemens
This isn't a great year to spend money, it's looking like. But that suits them just fine – like you said, there isn't a super clear hole on the roster aside from shortstop. And for me, backup at 3B because I dno't quite believe Durbin's torrid stretch. But I think I'd just be willing to keep some powder dry, basically. I think we've discussed their payroll situation some in recent weeks; it's really well set-up for next year, very few players leaving. Maybe they try to work out another year of Sonny Gray, maybe they just top up on pitching, but this is a great year to not need a bunch of players in FA, because the FA class is not good. I don't think they need to overcomplicate things too much – they went hard last winter, they can cool it this winter.
Rayball
Who do you have emerging in this final week between TEX and HOU?
Ben Clemens
Houston because they're like the bogeyman, they always seem to keep coming even when you think they're done. But no strong lean
drplantwrench
Also another note: it would be nice to make `Your questions awaiting the host` collapsible
Ben Clemens
Noted.
randomname1234
If you're the Red Sox, do you tank this week and hope to get WC#3 instead of WC#2? Almost certainly not catching NY for WC#1, and road games against AL West and AL Central winners sound much better than road games against Yankees and Tampa.
Ben Clemens
A few people asked versions of this earlier, I happened to like this phrasing most. But I'm answering all of your questions. No. I'd be happy if that happened, but I would not mess with wanting my good players to play well a week before the playoffs, for marginal gain. Matchups matter, but only so much, and there's no guarantee.
bosoxforlife
I do not understand why teams don't see players like Herrera as a potential career DH and as a very valuable third catcher. Mickey Gasper is presently showing just how valuable that type of player is even if doesn't keep hitting at this level. When a team has two catchers it really only has one but with three all can be used freely.
Ben Clemens
Oh I 100% agree. I think this is a leak among teams. And Herrera hits well enough, or at least projects to hit well enough, that you're not sacrificing offense anywhere, it's just free-ish value.
Phillip Denny
Do you think Luzardo's injury means he's just a glorified opener (or maybe gives you 2-3) in the WC/DS? If so, is there an argument for turning him into a late inning fireman instead?
Ben Clemens
I am unsure, but I am leaning towards him having very short starts, at which case yes, I'd prefer him as an impact reliever. I don't know if he is ready to warm up and play in that role, though, and given his at-times-injured past and his contract, if I'm the Phillies, I want him to give me a strong sign that he's interested in this role and thinks he'd do well at it
Ben Clemens
Okay everyone, this was a wonderful chat, but now I'm going to go have that aforementioned salmon and start working on an article for tomorrow.
Ben Clemens
Thanks for all the great questions, and for helping us test out the new chat interface. May the last week of the regular season be delightful for you, and let's get ready for the playoffs.
Ben is a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @benclemens.

item.content:encoded:
La postemporada de las Grandes Ligas tendrá presencia colombiana por partida doble. A falta de una semana para el final de la campaña regular, los Medias Rojas de Boston y los Bravos de Atlanta aseguraron sus respectivos lugares en los playoffs de 2026, con los relevistas Tyron Guerrero y Didier Fuentes dentro de sus nóminas.
Atlanta fue el primero en sellar su clasificación. Los Bravos aseguraron el título de la División Este de la Liga Nacional el domingo 20 de septiembre, al derrotar 4-2 a los Astros de Houston en el Daikin Park. El resultado les permitió conquistar por séptima ocasión en los últimos nueve años el campeonato divisional.
Fuentes ha sido una de las apariciones más llamativas en el bullpen de Atlanta. El derecho, nacido en Tolú, Córdoba, y de 21 años, figura entre los lanzadores más jóvenes de las Grandes Ligas y se convirtió durante la temporada en una pieza de confianza para el mánager Walt Weiss.
De acuerdo con los numeritos oficiales de la MLB, Fuentes suma en la temporada 2026 un registro de 7 victorias y solo dos derrotas (7-2), efectividad de 2.27, 71.1 entradas lanzadas, 91 ponches y un WHIP de 1.07 en 56 apariciones. Esta última estadística se refiere al promedio de corredores que un lanzador permite en base por cada entrada lanzada, ya sea por hit o base por bolas.
Leer también: Bolívar destrona a Atlántico y se queda con el título nacional sub-15 de béisbol
Fuentes llegó a Las Mayores como abridor, pero se ha consolidado como relevista. Redujo sus boletos y jonrones permitidos con respecto a su breve experiencia de 2025.
Fuentes también se convirtió en una alternativa de Atlanta para los episodios de mayor presión. En varios informes de la MLB se destaca su recta de tres dedos y la velocidad de 98 millas por hora que alcanza. Afronta los turnos con una mentalidad agresiva y ya marca 18 intervenciones positivas en hold (HLD), una estadística avanzada que indica las veces que un relevista ha mantenido la ventaja a favor de su equipo en un juego.
UN GUERRERO EN LA REMONTADA DE BOSTON
Al otro lado de la Liga Americana está Tyron Guerrero. El derecho de Bocachica, Bolívar, regresó este año a las Grandes Ligas después de no lanzar en el máximo nivel desde 2019 y encontró un lugar en el bullpen de los Medias Rojas.
A sus de 35 años, con sus 2 metros y 3 centímetros de estatura, fue seleccionado por Boston desde Triple-A Worcester el 22 de mayo.
Leer también: Trifulca empaña la coronación de Bolívar en el Torneo Nacional sub-15 de béisbol
El regreso tuvo como protagonista una de las armas más llamativas del colombiano: su sinker. En junio, MLB registró un lanzamiento de 102.8 millas por hora de Guerrero ante Spencer Jones, de los Yanquis de Nueva York. También se resaltó que el cartagenero llegó a promediar 100.2 millas por hora con ese lanzamiento durante la temporada.
Las cifras oficiales de la MLB registran a Guerrero con 39 apariciones en la temporada, marca de 1-2, efectividad de 3.18, 39.2 entradas, 38 ponches y WHIP de 1.11.
El colombiano, además, llega a la recta final después de superar una lesión en el hombro derecho. Boston lo colocó en la lista de lesionados el 1 de septiembre y lo activó nuevamente el 20 de septiembre. En su regreso ante Tampa Bay lanzó una entrada en blanco y ponchó a dos bateadores.
La clasificación de Boston se concretó el pasado domingo. Los Medias Rojas aseguraron uno de los cupos de comodín de la Liga Americana y disputarán desde el martes 29 de septiembre una Serie de Comodines al mejor de tres partidos como visitantes.

item.title: [mlb.com] Postseason FAQ: What's next for the Red Sox?
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne

item.content:encoded:
Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

item.title: [mlb.com] Who sits atop final Power Rankings of the regular season?
item.dc:creator: Will Leitch
item.description: These are the last MLB.com Power Rankings of the 2026 regular season. In exactly one week, 18 of these teams will go home, and 12 will be left. We have made it all the way through. Since these will be the final rankings, let’s take a look at each team, even the ones who did not make the playoffs, and find something positive its fanbase can feel about the 2026 season … now that it’s almost in the rearview mirror. item.content:encoded:
These are the last MLB.com Power Rankings of the 2026 regular season. In exactly one week, 18 of these teams will go home, and 12 will be left. We have made it all the way through. Since these will be the final rankings, let’s take a look at each team, even the ones who did not make the playoffs, and find something positive its fanbase can feel about the 2026 season … now that it’s almost in the rearview mirror.
These rankings, as always, are compiled from MLB.com contributors whose names you can find at the bottom of this (and every) piece, but the words are mine. If you dislike the rankings, yell at all of us. But if you dislike the words, feel free to yell at me.
Also, as we close the season, we note for each team the highest they were ranked in our Power Rankings all season -- when they hit the peak.
1. Brewers (previously: 1)
Season High Water Mark: 1, this week
It’s the best season in Brewers history. It sure looks like they’re going to win 100 games for the first time ever. They’ve got a Cy Young frontrunner in Jacob Misiorowski, they’ve got all the momentum, and they’ve got a team that wins by doing all the little things right. Last year was a huge postseason bummer. Now is the time to right that wrong.
2. Dodgers (previously: 2)
Season High Water Mark: 1, Aug. 17
The Dodgers have had a lot of drama this year, much of it revolving around a hugely disappointing first season at Chavez Ravine for Kyle Tucker and injury concerns for Shohei Ohtani. And yet here they are, one of the best teams in baseball, as always, and the team everyone knows is looming in October.
3. Rays (previously: 4)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 25
Don’t forget, almost no one picked the Rays to win the tough AL East this year. But it looks like it’s going to be theirs, with a deep, versatile roster led by Junior Caminero, who looks like he’s going to be a signature star in this league for the next decade-plus.
4. Braves (previously: 3)
Season High Water Mark: 1, June 15
Every year since their World Series title in 2021 has felt a little bit like a disappointment in its own way, even the 104-win season in '23. But this one sure hasn’t, with the Braves overcoming a '25 losing season by winning the division again. And check out Ronald Acuña Jr., who looks like a superstar again.
5. Yankees (previously: 5)
Season High Water Mark: 2, May 4
For a long time, it was assumed that if Aaron Judge was hurt for an extended period of time, the Yankees were cooked. But thanks to a fantastic pitching staff -- including Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler -- the Yankees look as strong as ever. But it still may all ride on Judge regardless.
6. Cubs (previously: 6)
Season High Water Mark: 1, May 11
What more can you say about Pete Crow-Armstrong at this point? He’s about to end the Shohei Ohtani MVP reign, and he’s doing so while becoming one of the most popular players in the sport and having one of the best seasons in Cubs history. And it sure feels like October is going to fit him like a glove.
7. Red Sox (previously: 8)
Season High Water Mark: 6, Aug. 5
This season looked absolutely lost in June, and Red Sox fans were tearing their hair out. Then, suddenly, the Sox were playing the best of any team in baseball, and they rode that run all the way to a playoff spot. And it's sure looking like we'll get another installment of The Rivalry in the Wild Card.
8. Padres (previously: 9)
Season High Water Mark: 3, April 20
The Padres have justified all the investments A.J. Preller and company have made in the offseason with this late-season run, but they still have won just one game past the Division Series round this century. The top of the NL is tough this year, but no one’s hotter than the Padres.
9. Phillies (previously: 7)
Season High Water Mark: 5, July 16
It has been a rocky road, with Don Mattingly taking over early in the season, the team righting itself, and then struggling down the stretch. But in this ear, all that matters for the Phillies is the postseason. All of their questions are about to be answered, one way or the other.
10. Guardians (previously: 12)
Season High Water Mark: 5, June 8
The Guardians’ fight back to the top of the AL Central wasn’t as dramatic as last year’s, but if they can end up atop the division when it’s all said and done, it won’t matter. And if they do … they might just get a first-round bye out of it.
11. White Sox (previously: 11)
Season High Water Mark: 6, June 15
If the White Sox aren’t able to get into the playoffs after the fun season they’ve had, it will feel like a heartbreaker, but it probably shouldn’t be. This is a team that has lost 100-plus games for three consecutive seasons! Look at where they are now! The playoffs would be wonderful. But what a major step forward they’ve made. With more to come.
12. Rangers (previously: 16)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 3
The Rangers have never gotten higher than three games over .500 this year … but that has not kept them out of the middle of the AL West, and even atop the division. They’ve only made the playoffs once in the last decade -- the year they won the World Series. That may well change this season.
13. Diamondbacks (previously: 10)
Season High Water Mark: 9, Aug. 17
The Padres’ torrid run down the stretch may end up keeping Arizona out of the playoffs, though the season’s final series between the two teams could have something to say about that. But a year of uncertainty ended up being a positive one, despite some off-field drama … and there’s still time left in this one.
14. Astros (previously: 13)
Season High Water Mark: 7, April 6
Yordan Alvarez had a fully healthy season and responded with an all-timer of an offensive performance. The only question now is whether they can catch the intrastate-rival Rangers for the AL West crown -- and it looks like they're going to have to, if they want to make the playoffs at all.
15. Blue Jays (previously: 14)
Season High Water Mark: 2, March 23
It looked for a while like the Jays, after the brutal way they lost the World Series last year, would make up for a disappointing season by sneaking into the final Wild Card spot. How fans feel about this season may depend on whether or not they can crawl their way back in. It’s going to be an uphill climb.
16. Pirates (previously: 15)
Season High Water Mark: 5, April 20
Pirates fans had big hopes for this year, and while they weren’t the playoff team that some had expected, they nevertheless have won 79 games and could notch their first winning season since 2018. It’s progress.
17. Orioles (previously: 19)
Season High Water Mark: 10, March 23
It may have hurt to do it, but the O’s did maximize their return for Adley Rutschman with even more young players to add to the ones they already have. It’s understandable if O’s fans are skeptical, but you can’t argue that Pete Alonso was a great investment, and really a North Star for the whole franchise at this point.
18. Marlins (previously: 18)
Season High Water Mark: 8, July 16
Take away that 12-game losing streak, and the Marlins are a playoff team this year. You obviously can’t do that, but the different way the Marlins have been doing things started to pay off this year. And they may well have a star in Otto Lopez.
19. Tigers (previously: 21)
Season High Water Mark: 8, April 27
This turned out to be their first losing season since 2023, which is frustrating because hopes were so high heading into the year, but there is still a ton of young talent here, led by Riley Greene, who is quietly putting together a stellar start to his career. And with the Tarik Skubal trade, there’s even more young talent on the way.
20. Cardinals (previously: 17)
Season High Water Mark: 8, May 18
The bullpen fell apart down the stretch, making the record look worse than the season felt, but the Cardinals made many steps forward this year, particularly with the lineup: Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt, Joshua Báez, Alec Burleson and Leo Bernal all look like lineup mainstays … with even more talent coming down the pipe.
21. Nationals (previously: 24)
Season High Water Mark: 12, June 22
James Wood is a star, but he was hardly the only National to emerge in 2026, with CJ Abrams and the recently extended Cade Cavalli setting themselves up as players the Nationals can build around. The offense was terrific this year: That’s the first time you’ve been able to say that in a long time.
22. Mariners (previously: 20)
Season High Water Mark: 3, March 23
So, yeah, it was a bit of a disaster season for the Mariners, in just about every possible way. But this was not a now-or-never season for the M’s: They have a very exciting rotation for 2027, and note that Cal Raleigh started to warm up as the season came to a close as well.
23. Mets (previously: 23)
Season High Water Mark: 5, March 23
That most of the offseason moves blew up in their faces is the reason they’re not in the playoffs, but they certainly played well enough in the second half to look like a playoff team, thanks largely to rookies Carson Benge, A.J. Ewing and Nolan McLean. The Mets will look different next year, but that’s a good thing.
24. Twins (previously: 22)
Season High Water Mark: 15, Aug. 5
The next generation of Twins stars has arrived: Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez all made their debut this year (and still have Rookie of the Year eligibility for next season). This was a transition year for the Twins. There’s plenty of reason to think they can turn the corner in 2027.
25. Reds (previously: 25)
Season High Water Mark: 6, April 27
This was the superstar step forward the Reds have been waiting for from Elly De La Cruz. They no longer have to wonder if he’s ever going to make the leap: He now has. And remember, he is still only 24 years old.
26. Royals (previously: 26)
Season High Water Mark: 14, May 11
Not much went the way it was supposed to this year, but there’s still a lot of young talent here. And there is Bobby Witt Jr., who, even in a down power year (for him), leads the American League in WAR, per FanGraphs.
27. Giants (previously: 27)
Season High Water Mark: 18, March 23
The terrible start, and the occasional discord and chaos, made this season feel like it was over with before it even began. But don’t overlook the fact that Rafael Devers, for most of this season, looked like the superstar the Giants traded for.
28. Angels (previously: 29)
Season High Water Mark: 19, April 20
A potential sale of the team is something that fans have wondered could change the trajectory of this franchise, and they’re going to get the opportunity to find out. There’s some young talent starting to percolate here, perhaps most notably Walbert Ureña, a 22-year-old who looks like he might already be an ace.
29. A’s (previously: 28)
Season High Water Mark: 10, May 11
The onslaught of injuries to their position players made people forget how good this lineup was at some point, and how late in the year they were in contention. As they move closer to their move to Las Vegas, there’s still plenty to build on here … and plenty of reason to have optimism for the future.
30. Rockies (previously: 30)
Season High Water Mark: 27, May 4
It does not look like the Rockies are going to avoid 100 losses this year, alas, marking four straight years with 100-plus losses. But they’ll still be double-digit games better than they were last year, and they’ll do so with a front office that seems, at last, to have a clear plan moving forward.
Voters: Jason Catania, Dan Cichalski, Theo DeRosa, Rick Gold Jr., Jared Greenspan, Will Leitch, Brent Maguire, Travis Miller, Brian Murphy, Arturo Pardavila, Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, Andrew Simon, David Venn, Andy Werle.

item.content:encoded:
A scary scene took place on Sunday when Chicago Cubs star Alex Bregman was hit in the face by a foul ball and force to exit the game against the Cincinnati Reds. After the game, Bregman posted a photo on his Instagram, telling fans that he will be fine, but also showing the damage the foul ball did.
Bregman may ultimately end up being just fine in the next week, but there is at least a chance he could land on the injured list and miss the rest of the regular season while the Cubs try to zero in on clinching a playoff spot.
How Bregman's injury impacts Cubs, playoff race
The Cubs would have the top wild card spot if the regular season ended today. They begin a three-game series on Tuesday night against the Miami Marlins, while the San Diego Padres face the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Philadelphia Phillies face the Milwaukee Brewers.
By strength of schedule, the Cubs have the easiest week of the three teams in wild card spots. But without Bregman, things could get a little bit more difficult. They'll face Bregman's former team, the Boston Red Sox over the weekend.
This could potentially hurt their chances of securing the top wild card spot and knock them down a bit in the standings, creating room for Philadelphia and San Diego to climb to the top. And if the Cubs are without Bregman at all in the postseason, then they will have tougher time getting out of the wild card round, as they could find themselves playing one of the other two wild card teams, or possibly even the Atlanta Braves.
The Cubs lost the NLDS last year to the Milwaukee Brewers, and they'll hope to make a deeper run this October, but any time without Bregman will make that task all the more difficult.
Bregman could be back in time for the postseason, so that could give the Cubs a better chance, but the timing of the injury certainly isn't good, especially with Chicago still trying to secure their wild card berth now that Milwaukee has already won the National League Central. It's going to be difficult to stay hot if he ends up landing on the injured list.
It will be interesting to see how he recovers and if he will be able to recover in time to help the Cubs in the playoffs.
Curt Bishop is a freelance sports writer who graduated from Maryville University of St. Louis with a Bachelor of Arts degree in the field of Communication and currently writes as a contributor for various platforms covering Major League Baseball. Curt’s work includes covering trade and free agency predictions, as well as rumors and news. item.title: [UnionLeader.com] Red Sox reaching the playoffs provides a measure of vindication for Breslow
item.dc:creator: Sean McAdam masslive com
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — After all the champagne bottles had been emptied and all the beer had been consumed or sprayed, a lone figure emerged from the joyous Red Sox clubhouse late Sunday afternoon. Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow was barefoot, his clothes somewhat damp from the proceedings inside, and his sense of satisfaction evident. Back in late April, Breslow had made the boldest of moves when he fired popular manager Alex Cora and most of his coaching staff, and replaced him wi
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — After all the champagne bottles had been emptied and all the beer had been consumed or sprayed, a lone figure emerged from the joyous Red Sox clubhouse late Sunday afternoon.
Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow was barefoot, his clothes somewhat damp from the proceedings inside, and his sense of satisfaction evident.
Back in late April, Breslow had made the boldest of moves when he fired popular manager Alex Cora and most of his coaching staff, and replaced him with a manager with no major league experience — playing, coaching or managing — and a makeshift coaching staff.
At the time, Breslow said the changes were necessary to save an underperforming team in a season that was quickly slipping away. But in his mind, these Red Sox could still be salvaged. More than once, he mentioned that the Red Sox, then owners of a 10-17 record, still had 135 games left to play.
To many, it seemed like a thin rationalization. As it turned out, Breslow was correct and Sunday, as the Red Sox assured themselves of a playoff spot, he appeared almost prophetic.
“This has been a turbulent season,” said Breslow. “But ultimately, we talked about putting together a team that was capable of getting to the postseason and having a deep postseason run. This (getting into the playoffs) is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here, so we still have a bunch of important games ahead of us.”
Asked if he had truly believed that the Red Sox were capable of this kind of turnaround, he didn’t hesitate to respond in the affirmative.
“I believed in the players that we had and I believed it was really important to act definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded.
“And while there may have been some people who questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered resoundingly.”
On Sunday, Breslow singled out interim manager Chad Tracy for extra praise.
“I talked about Trace back in April and just the consistency and stabilizing presence that he can be,” said Breslow. “He’s got an incredibly unique ability to connect with players — young players, veteran players — and I think they really respect the authenticity and the honesty that he approaches them with daily.”
As Breslow spoke, it was hard not to hear some indirect criticism of Cora and the coaches with whom he was most closely associated.
Recounting the 32-5 run that lifted the Red Sox from the division basement, Breslow referenced how the Sox had, after the firings, changed “the way that we practiced, the way that we trained, the way that we delivered information to our players, the way we supported our players. When you put all those things together, they compound and ultimately the performance on the field, by way of wins and losses, was the last thing to catch up.”
Breslow said he noticed a sense of pride displayed by the players as they celebrated qualifying for the postseason for the second straight season and detected some satisfaction in proving their naysayers wrong.
“I think we’ve shown what we’re capable of,” he said.
As a player, Breslow was part of a long playoff run that resulted in a World Series championship in 2013. Now, as an executive, he’s experiencing it from a different perspective.
“The obvious difference is,” he said, “I didn’t have a direct impact on outcomes of games in this role, whereas I did as a player. But I think there’s a different set of gratification when you’re part of this massive effort to identify players and bring them in and help support the coaching staff. It’s very different and in some ways it’s maybe a couple of layers removed. But it’s certainly as satisfying.”

item.content:encoded:
It’s not remotely the right time to start talking about offseason movement, but there is movement afoot. Two of Craig Breslow’s assistant GMs, Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith, have already conducted preliminary interviews for the big chair in Sacramento after the A’s fired Dave Forst back in August. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
Here in Boston, though, we’re unlikely to see a search for a new boss in a while. Craig Breslow earned himself quite a bit of rope this season, thanks to a decisive move that paid off big time in firing Alex Cora. “I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said. “And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
And here’ s a look at some of the key moments of the season that got this team where it is today. Remember the ninth inning comeback against the Mets that came after that long-delayed flight? How about Caleb Durbin’s home run off Cam Schlittler? (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
But, strangely enough, when it came time to clinch the playoffs, it wasn’t a Red Sox player who did the dirty work, though it was a Red Sox legacy player. “And the man with the game-winning three-run homer that would, in the end, send both the Braves and the Red Sox to the postseason? Well, baseball is quite sentimental, and it also has a sense of humor, so, obviously, it was Mike Yastrzemski.“ (Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, MLB.com)
But the fact that the Sox clinched on a loss didn’t dampen the celebration. “There was a lot of beer!” said Payton Tolle. “It was a slobberknocker.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
But before the slobberknocker could get slobbin’, Chad Tracy addressed his team to sum up the season that was. “I want to express gratitude for everyone in the room,” he said. “I’m so grateful for you guys, for our staff, for everybody. You stared impossible in the face. The position we were in, you beat it back and said, ‘The hell with that, we’re going to the playoffs.’ And you did.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
So the Sox are in the dance. But for how long? That’s anyone’s guess, but Red Sox fans are apparently more optimistic than the fans of any other American league team. (Stephen J. Nesbitt, The Athletic)

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have secured a spot in baseball's postseason, making history by becoming the first team to clinch a playoff berth after being 14 games below .500. As of Sunday (September 20), the Red Sox have achieved an 84-72 record under interim manager Chad Tracy, following a remarkable second-half surge. Their playoff spot was confirmed with the Houston Astros' loss to the Atlanta Braves.
Despite a 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays, the Red Sox celebrated their postseason berth with a clubhouse party. The team, led by spiritual leader Willson Contreras, has shown resilience throughout the season. Tracy, who took over from Alex Cora on April 26, has been credited with stabilizing the team and fostering a supportive environment.
The Red Sox's journey to the playoffs included a significant turnaround starting with a four-game sweep of the New York Yankees in late June. They went on to achieve a 15-game winning streak, tying a franchise record set in 1946. This impressive run has positioned them as the No. 5 seed, likely facing the Yankees in the AL Wild Card round.
The team overcame early-season challenges, including the dismissal of Cora and several coaches. Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow emphasized the importance of decisive action in creating a thriving environment for the players. Looking ahead, the Red Sox aim to continue their momentum into the postseason, with the first game of the Wild Card Series expected to take place at Yankee Stadium on September 29.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] New York Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays: Series Preview
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Farrar
item.description: So it all comes down to this? After the Yankees dropped the last two games of their series against the Diamondbacks in the desert, the math is at least simple for the Yankees in their last-ditch Hail Mary: win all four games to flip the season series with the Rays to 7–6 in their favor, shrinking the division deficit to two games and securing the tiebreaker.
