item.content:encoded:
So it all comes down to this? After the Yankees dropped the last two games of their series against the Diamondbacks in the desert, the math is at least simple for the Yankees in their last-ditch Hail Mary: win all four games to flip the season series with the Rays to 7–6 in their favor, shrinking the division deficit to two games and securing the tiebreaker. Should such a miracle occur, then each team’s final series of the regular season comes into play (Phillies for the Rays, Orioles for the Yanks). Anything less than a sweep, and the Rays will celebrate clinching the AL East on the Yankee Stadium infield.
Both offenses come in having played pretty well over their last 10 games. Even with Aaron Judge not doing much and then returning to the IL, the Yankees have averaged 5.4 runs per game, while the Rays have averaged 5.7 over that span. This series, much like the whole year, will of course not feature the Yankees’ captain. With postseason baseball right around the corner, there are no longer places to hide or excuses to be made.
After the offday for both clubs today, the bullpens will come in ready to handle the doubleheader on Tuesday and the following two games. The Rays have three standouts ready to roll in Bryan Baker, who has a major-league-leading 40 saves while posting a 1.49 ERA and a 0.91 WHIP. Right behind him, Kevin Kelly has made 68 appearances, tossing 72.0 innings while maintaining a 0.90 WHIP and a solid 2.49 ERA. Meanwhile, left-hander Cam Booser has provided 38.1 innings with an outstanding 42:6 strikeout-to-walk ratio and a 0.78 WHIP on the year. Now let’s dive into the starting pitching matchups.
Tuesday, Game 1: Carlos Rodón vs. Nick Martinez (1:05 p.m. ET)
The Yankees will send Rodón out for game one of the doubleheader. Rodón has fully settled into his normal rhythm of ugly, but quality starts. He actually hasn’t allowed more than three runs in any start all year long, though elbow inflammation cost him about seven weeks. Across 15 starts, he has delivered a sharp 2.95 ERA and a 1.13 WHIP with 83 strikeouts in 76.1 innings, limiting opponents to a .178 batting average. Over his last three outings, Rodón has showcased his usual grind, allowing a total of just four earned runs over 17.1 innings while racking up 20 strikeouts.
Martinez takes the hill for the Rays to counter Rodón. The righty has quietly had a phenomenal campaign for Tampa Bay. Spanning 29 starts, he has an impressive 15-4 record with a 2.94 ERA and a 1.07 WHIP across 171.1 innings of work, all while walking only 24 batters all season. The journeyman was an All-Star for the first time in 2026 and won his most recent start on September 16th, throwing an efficient 72 pitches over five innings against the A’s. Martinez has given up five earned runs over his last three turns through the rotation and has been pulled with varying lower-pitch counts each time. Martinez’s primary weapon is a high-spin changeup that completely neutralizes left-handed bats.
Tuesday, Game 2: Max Fried vs. Drew Rasmussen (7:05 p.m. ET)
The Yankees hand the ball to another veteran lefty in Fried for the nightcap of the twin bill. Despite managing his workload (and bone bruise) carefully down the stretch to stay completely fresh for October, Fried’s “full”-season body of work has been spectacular. In 19 starts this season, he has pitched to a 2.63 ERA and a 0.981 WHIP, racking up 100 strikeouts over 106 frames while holding opponents to a meager .198 average. In his last two starts, Fried struggled against the Rockies (only allowing a run on one hit but needing 80 pitches to record 10 outs) before rebounding in Minnesota, going seven strong innings of one-run ball on September 15th.
Tampa Bay counters with their top guy in the right-handed Rasmussen to finish out the doubleheader. The 31-year-old has put together a great season for the Rays and is the most likely candidate to start Game 1 of a playoff series for them, logging a 15-5 record over 29 starts and a 2.72 ERA, a 0.925 WHIP, and 163 strikeouts in 165.1 innings. Rasmussen is coming off a good performance against the A’s, firing five scoreless innings before being lifted with a comfortable 6-0 lead. Over his last three starts, he has surrendered just two earned runs in 19.0 innings. Rasmussen attacks hitters with a dose of high-velocity cutters and hard-sweeping sliders.
Wednesday: Gerrit Cole vs. Ian Seymour* (7:05 p.m. ET)
The mid-week spotlight features the Cole train hoping to find the rails he and Scranton have both abandoned of late. On the year, Cole has a 9-9 record with a 3.63 ERA, a 1.10 WHIP, and 123 strikeouts across 121.1 innings. Cole has been a bit volatile in his last three outings. He was tagged for five runs by the Mets on September 12th and four runs by the Padres on September 6th, but bounced back in his most recent start on September 18th in Arizona, firing six innings of four-hit, two-run ball with six strikeouts. Although Cole coughed up a combined seven long balls to the Mets and Padres, he at least kept the D-backs to one shot by Corbin Carroll. Aaron Boone has said that the old ace will get a playoff start, so it’s vital that he keeps the homers in check in his regular-season finale.
The Rays haven’t officially announced their Wednesday starter yet, but the next man in the rotation after Rasmussen is Seymour, and he would be on normal rest. The lefty from Madison, Connecticut has compiled a 9-7 record with a 4.38 ERA, a 1.17 WHIP, and 155 strikeouts in 127.1 innings. Over his last three starts, he struck out 10 in a six-inning performance against Houston on September 12th, but was touched up for four runs by Boston on September 18th and three runs by Texas on September 6th. Seymour leads with a low-90s four-seam fastball that plays up due to a unique extension and arm slot, paired with a good changeup and a sweeping slider.
Thursday: Cam Schlittler vs. Freddy Peralta* (7:05 p.m. ET)
Schlittler has gone from a rising young fan favorite to the runaway favorite to win the AL Cy Young Award. Over a sample size of 32 starts, Schlittler has thrown 190.2 innings and posted a stellar 1.94 ERA (ranking second in MLB) alongside a 0.91 WHIP (third in MLB) and 234 strikeouts against an unfair .184 opponent batting average. Schlittler has not given up more than a single earned run in a start since August 3rd. Here is to hoping Schlittler has another few amazing starts left in store for us in 2026. What a season! This will be his final tune-up before the playoffs.
The Rays are on track to wrap up the series by sending the veteran right-hander Peralta to the hill to counter Schlittler. Since coming over to the Rays at the 2026 Trade Deadline following a regrettable short stint with the Mets, he is throwing his changeup more and is showing a change in arm angle. On the year, he has a 9-11 record, a 4.56 ERA, a 1.335 WHIP, and 146 strikeouts over 158 innings. In his last three outings, he allowed one run over 5.2 innings against Boston on September 19th, spun five scoreless against Houston on September 13th, and gave up just four hits and a run over six innings in Atlanta on September 8th. That computes for a superb 1.08 ERA over his last 16.2 innings. Nicknamed “Fastball Freddy,” Peralta features a delivery that makes his mid-90s four-seam fastball almost pop into view for hitters. He relies heavily on that fastball, pairing it with a sweeping slider and that aforementioned fading changeup.
*Starter not yet finalized
Who will win the Yankees/Rays series?
New York needs a clean sweep to stay alive in the AL East; otherwise, Tampa Bay clinches the division title and a first-round bye.

item.title: [FanSided] Yankees can deliver Sonny Gray the ultimate karma in potential final game
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: Having owned a Coonhound named “Karma” for 13 years, I’m well familiar of the idea that what goes around comes around. Even the dog who would stare at the wall during thunderstorms would join us in being amused by veteran Boston Red Sox pitcher Sonny Gray’s upcoming predicament. As things stand entering the regular season’s final week, the 36-year-old right-hander would likely start next Wednesday’s second game of the Wild Card Series. Fittingly, Gray would make his Red Sox playoff debut against
item.content:encoded:
Having owned a Coonhound named “Karma” for 13 years, I’m well familiar of the idea that what goes around comes around.
Even the dog who would stare at the wall during thunderstorms would join us in being amused by veteran Boston Red Sox pitcher Sonny Gray’s upcoming predicament. As things stand entering the regular season’s final week, the 36-year-old right-hander would likely start next Wednesday’s second game of the Wild Card Series.
Fittingly, Gray would make his Red Sox playoff debut against a Yankees team he’s publicly admitted to despising. The three-time All-Star pitched in 41 games for the Yankees from 2017-18, a stint that resulted in him being demoted to the bullpen midway through that second season.
“It feels good to me to go to a place where it’s easy to hate the Yankees,” Gray said this past offseason. “I never wanted to go there in the first place.”
Good news, Sonny: Your next trip to the Bronx could also mark the last start of your impressive 14-year career.
Could Boston Red Sox pitcher Sonny Gray retire after the 2026 season?
We’ve done plenty of speculating about players’ futures lately, but this isn’t one of those instances. Gray recently told the Boston Globe that he’d retire in a “heartbeat” if his family wanted him to, and the organization is reportedly preparing for the possibility that he won’t return in 2027.
Gray turns 37 in November and has a $30 million mutual option for 2027, though he can opt out and forfeit a $5 million buyout. Assuming that he wants to return next year, it’s difficult to envision the Red Sox passing on his option given his performance and his outspoken love of pitching in Boston.
Garrett Crochet gets all of the attention, but don’t sleep on Gray’s impact. He climbed the 2,000-strikeout threshold earlier this year, and he's already recorded a career-high 17 wins. The journeyman starter’s 2.82 ERA and 4.0 bWAR both mark his best since 2023, his final year with the Twins.
The only thing left on Gray’s to-do list is pitching in the World Series, which is far easier said than done. Boston is all but locked into the AL’s No. 5 seed, and the Red Sox would play the entire Wild Card Series on the road. If they were to knock off the Yankees, the Red Sox would start the ALDS away from Fenway Park, and the only way they’d have home-field advantage in the ALCS is if the No. 6 seed — currently the White Sox — embarks on a miracle run.
Hey, we’ve seen stranger things. Who else is old enough to remember the 2007 Rockies going from a controversial Game 163 win to sweeping the NLDS and NLCS as a Wild Card team? Of course, they suffered their own sweep at the hands of the Red Sox. It’s like poetry.
And what would be more poetic than Gray either exacting revenge on the Yankees or seeing his career end against that same team?
"We’ll see what the future holds for me," Gray said. "But if this is it, no better way to go out and try to do something special here the next couple months."

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Payton Tolle Can Make Red Sox Playoff History 108 Years After Babe Ruth
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox kick off postseason action, if they turn to red-hot rookie Payton Tolle in either Game 1 or Game 2 on the mound, he will make a bit of absurd team history.
It's a real discussion right now about where to slot in Tolle. Boston's top three starters clearly are him, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez. Boston is very likely going to face the New York Yankees in the first round of the playoffs and Tolle has had success against the Red Sox's biggest rival this season. Saturday, Rob Bradford of WEEI shared that Tolle has a "good shot" at being the team's Game 1 starter in a playoff series, which would've been a shocking statement a few months ago. If Tolle does get the ball in Game 1 — or Game 2 — he'll become the youngest pitcher to start the first or second game of a playoff series for Boston since Babe Ruth back in 1918, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
"At 23 years old, Payton Tolle could become the youngest pitcher to start Game 1 or Game 2 of a Postseason series for the Red Sox since Babe Ruth (1918 World Series Game 1),"
How crazy is that? It's been over 100 years since Ruth took the mound in Game 1 of the 1918 World Series and no one has been able to start a Game 1 or Game 2 for Boston in a playoff series since.
Payton Tolle Has A Shot At History
Tolle is 23 years old and 324 days old. So far this season, the big lefty has a 3.02 ERA and a 166-to-38 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 143 innings pitched for Boston. For as good as Tolle has been, it's easy to forget that he actually didn't make Boston's Opening Day roster out of Spring Training.
The Red Sox promoted the lefty on April 23 and he has been incredible ever since. He should get votes in the American League Rookie of the Year race, despite the fact that it's seemingly a foregone conclusion that Kevin McGonigle is going to win the award.
When it comes to Boston's playoff rotation, you can't go wrong with any of these three guys, at least on paper. Tolle, Gray and Suárez are all pitching very well right now, to the point that any could realistically be the Game 1 starter. Tolle has done the best specifically against the Yankees this season and New York struggles against lefties, that should work in the rookie's favor. Gray has been Boston's ace all season and Suárez has plenty of playoff success and is also a lefty.
On paper, any of these three would be a good choice. When it comes to Tolle, it would be historic.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras Shares Honest Message After Red Sox Clinch originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Willson Contreras never stopped believing in the Boston Red Sox.
After Boston clinched a spot in the 2026 MLB postseason Sunday, the veteran first baseman reflected on the team's journey and made it clear how proud he is of the clubhouse.
"I did believe in my team," Contreras said in an interview. "I did believe in everybody who was here. I never had a doubt that we can turn the season around."
Contreras recalled sending a message to his teammates during Boston's struggles.
"I just said, 'Keep believing in ourselves,'" Contreras said, per Ian Browne of MLB.com. "I said, 'Believe.' That was our main word. And that's what we believed from Day 1."
The Red Sox eventually turned their season around, but Contreras credited the entire clubhouse for continuing to work through adversity.
The full speech from Willson Contreras to the team. Electric stuff. Clearly the guy who leads this entire group. Of course he had to throw a trash barrel lol. https://t.co/pF1S0TpPyz
— Tyler Milliken (@tylermilliken_) September 20, 2026
"We created a good family here, good chemistry throughout the season," Contreras said. "We just needed time and the time came for us."
Contreras also pointed to the injuries and other challenges Boston faced throughout the season.
"We played through injuries, we played through mental stuff, physical stuff but we never stop believing in each other and that's why we're here," he said.
Contreras joined the Red Sox from the St. Louis Cardinals last offseason and quickly became an important voice in the clubhouse.
Following Sunday's clinching celebration, he addressed his teammates and made sure they knew how much he appreciated the group.
"I'm really thankful, first of all, for playing for Boston," Contreras said. "Thankful for the front office for asking me to come here and all of the good human beings that are here on this team."
For Contreras, reaching the postseason is an accomplishment worth celebrating, but he views it as only the beginning.
"This is just the first step ahead," Contreras said. "I just wanted to let everybody know that I'm proud of every one of you."

item.content:encoded:
A lot has gone right for the Red Sox on their path since firing manager Alex Cora toward the start of the 2026 season.
Arguably no top performer for Boston, however, has come on more suddenly than left-handed pitcher Payton Tolle. The 23-year-old struggled in his seven games in 2025, but has been terrific throughout his second MLB season.
During the Red Sox's postseason clinch celebrations on Sunday, Tolle acknowledged his breakout campaign with a hilarious quote.
Here's what Tolle said about his contributions to this year's Red Sox playoff team after his 2025 struggles.
Payton Tolle's Hilarious Quote About Breakout 2026 Season
In the midst of Boston's locker-room celebrations on Sunday after clinching a postseason berth, Tolle answered questions from reporters.
The young starter said he believes the Red Sox can "make a run" in October. He also acknowledged that his 2025 contributions to Boston's playoff roster paled in comparison to 2026.
"Last year, it kind of felt like I got an 'A' on the group project and didn't do anything," Tolle said. "I'm super proud to be a part of this group, just excited to keep going."
"Last year, it kind of felt like I got an A on the group project and didn't do anything... I'm super proud to be a part of this group, just excited to keep going."
Payton Tolle, quote machine 😭 pic.twitter.com/vMQJi5W5fZ
Tolle, through 25 starts this season, has a 9-6 record with a 3.02 ERA and 166 strikeouts. He's become one of the most reliable arms in Boston's rotation — something that will certainly continue into the postseason.
He seemed to have plenty of fun celebrating on Sunday as a new fan favorite:
Payton Tolle is ready to celebrate. pic.twitter.com/FqwwEuioK9
— Daniel Álvarez-Montes (@DanielAlvarezEE) September 20, 2026

item.content:encoded:
MLB: ¡Qué golpazo! Alex Bregman de los Cachorros de Chicago sufre impactante pelotazo en la cara y es llevado al hospital VIDEO
El incidente ocurrió en la parte alta de la cuarta entrada, con dos outs. Michael Busch, compañero de Bregman, conectó una pelota de foul que terminó golpeando al tercera base en el pómulo izquierdo, debajo del ojo
Alex Bregman vivió un momento de preocupación durante la victoria de los Chicago Cubs por 9-1 sobre los Cincinnati Reds, luego de recibir un pelotazo en el rostro mientras se encontraba en el círculo de espera del Great American Ball Park.
El incidente ocurrió en la parte alta de la cuarta entrada, con dos outs. Michael Busch, compañero de Bregman, conectó una pelota de foul que terminó golpeando al tercera base en el pómulo izquierdo, debajo del ojo.
Bregman se dirigió inmediatamente al dugout y ya no regresó al encuentro. Matt Shaw entró en su lugar, mientras el cuerpo médico de los Cubs atendía al jugador.
La escena generó preocupación entre sus compañeros debido a que el pelotazo impactó directamente en el rostro.
ESTO TE INTERESA: MLB: Jugadores latinoamericanos que aspiran al premio Roberto Clemente 2026 ¿Hay mexicanos?
El jugador fue trasladado a un hospital
Después de abandonar el terreno de juego, Bregman fue llevado a un hospital local para someterse a radiografías y una tomografía computarizada, con el objetivo de conocer el alcance de la lesión.
El manager de los Cubs, Craig Counsell, explicó que el pelotero tenía una cortada debajo del ojo, sangrado nasal y una inflamación considerable en la zona donde recibió el impacto.
“Tenía una cortada debajo del ojo. Le sangraba un poco la nariz. Está bastante hinchado”, explicó Counsell tras el encuentro. El manager también señaló que inicialmente pensó que el pelotero podía haberse fracturado la nariz, aunque todavía esperaban los resultados de los estudios médicos.
TAMBIÉN PUEDES LEER: Abner Meza, pitcher mexicano, gana el premio al lanzador del año 2026 para los New York Mets
El accidente ocurrió mientras Chicago se encaminaba a una cómoda victoria sobre Cincinnati. Bregman había contribuido previamente al triunfo con un sencillo productor de carrera y una base por bolas antes de abandonar el partido.
Bregman muestra su rostro y manda mensaje a los aficionados
Horas después del incidente, Bregman utilizó sus redes sociales para compartir una fotografía en la que mostró la inflamación y el golpe que sufrió en el lado izquierdo del rostro.
El jugador de los Cubs también agradeció los mensajes que recibió de los aficionados y compañeros después del accidente.
“Gracias por todos sus mensajes. Estaré de regreso”, escribió Bregman en Instagram.
Buscan un lugar en postemporada
Por ahora, los Cubs deberán esperar la evaluación médica para determinar el alcance de la lesión y cuándo podrá volver a jugar. El equipo se encuentra en plena lucha por un lugar en la postemporada, por lo que la disponibilidad de Bregman será un tema a seguir en los próximos días.
TE RECOMENDAMOS: ¡Tremendo susto en MLB! Jared Young sale en carrito tras fuerte golpe en la cabeza VIDEO
Tienen récord de 87 partidos ganados y 69 perdidos y se ubican en la segunda posición de la división Central de la Liga Nacional, por detrás de los líderes Milwaukee Brewers.

item.content:encoded:
Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman has returned to Chicago a day after being hit in the face by a foul ball while standing in front of the on-deck circle during a road game against the Cincinnati Reds.
Bregman shared that information — as well as a photo that appears to show that his left eye remains swollen shut — Monday morning on his Instagram Stories.
"Back in Chicago," wrote Bregman, who also appeared to have a cut and bruising near his left cheekbone where the ball off teammate Michael Busch's bat made contact during the fourth inning of the Cubs' 9-1 victory.
Read more: Is it still a rivalry? Dodgers complete sweep of woeful Giants
It was the second photo and update posted by Bregman since the gruesome injury occurred. On Sunday evening, the three-time All Star shared a photo that appeared to have been taken in the team's clubhouse. In addition to his eye being swollen shut and cheek cut, Bregman also has gauze inserted in his left nostril, where some bleeding had occurred.
"Thanks for the messages yall," Bregman wrote. "I'll be back."
Before the incident occurred, Bregman hit a run-scoring single in the first inning and walked and eventually scored in the third. He was standing several feet in front of the on-deck circle when Busch fouled off a pitch by Cincinnati's Luis Mey on a checked swing.
Read more: Dodger Stadium has a botanic garden tour. Meet the man entrusted with making it a draw
Bregman lost his bat but maintained his footing as the ball struck him. He covered his face with his left hand and was able to jog toward the Cubs dugout, where a trainer helped him down the steps and into the clubhouse. The 11-year veteran was taken to a hospital for testing.
"It's a terrible, terrible accident," Cubs manager Craig Counsell said after the game. "We hope he's OK."
Bregman is batting .262 with 26 home runs and 89 RBIs in his first season with the Cubs. He is probably best known to Los Angeles fans as a member of the Houston Astros team that defeated the Dodgers in the 2017 World Series and were later found by MLB to have illegally used technology to steal signs during that season. Bregman and the Astros also won the 2022 World Series.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times.

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Cubs somber after Alex Bregman's scary injury
item.dc:creator: Bill Ladson
item.description: CINCINNATI -- The Chicago Cubs were somber after they defeated the Cincinnati Reds, 9-1, at Great American Ball Park on Sunday because Chicago was thinking about third baseman Alex Bregman, who was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch. item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI -- The Chicago Cubs were somber after they defeated the Cincinnati Reds, 9-1, at Great American Ball Park on Sunday because Chicago was thinking about third baseman Alex Bregman, who was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of teammate Michael Busch.
Bregman was injured in the fourth inning with two outs. With the count, 1-2, Busch checked his swing at a pitch thrown by Reds right-hander Luis Mey. The ball made contact with Busch's bat, however, and then hit Bregman while he was in the on-deck circle. Bregman then ran towards the end of the Cubs' dugout before finally going into the clubhouse to get looked at by the team’s trainer.
Bregman was taken to a nearby hospital for X-rays and a CT scan, but the Cubs have yet to announce the seriousness of Bregman’s injury.
“I don’t know anything more than that,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell told reporters. “He had a cut under his eye. He was bleeding from his nose a little bit. It’s pretty swollen. It was below the eye. I honestly thought it hit him in the nose. I thought he had a broken nose, but I knew it hit him somewhere in the face. It’s just an unfortunate accident. I’m hoping and praying he is all right.
“We have to get good results from the hospital first. [Bregman] got hit in the face, so you are worried about his general well-being first. If we get a good report, we’ll move to the next step. I want to get a good report.”
Bregman is in his first season with the Cubs after signing a five-year, $175 million contract last January. He is having a productive season with the Cubbies, slashing .262/.352/.452 with 26 home runs and 89 RBI.
Before Sunday’s game, Bregman spoke to Yardbarker about his first season with the Cubs.
"The first half didn’t start out how I wanted it. (I) kept fighting. (I) trusted the process,” Bregman said. “I felt like myself over the last two months. That’s what I expect from myself. I’ve also been super thrilled to be in a position to continue to play postseason baseball, play meaningful games in October. I’ve been fortunate to do that every year of my career, which I don’t take lightly. I’m happy that we put ourselves in the position, so far, to be in.”
Bregman even had a word to say about teammate Pete Crow-Armstrong. To Bregman, PCA is the National League Most Valuable Player, and he has the stats to back it up.
Entering Tuesday’s action against the Marlins, Crow-Armstrong is leading the Majors with 10.5 wins above replacement (per FanGraphs) and 118 runs scored. He could also become the seventh player in MLB history to reach the 40-40 plateau.
“He has been the best player in the sport. It’s not even close,” Bregman said about PCA.
All quotations obtained firsthand unless otherwise noted.

item.title: [fansided.com] MLB Power Rankings: Playoff stakes rise as October contenders make their move
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers; Mark Powell
item.description: The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series. "Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not
item.content:encoded:
The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.title: [bostonglobe.com] Why are all the streets in this Utah subdivision named for Red Sox players? We asked. - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Camilo Fonseca
item.description: On the edge of the wind-scoured Salt Lake Valley, between rows of gray and white houses and sunbaked driveways, you can find a little taste of Fenway Park. A housing subdivision in Herriman, Utah, is turning heads online for its streets, each of which bears the name of a Red Sox star from the annals of team history: Pesky Lane, Pedroia Street, and Varitek Drive, to name a few. item.content:encoded:
On the edge of the wind-scoured Salt Lake Valley, between rows of gray and white houses and sunbaked driveways, you can find a little taste of Fenway Park.
A housing subdivision in Herriman, Utah, is turning heads online for its streets, each of which bears the name of a Red Sox star from the annals of team history: Pesky Lane, Pedroia Street, and Varitek Drive, to name a few.
The names, which could be ripped straight from the banners on Van Ness Street, stand out in a place like Herriman, a Salt Lake City suburb 500 miles from the nearest Major League Baseball stadium. There’s little else to suggest Copper Fields, a neat grid of roughly 200 houses completed by Edge Homes in 2024, has a link to Boston.
But once social media caught wind of the Sox-heavy ‘hood over the weekend, fans were ablaze with speculation.
“Ready to blow my savings and move to Utah so I can live on Pedroia Street,” one commenter wrote on X, posting an image of a three-bed, three-bath home on sale for $669,000 (slightly cheaper than a 700-square-foot condo in the South End).
“[I don’t care] about getting priced out of Boston,” opined Anna Caruso of Section 10, a Red Sox podcast, beneath a photo of the development. “You’ll find me here.”
Another commenter said that, in person, the neighborhood is “brand-new and pretty nice,” though “all of the houses look basically the same.”
“I wonder what [percentage] of families that live here have no idea what the streets mean,” they added.
So, who’s behind all these names? There’s not much of a Red Sox connection in the area to speak of, aside from the fact that a young David Ortiz played with Salt Lake’s minor league team while still a Minnesota Twins prospect.
But that didn’t matter to Brandon Parr, the Edge Homes project manager who selected the names. Parr, 47, was born and raised in Utah — but he lives and breathes the Red Sox all the same.
“I liked Wade Boggs a lot, and he just happened to play for them, so I became a fan,” he said. “The rest is history.”
When Parr got the chance to name an entire new subdivision, his vision was clear.
“I don’t think anybody on my team really knew what I was doing until they saw the first flat be recorded [on the master plan],” he said.
Parr made sure to include a (Wade) Boggs Way, as well as a (Jerry) Remy Road, named after the late broadcaster and former player, and a Xander (Bogaerts) Lane. The neighborhood even has a Yawkey Way, named after the controversial Red Sox owner whose name once marked what is now Jersey Street. (Edge Homes seems to have missed the memo on that one.)
Plenty of fans online wondered why Parr didn’t nod toward other Red Sox legends. The answer, he said, was that some names were hard to get local approval for. Ted Williams, for example, had a surname common enough that there’s already a Camp Williams Road in town.
“Some of them are personal favorites,” Parr said of the player names. “I was a big fan of Nathan Eovaldi and his performance in 2018, so he’s on there. ... Boggs was the reason I started liking the Red Sox, so I had to get him. I was just trying to pick some names that meant something to me, and to the organization as well.”
It’s not the first time Parr has gotten creative with street names. Edge Homes takes on anywhere from 10 to 12 development projects a year, and naming all those streets can be “a little bit of a daunting task sometimes,” he said.
Aside from Red Sox players, Parr has also referenced comic book movie actors. A subdivision in Riverton, Utah, includes a Hemsworth Lane and a Hiddleston Drive, named after Chris Hemsworth and Tom Hiddleston, the actors who play Thor and Loki in Marvel films.
“My company encourages us to be creative,” he said. “It’s just something fun that we do as a team.”
Parr, who carries a Red Sox water bottle and owns a replica championship ring, has taken his family to a few games at Fenway. But he admits that Red Sox fans aren’t exactly plentiful in Salt Lake City.
“I’m kind of alone,” he said. “At the office, I would say there’s definitely more Yankees fans around me than Red Sox fans. But I’ll be a Red Sox fan till the day I die.”
At least one Herriman resident recognizes the significance of the street names.
Chris Watson, 56, a graphic designer and photographer, has lived in Utah for over two decades. But he was raised in Framingham, collecting Red Sox trading cards and watching Luis Tiant and Jim Rice and Carl Yastrzemski.
“I don’t keep up with [the team] as much anymore,” he said. “But the only baseball hat I’ll wear is a Red Sox hat.”
When he was searching for a place to build a new home a few years back, he realized “really quickly” the names on the lot were something special.
It was a “really fun coincidence” to end up living on Fisk Road — named after Carlton Fisk, Watson’s favorite player on the (in)famous 1978 team. Even that team, lamented for its end-of-season collapse against the Yankees, still holds a special place in his heart.
“That was the peak of fandom for my 8, 9-year old self,” he said. “He would have thought it was really cool [to be living here].”
Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

21 Sep 2026, 19:10 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Reinhold Matay)
It has taken a pair of pitchers whose careers were on hold due to Tommy John surgery all season to finally make their 2026 debuts.
Right-hander River Ryan is scheduled to make his Tigers debut against left-hander DJ Herz of the Washington Nationals when the teams open a three-game series on Monday in Detroit. Both pitchers missed the 2025 campaign and the first 156 games of this season following the elbow surgery and a setback.
Ryan, then with the Los Angeles Dodgers, made his only four appearances in the majors in 2024, registering a 1-0 record and 1.33 ERA. The 4 2/3 shutout innings he threw in a start against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Aug. 10 were his last of that season. A hamstring injury slowed the return to action for the 28-year-old.
Herz, 25, made 18 starts for the Nationals in 2024, finishing 4-9 with a 4.15 ERA. He walked 36 batters, struck out 106 and gave up 11 home runs in 88 2/3innings. For Herz, the elbow injury occurred in spring training in 2025, and a flexor strain suffered in a minor league rehab assignment kept him off the mound for the Nationals.
Now, both have been cleared for action, and with both the Tigers and Nationals at 73-83 and out of the playoff picture, there is no reason for the teams not to take a look at the pitchers.
Unlike Herz, Ryan will be walking into an unfamiliar clubhouse in Detroit. He was one of three Dodgers minor league prospects acquired by the Tigers in an Aug. 2 trade for two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal.
'Hopefully we can get him a couple of outings,' Tigers manager A.J. Hinch said of Ryan. 'We expect him to be a big part of what we're doing moving forward. He's really talented and he's been here before. It's not like a (big-league) debut, but it'll feel like it given that he's brand new to the organization.'
Ryan gave up two runs in 4 2/3 innings during his rehab starts with four strikeouts.
'He's very talented,' Hinch said. 'As much as we talk about a guy we traded for and want to get into our organization, it's because he's good. He's demonstrated that.'
Keider Montero, originally listed as the starter, is expected to pitch multiple innings in bulk relief. Montero (9-9, 3.58 ERA) gave up two runs in four innings of a 4-1 loss to the Toronto Blue Jays on Wednesday.
Assuming the Tigers stick with the plan, Montero will be making his seventh relief appearance this season. Montero has started 25 games.
The Nationals have won six of their past eight games but one of those losses came Sunday as they fell 5-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals.
'We got so many guys here that are just so talented, really young, really hungry,' starting pitcher Jake Irvin told MLB.com. 'The goal in here is just to continue to get better, continue to grow, continue to build a culture. I think we've done a really good job of that, and it's a huge step forward for this organization.'
The Nationals have gotten better this season. They haven't finished above .500 since they won the World Series in 2019, and in the five seasons since the pandemic, they have lost 91 games twice, 96 games in 2025, 97 in 2021 and 107 in 2022.
Washington won the first two games against the Cardinals and had a 3-2 lead entering the eighth inning but the bullpen squandered the lead in what became a 5-3 loss.
'I thought we should have won all three games,' manager Blake Butera said. 'You leave winning two, and you should feel good about it, but it doesn't feel very good because I feel like we should have won all three.'
CJ Abrams continued his big offensive season with a two-run homer, his 31st of the season, on Sunday. He needs one more RBI to reach 100.
The Tigers were in Chicago over the weekend, losing two of three to the White Sox.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [fansided.com] Grading Bleacher Report's latest Paul Skenes trade proposals to the Yankees and Mets
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: You know that the Pittsburgh Pirates’ offseason has officially arrived when we’re talking about a potential Paul Skenes trade. It’s been a bit, hasn’t it? The Pirates remained in NL Wild Card contention throughout the second half, which ordinarily would be enough to halt the annual speculation. item.content:encoded:
You know that the Pittsburgh Pirates’ offseason has officially arrived when we’re talking about a potential Paul Skenes trade.
It’s been a bit, hasn’t it? The Pirates remained in NL Wild Card contention throughout the second half, which ordinarily would be enough to halt the annual speculation. But Skenes has looked nothing like his Cy Young self, and he could realistically end the year with an ERA above 4.00. This is the same pitcher who had a 1.96 ERA through his first 320.2 innings and looked unhittable most nights.
In the grand scheme of things, nothing has changed. Skenes hasn’t publicly requested a trade, and the Pirates have insisted they won’t trade the three-time All-Star. Objectively, we imagine he’ll be toeing the mound on Opening Day 2027, whenever that might be.
Bleacher Report’s Zachary D. Rymer nonetheless pitched (pun intended) two possible Skenes trades, one involving the Yankees and another featuring Mets. Needless to say, we have plenty of thoughts.
Yankees send Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, and two pitchers to the Pirates for Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: C+
Yankees grade: C-
Those who spend much of their free time scrolling X/Twitter (hey, we know the feeling all too well) are likely familiar with the meme of Bugs Bunny squinting his eyes and saying “No.” That’s exactly how we felt upon initially seeing this trade offer.
Let’s start with the obvious: the Yankees aren’t trading Rice. At no point did we hear his name floated amid the Tarik Skubal rumors, and his left-handed power makes him a perfect fit for Yankee Stadium’s short porch. He’ll either open next season as the starting first baseman or designated hitter, depending on what Giancarlo Stanton’s future looks like; the 2017 NL MVP has one year left on his deal, and he’s been an injury liability since the start of 2019.
We’re skeptical that Jones would be moved unless the return involves an MVP-caliber outfielder. Trent Grisham is a pending free agent, and we’re genuinely unsure what Jasson Domínguez’s future in New York looks like, especially after his recent demotion to Triple-A. When a team doesn’t want you on the big-league roster ahead of the playoffs, what does that say?
Reynolds has had a fine year, and he entered Sunday leading the league in doubles. But if you’re the Yankees, do you really want to give up Jones and Lagrange for an outfielder who turns 32 in January? Reynolds is under contract through 2030 (with a $20 million team option for 2031), and that’s a significant commitment to someone who, at his best, is a mid-3 bWAR player.
We must also note that Rymer claimed that Rodríguez ranked No. 82 and Lagrange placed No. 100 on MLB Pipeline, which is simply untrue. Shortstop Dax Kilby is the only Yankees player on the most recent MLB Pipeline list, and he placed No. 83. So the Pirates wouldn’t even be landing a top-100 prospect? Hard pass.
That said, we’ll give the Yankees a C- for their return, because an elite Skenes ranks among the game’s best pitchers. But will we see him regain that 2024-25 form? That we’re even asking the question should say enough.
Mets give up Carson Benge and two prospects for Pirates teammates Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: D
Mets grade: C
At least the proposed Pirates-Yankees trade made some sense. We can’t say the same about Pittsburgh theoretically shipping Skenes and Reynolds to the Mets for Benge, Rojas, and Tong.
First off, why would the Mets only need to give up three players rather than the Yankees’ four? Rymer listed Rojas as the No. 79 prospect and Tong at No. 88, neither of which is accurate; Rojas is No. 73, and MLB Pipeline no longer lists Tong among its top 100 prospects, for reasons we don’t understand. Mariners lefty Kade Anderson has thrown 25.1 big-league innings, and he's still ranked No. 5, but Tong and his 39.2 innings over two seasons no longer qualify. Huh?
Benge has quietly enjoyed a solid rookie season, hitting .276 with 19 home runs, 61 RBIs, 22 steals, and a .760 OPS through his first 149 games. But for him to be the centerpiece of a deal involving both Skenes and Reynolds is absurd. Oh, and Benge turns 24 in January, so he’d be a slightly older second-year starter.
As for the Mets, adding yet another long-term contract isn’t the answer to putting their disastrous 2026 season behind them. As we’ve said before, Bo Bichette would be foolish to exercise his opt-out clause and leave $42 million in guaranteed money on the table. Marcus Semien has two years and $46 million left on his deal, and we’re not even factoring in Francisco Lindor’s contract.
That said, we’ve seen enough positives from Benge thus far to hold off on giving the Pirates’ theoretical return an “F” grade. But both teams should pass on even contemplating such an offer.

item.title: [fansided.com] Scott Harris and more eliminated Tigers to blame for an inexcusable season
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman

item.content:encoded:
Even us ‘90s kids have seen some bad Detroit Tigers teams over the years, though few have been more disappointing than the 2026 club.
Not only were the Tigers expected to compete for another AL Central crown, but they were considered a dark horse team to win their first pennant since 2012. Instead, Sunday’s 8-1 loss to the rival White Sox ended any outside hopes of A.J. Hinch’s club making its third consecutive playoff appearance.
With six games left, the 73-83 Tigers will at least avoid hitting the 90-loss mark. That’s not much of a consolation, though, and many of the team’s veterans shoulder the blame for an ugly season in the Motor City. Did you know that the Tigers’ Pythagorean win-loss record is 85-71 entering Monday?
In a decision that might generate debate, we’ve omitted Justin Verlander from this list. The expectations for him shouldn’t have been overly high, and he’s fought hard to recover from hip and hamstring problems. He’s expected to make his final MLB appearance against the Pirates this coming weekend, and we expect a heartwarming atmosphere around Comerica Park.
Should Detroit Tigers fans blame Scott Harris for the team’s disappointing 2026 season?
Objectively speaking, most of Harris’ notable moves haven’t entirely backfired. Kevin McGonigle fell to Detroit in the 2023 draft’s second round, and he’s widely expected to be the AL Rookie of the Year recipient. Veteran second baseman Gleyber Torres has been solid when he’s been healthy over the last two years, and we won't even hold the Verlander signing against Harris.
We must also reiterate that Harris inherited Javier Báez, who has indisputably been one of the worst free agent signings in Tigers history. And although he drew significant pushback for the seemingly underwhelming return for Tarik Skubal, the early returns haven’t been awful on the Tigers’ end.
Top outfield prospect Zyhir Hope has an .822 OPS in nearly 150 plate appearances at Double-A Erie, and we’ll see whether he contends for an Opening Day spot next spring. River Ryan will make his Tigers debut when he starts against the Nationals on Monday night, though Brady Scott has missed much of the last month-plus with an arm injury.
We’ve seen far worse performances by lead baseball executives this year, and Harris shouldn’t warrant being the scapegoat. But you know what they say about deserving…
Framber Valdez, SP
The most significant black mark against Valdez is his three-year, $115 million contract. Had he been a veteran who’d signed a two-year deal worth $30 million, it’d have been easy for the Tigers to accept his 4.06 ERA and diminished strikeout rate. By no means would they have been encouraged heading into 2027, but the context of someone’s salary matters.
Valdez is due nearly $43 million next season and has a $35 million player option for 2028. We'd be shocked if he doesn't opt into the latter year, but could the Tigers possibly dump his salary elsewhere? Probably not, seeing as he also has a $40 million mutual option for 2029.
When you factor in Valdez’s suspension for allegedly throwing at Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story and the subsequent accusations of immaturity, we’re not exactly optimistic about how he’ll fare next year.
Javier Báez, SS/CF
How bad has Báez been in a Tigers uniform, you ask? He's managed just 0.8 bWAR since the start of 2023, and he has a .606 OPS in that time. Across a full 162-game season, the three-time All-Star would have averaged 12 home runs, 69 RBIs, a .262 on-base percentage, and 0.3 bWAR.
This year has been a complete disaster, with an ankle problem costing Báez several months on the injured list. He’s provided Detroit with -0.8 bWAR in nearly 200 plate appearances, and his five walks against 38 strikeouts aren’t exactly encouraging about what lies ahead.
If Báez still has any diehard fans, please step up to the podium. He has one year left on his contract, and his $24 million salary might guarantee he remains in Detroit for the foreseeable future.
Matt Vierling, CF
Vierling lacks the kind of lucrative contract that Valdez and Báez signed, but he’s right alongside the latter among the team’s lowest bWAR scores. The 30-year-old center fielder managed -0.9 bWAR and a .590 OPS in 291 plate appearances before groin and heel injuries prematurely ended his season.
At this point, we’re not sure why Harris — or his potential replacement — would keep Vierling around. He's been worth -1.1 bWAR in only 122 games since the start of last year, so claiming that he lacks value is the understatement of the month.
Zach McKinstry, RF/SS
Of the four players on our list, McKinstry leads the pack with 1.5 bWAR through 124 games. It's too bad that he's managed only 26 RBIs and a .584 OPS across 366 plate appearances. How do you have such a low RBI total with that many plate appearances? Even the argument about him usually hitting no higher than sixth doesn’t work, because we’ve seen plenty of No. 7 hitters have at least 60 RBIs.
Assuming that the Tigers plan to upgrade their outfield this winter, keep your eye on the Yankees’ Trent Grisham; the two-time Gold Glove winner played this year on the qualifying offer, and Detroit might be desperate enough in hoping he can replicate his 34 homers from last season.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Boston Red Sox Announce Major Aroldis Chapman News
item.dc:creator: Jake Rogers
item.description: The Boston Red Sox will take Monday off after dropping two of three games to the Tampa Bay Rays in Florida, but they return home Tuesday for a three-game series against the Cleveland Guardians with encouraging news on their closer. Aroldis Chapman has not pitched since Sept. 13 against Kansas City. The 38-year-old left-hander has been dealing with lat tightness that kept him unavailable over the weekend. The club indicated Chapman should be ready for the final homestand that begins Tuesday at Fe
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox will take Monday off after dropping two of three games to the Tampa Bay Rays in Florida, but they return home Tuesday for a three-game series against the Cleveland Guardians with encouraging news on their closer.
Aroldis Chapman has not pitched since Sept. 13 against Kansas City. The 38-year-old left-hander has been dealing with lat tightness that kept him unavailable over the weekend.
The club indicated Chapman should be ready for the final homestand that begins Tuesday at Fenway Park.
Chapman is in the midst of another strong season. He is 3-4 with a 1.95 ERA, 34 saves and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings across 52 appearances. His WHIP sits at 1.14.He has converted 34 of 36 save chances. His four-seam fastball has averaged 96.9 mph this year.
The Cuban-born reliever reached 401 career saves earlier this season. He also became the all-time strikeout leader among relief pitchers in July.
Boston clinched a wild-card berth Sunday despite a 5-1 loss to the Rays. The Red Sox are 84-72 and sit third in the AL East, 11 1/2 games behind Tampa Bay.
They have gone 52-25 since sitting 32-46 and 15 1/2 games out of first place on June 24. Interim manager Chad Tracy is 74-55 since taking over in late April.
The team holds a four-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for the second wild-card spot with six games remaining.
Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller handled recent save situations while Chapman was sidelined. Whitlock recorded his fourth save of the year last week.
Chapman is under contract for $13.3 million this season. A $13 million mutual option for 2027 becomes guaranteed if he remains healthy and passes a physical after the season. He has already surpassed the 40-inning threshold attached to that clause.
The Red Sox bullpen has been a strength throughout the year. Chapman’s availability for the Guardians series and the following set against the Chicago Cubs would give the club a clearer picture heading into the postseason.
Boston is projected to face the New York Yankees in a best-of-three Wild Card series beginning Sept. 29 on the road unless the standings shift in the final week.
The Guardians arrive at Fenway after their own late-season push. Cleveland remains in the mix for an AL Wild Card berth.
Chapman first felt the lat tightness last Tuesday. He has reported improvement through the week and was not placed on the injured list.
The Red Sox have been cautious with their veteran closer given the proximity of the playoffs. They have enough of a cushion in the wild-card race that they do not need to rush him back.
Chapman’s last outing was a scoreless ninth inning with three strikeouts against the Royals. He walked two in that appearance.
His 2026 numbers include a 12.08 strikeouts-per-nine-innings rate and just three home runs allowed.
The left-hander was named an All-Star for the ninth time this summer. He also earned All-Star honors in 2025.
Boston’s remaining regular season games are all at Fenway Park. The homestand offers a chance to get Chapman work before the postseason begins.
The clubhouse celebrated the playoff clinch Sunday night in St. Petersburg after the Houston Astros lost to Atlanta, which officially locked in Boston’s berth.
Players and staff gathered for a team photo on the field after the result became official.
The Red Sox now shift focus to finishing the regular season healthy and sharp. Chapman’s expected return is a key piece of that preparation.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Red Sox Minor Lines: The season that was for Kristian Campbell, Franklin Arias, and others in Worcester

item.content:encoded:
Worcester: Cancelled (rain), end of season
Remember when Portland’s last game of the season was cancelled due to rain? Oh, that was just last week.
Well, as we’re stuck in a cycle of weekend storms, the last game of the season was cancelled for the WooSox. A factor in this decision was Worcester being eliminated from playoff contention on Saturday night. Still, for the season to end so unceremoniously calls for at least some commemoration, and so I’d like to shout out some names on the roster. I originally intended on going down the line on the website and speculate on future contributions to the team, but, by my estimation, especially since the trade for Adley Rutschman that had a ripple effect through the organization, a good portion of Worcester’s roster are either one-year placeholders until the farm gets replenished with the next couple of drafts or guys that are dealing with significant injuries. So, here’s to the guys that may not be that:
Allan Castro finished the season with 77 RBIs, two behind Bobby Dalbec for the team record since they relocated to Worcester five years ago… and saying that relocation happened six seasons ago is crazy for someone who went to the first home stand under pandemic crowd protocols. Castro really was a constant for the offense amidst a handful of platoon guys cycling through the team and that can’t be understated. He batted doubtful games back into contention and sealed close games away. If I pick a workhorse/general player of the year, it’s him or Braiden Ward, but only because Franklin Arias started the year in Portland.
Speaking of Braiden Ward, I personally was sad to see Brennan Bernardino go this offseason but loved the return from Colorado. And he performed fantastically, particularly near the end of the season. He ended up swiping 61 total bags and ther’s some clamor around a potential call-up to the Sox who, despite being a generally quick team in terms of baserunning, lack a real Dave Roberts-esque “when you see him, you know he’s going to steal” threat. Ward provides that, is defensively versatile, playing second as well as center field, and is pretty reliable with the bat in a pinch.
Franklin Arias is banging on the door and he will definitively be getting the call either in 2027 or Opening Day 2028, depending entirely on the length of the lockout. Either way, though, keeping him off the 40-man roster for now means, even with a lockout, he’ll get valuable time to improve his exceptional swing even more, though not against Major League arms. His totals across Portland and Worcester read like an All-Star caliber player: 28 home runs, .323/.400/.557 slash line, a 14% strikeout rate, and a plus glove in the infield to boot. Arias may or may not live up to his sky high prospect status, but pencil him in to the next iteration of this Red Sox team, whenever that comes.
John Holobetz will also likely be given the call in 2027. He’s still just 24. The 6’3” righty struck out 132 in 119 innings, walked just 36, had a WIP of a hair under 1.25, but even more comforting is he outperformed his Portland numbers in Worcester, signaling quick growth. While it’s sad that Quinn Priester missed 2026 with an injury, he was a world-beater in 2025, and the value of having steady presence in the rotation can’t be understated Depending how he bounces back in 2027, especially with the Brewers emerging as an NL front runner, expect that trade to go down in the history books as a win-win.
Hayden Mullins also put in his best work in 2026, and more specifically, directly before his promotion to Triple-A right before the end of the season. He celebrated his 26th birthday last Monday and so, in his age-25 season, Mullins was exactly what Portland needed in a rotation guy, especially following Anthony Eyannson’s departure. He struck out 132 in 92 innings, walked 49, lacked the longevity that Holobetz and others in the rotation had but did not give up long balls, getting taken yard just seven times all season (and even one of those was in his only Worcester appearance.) The 6’0” lefty will continue his development in 2027 before likely a late season call-up; it’s possible the team explores some multi-inning reliever roles depending on how this development goes.
Of course, too, the team’s former first-round draft pick Mikey Romero and current millionaire Kristian Campbell are still kicking around Wrocester, and the latter wants a redemption arc after a rough 2025. Neither saw any Major League time due to a cluttered roster and a multitude of other reasons, but don’t count either out for a platoon role next year, pending a lengthy lockout. You want guys looking better in September than they did in April, and while Campbell swung somewhat of a hot bat in the spring, I think that notion is true for both of these guys. The same is even true with Jedixson Paez (who saw Major League action, but don’t mention this to him) Blake Wehunt and Gage Ziehl. These are all guys to watch in 2027, provided some trade for a hole on the roster doesn’t call for dealing one of them (I think Campbell is pretty set on this roster given his price tag.) But, depth is a good problem to have.
And so ends my fourth full season providing Minor Lines for Over The Monster. You’ll see me kicking around during the playoff push and the offseason providing input on pieces that can make this 2027 team - and farm - even better than the 2026 version. Thanks so much for reading all season, and Go Sox!

item.title: [Publimetro México] ¡Drama en las Grandes Ligas! Alex Bregman queda con el rostro desfigurado tras pelotazo en la MLB
item.dc:creator: Yunior Carteño
item.description: Un momento completamente accidental encendió las alarmas en las Grandes Ligas. Alex Bregman, tercera base de los Chicago Cubs, terminó en el hospital después de recibir un fuerte pelotazo en el rostro durante el juego contra los Cincinnati Reds, pese a que ni siquiera se encontraba bateando cuando ocurrió el impacto. ¿Cómo ocurrió el accidente de Alex Bregman? item.content:encoded:
Un momento completamente accidental encendió las alarmas en las Grandes Ligas. Alex Bregman, tercera base de los Chicago Cubs, terminó en el hospital después de recibir un fuerte pelotazo en el rostro durante el juego contra los Cincinnati Reds, pese a que ni siquiera se encontraba bateando cuando ocurrió el impacto.
¿Cómo ocurrió el accidente de Alex Bregman?
El incidente se produjo este domingo 20 de septiembre en el Great American Ball Park, cuando Michael Busch estaba en la caja ante los lanzamientos del dominicano Luis Mey. El pelotero de Chicago realizó un swing contenido y alcanzó a desviar la bola de foul, que tomó una trayectoria inesperada hacia donde Bregman esperaba su turno.
Con dos outs en la cuarta entrada, la pelota golpeó directamente a Bregman en el pómulo izquierdo, debajo del ojo. El antesalista reaccionó inmediatamente, soltó su bat y caminó hacia el dugout mientras se cubría la zona afectada con una mano.
La escena generó preocupación entre sus compañeros debido a la fuerza y ubicación del impacto. El manager de los Cubs, Craig Counsell, reveló posteriormente que el jugador presentaba una cortada debajo del ojo, inflamación y también sangrado por la nariz.
“Es un accidente terrible. Esperamos que esté bien”, señaló el estratega, quien admitió que inicialmente creyó que su pelotero podía tener la nariz fracturada debido a la violencia del golpe.
Chicago decidió retirarlo inmediatamente del encuentro. Matt Shaw entró como bateador emergente, mientras Pedro Ramírez posteriormente pasó a cubrir la tercera base. Los Cubs terminaron imponiéndose 9-1 sobre Cincinnati.
Alex Bregman fue trasladado al hospital
Debido a que la bola alcanzó una zona particularmente delicada, Bregman fue enviado a un hospital para someterse a radiografías y una tomografía computarizada (CT) con el objetivo de conocer la gravedad de la lesión y descartar daños mayores.
Michael Busch reconoció que continuar jugando después del episodio resultó complicado. El beisbolista explicó que todo sucedió en cuestión de segundos y manifestó su preocupación debido a que cualquier golpe en la cabeza genera alarma dentro del diamante.
Horas después, el propio Bregman dio señales alentadoras mediante sus redes sociales. El estadounidense publicó una fotografía donde apareció con el ojo izquierdo completamente inflamado, moretones y restos de sangre alrededor del rostro, una imagen que evidenció la fuerza del impacto.
Pese a lo aparatoso de su aspecto, acompañó la publicación con un breve mensaje para tranquilizar a sus seguidores: “Gracias por todos los mensajes. Volveré”.
El accidente llegó además durante una campaña importante para Bregman con los Cubs. El tercera base registra promedio de .262, 26 cuadrangulares y 89 carreras impulsadas en la temporada 2026, por lo que su evolución médica será seguida de cerca por Chicago en la recta final de la campaña.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox SP Payton Tolle Explains the Difference Between 2025 and 2026 For Him
item.dc:creator: Dan Morrison

In many respects, 2025 and 2026 look very similar, with the Red Sox heading for a Wild Card matchup and a likely opening-round series against the New York Yankees in the Bronx.
