item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox enter Saturday with the opportunity to clinch a postseason berth.
In Friday’s series opener, Roman Anthony hit the longest home run of his career en route to a 4-2 victory, which snapped Tampa Bay’s six-game winning streak.
The Sox’ magic number is down to two following the win. Two scenarios would secure a postseason berth for Boston on Saturday: A Sox victory and Blue Jays victory over the Rangers, or a Sox victory, Blue Jays loss, and Braves win over the Astros.
The Sox will turn to righthander Brayan Bello, who pitched 1 ⅔ scoreless innings out of the bullpen in his last appearance against Texas on Tuesday.
Righthander Freddy Peralta will take the mound for the Rays. He faced the Sox on July 11 while a member of the Mets, allowing two runs on three hits in 4 ⅓ innings.
Here’s a preview.
RED SOX (84-70): Anthony LF, Gasper DH, Rutschman C, Wilyer Abreu RF, Sogard 1B, Story SS, Durbin 3B, Duran CF, Kiner-Falefa 2B
Pitching: RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.74 ERA)
RAYS (93-60): Diaz DH, Aranda 1B, Caminero 3B, Hicks C, Simpson LF, Mesa Jr. RF, Palacios 2B, Mullins CF, Mateo SS
Pitching: RHP Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA)
Time: 4:10 p.m.
TV, radio: NESN, WEEI-FM 93.7
Red Sox vs. Peralta: Wilyer Abreu 0-5, Willson Contreras 7-26, Jarren Duran 3-7, Caleb Durbin 1-1, Isiah Kiner-Falefa 4-9, Andruw Monasterio 1-1, Adley Rutschman 0-3, Nick Sogard 0-2, Trevor Story 1-9, Connor Wong 1-2
Rays vs. Bello: Jonathan Aranda 6-19, Junior Caminero 1-9, Jonny DeLuca 0-2, Yandy Diaz 8-21, Jake Fraley 3-5, Nick Fortes 1-5, Liam Hicks 0-3, Richie Palacios 0-2, Jorge Mateo 2-7, Cedric Mullins 4-16, Chandler Simpson 1-3, Taylor Walls 2-17
Stat of the day: Opponents were batting .280 off Peralta’s changeup with the Mets, but they’ve hit .097 off it over the last month.
Notes: Peralta posted a 4.99 ERA in 22 starts with the Mets, but since being acquired by Tampa Bay on Aug. 2, he’s posted a 3.86 ERA in eight starts. Over his past four outings, he’s allowed just two runs on 10 hits, with 17 strikeouts and a 0.78 ERA … Willson Contreras remains day-to-day after getting hit on the right hand in Thursday night’s victory at Texas, and the Sox are confident he dodged a serious injury. Tracy said Friday he would not rule out Contreras playing this weekend …. The Sox enter Saturday 5½ games behind the Yankees for the first wild card spot. The Yankees trail Tampa Bay by 4 games for the AL East division lead.

item.dc:creator: Matías Persuh
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have been one of the major storylines in the AL East right up until the final stretch of the season. Behind the Tampa Bay Rays and New York Yankees, the team managed by interim manager Chad Tracy needs a series of results to secure a Wild Card berth and keep its postseason hopes alive. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have been one of the major storylines in the AL East right up until the final stretch of the season. Behind the Tampa Bay Rays and New York Yankees, the team managed by interim manager Chad Tracy needs a series of results to secure a Wild Card berth and keep its postseason hopes alive.
Beating the Rays on the road at Tropicana Field is a must. On top of that, the Red Sox need either the Texas Rangers or the Houston Astros to lose their game in order to finally punch their ticket to the postseason.
Both the Rangers and the Astros will play at home in the evening. Texas will host the Toronto Blue Jays at Globe Life Field, while Jose Espada’s team will welcome the Atlanta Braves to Daikin Park.
Boston wants to return to the World Series
The Boston Red Sox are itching to make a serious Fall Classic run, aiming to bring the Commissioner’s Trophy back to Fenway for the first time since their dominant 2018 championship. Sitting at an impressive 84-70 record late into the campaign, the club has completely revitalized its season under manager Chad Tracy, who took the helm and turned things around after a rough start.
Chad Tracy of the Boston Red Sox.
With the squad clicking at the right time and buying into Tracy’s energetic leadership, Boston looks ready to cause standard postseason chaos and prove they belong back on baseball’s biggest stage.
More chances to clinch a postseason spot
If the Red Sox can’t lock up their Wild Card spot today against Tampa Bay, they still have plenty of chances left on the schedule to seal the deal. They’ll wrap up their road trip at Tropicana Field on Sunday against the Rays before returning home for a critical six-game homestand to close out the regular season.
BoSox will host a three-game series against the Cleveland Guardians mid-week, followed by a final three-game Interleague matchup against the Chicago Cubs at Fenway Park from September 25-27. With those remaining games right in front of their home crowd, the Red Sox hold their postseason destiny firmly in their own hands.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Cam Schlittler llega este sábado al Chase Field con otra oportunidad de convertir una temporada que ya es dominante en algo aún más difícil de alcanzar para el resto de la Liga Americana.
El lanzador diestro de los Yankees llega a su partido contra Arizona con un balance de 14-6, una efectividad de 1,95, un WHIP de 0,90 y 228 strikeouts en 184 2/3 entradas. Ha cedido una carrera o menos en siete salidas seguidas, una racha que le ha llevado de ser un simple aspirante a situarse en el centro de las conversaciones sobre el premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, mientras que los Yankees se han asegurado otra plaza en la postemporada.
El contraste con su rival más cercano se acentuó el viernes por la noche sin que Schlittler lanzara ni una sola bola. El as de Toronto, Dylan Cease , solo aguantó 2 2/3 entradas en la derrota por 7-1 ante Texas. Concedió seis bases por bolas, encajó cuatro carreras (solo una limpia) y solo 36 de sus 74 lanzamientos fueron strikes. Sportsnet también midió su bola rápida a 93,6 mph, 3,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Cease sigue teniendo una temporada de élite. Tras la derrota, tiene un balance de 11-6, con una ERA de 2,40, un WHIP de 1,10 y 239 strikeouts en 169 entradas, lo que le sitúa a la cabeza de la Liga Americana. Su total de ponches sigue siendo mejor que el de Schlittler. Sin embargo, su promedio de carreras limpias, la eficiencia en su carga de trabajo y su control reciente marcan ahora un contraste estadístico más marcado, justo en el momento en que las opiniones sobre los premios se van consolidando.
Para los Yankees, eso va más allá de los trofeos. Schlittler se ha convertido en el miembro más estable de un cuerpo de lanzadores de los Yankees que ha tenido que lidiar con las ausencias de Gerrit Cole, Max Fried y Carlos Rodón. Además, está previsto que sea el primero en lanzar en la rotación de Nueva York en octubre, lo que hace que sus últimas salidas en la temporada regular cobren importancia tanto para la lucha por los playoffs como para la carrera por los premios.
Los Yankees llegan al sábado con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay, así que cada salida que le queda sigue teniendo un interés inmediato más allá de la carrera por los premios.
Una votación unánime cambia el panorama de la carrera
Esta semana ha llegado la señal más clara hasta ahora. En la última votación del premio Cy Young de la temporada en MLB.com, los 32 votantes eligieron al as de los Yankees como el número uno de la Liga Americana. Consiguió el máximo de 160 puntos. Cease quedó segundo con 126.
El jurado pidió a los votantes que clasificaran a cinco lanzadores en una escala del 5 al 1 (5-4-3-2-1), teniendo en cuenta tanto lo que había pasado como cómo podrían desarrollarse las dos últimas semanas. Esa distinción es importante. La encuesta no es la votación oficial de la BBWAA y no decide el premio, pero la unanimidad entre los 32 votantes de MLB.com muestra lo mucho que ha subido la posición del as de los Yankees.
El último modelo de premios de ESPN apunta en la misma dirección. Su sistema AXE sitúa a Schlittler en primer lugar entre los lanzadores de la Liga Americana con 153,1, por delante de Cease, que tiene 145,8. ESPN señaló que Schlittler ya llevaba un balance de 12-6 con una efectividad de 2,09 hasta agosto, y que luego empezó septiembre con un 2-0 y una efectividad de 0,89 en sus tres primeras salidas del mes.
El caso de Cone explica por qué los números tienen más peso
David Cone ha definido el valor de Schlittler basándose en algo más sencillo que una fórmula para los premios. El exganador del premio Cy Young de los Yankees destacó la constancia con la que este lanzador diestro ha aliviado la presión de anotar sobre la alineación y el bullpen.
«¿Dónde estarían los Yankees sin él?», dijo Cone.
A continuación, Cone situó a Schlittler al mismo nivel que las estrellas más valiosas de la liga al hablar de lo mucho que Nueva York ha dependido de él a lo largo de una temporada marcada por los cambios constantes en la rotación.
«Schlittler está entre los mejores. Se lo merece, sin duda hay que tenerlo muy en cuenta», dijo Cone.
Ese argumento viene respaldado por la trayectoria de Schlittler esta temporada. Cone señaló esta semana que el lanzador diestro ya había hecho 21 salidas en las que solo había cedido cero o una carrera. En las últimas siete salidas de Schlittler, las estadísticas actuales de la MLB muestran una efectividad de 1,00 en 45 entradas, con 57 ponches y un WHIP de 0,76.
El tropiezo de Cease marca la diferencia en los últimos compases
Lo más revelador es el momento en que se hizo la encuesta. La encuesta de MLB.com se publicó antes de la salida más corta de Cease esta temporada, el viernes en Arlington. Eso significa que el resultado unánime no necesitó su último tropiezo para diferenciar a los dos lanzadores.
Las estadísticas de Cease siguen siendo lo suficientemente buenas como para que la carrera siga siendo reñida. Tiene 11 strikeouts más que Schlittler en 15 2/3 entradas menos. Pero también ha concedido 78 bases por bolas frente a las 44 de Schlittler, y el viernes fue la tercera salida consecutiva en la que Cease no logró completar seis entradas.
Schlittler tendrá la próxima oportunidad de demostrar su valía. Los Yankees lo alinearán contra Brandon Pfaadt el sábado, con Nueva York con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Una buena actuación no garantizaría oficialmente el premio, pero dejaría aún menos margen para que algún rival cambie el panorama de esta recta final de la temporada.
Queda una última prueba antes de octubre
A los Yankees aún les queda más de una semana antes de que termine la temporada regular, y los aficionados de los Yankees saben que las votaciones para los premios no se basan en encuestas de predicción. Una o dos malas salidas finales aún pueden cambiar el panorama. Esa es la incertidumbre que Schlittler debe afrontar.
Lo que ha cambiado es la carga de la prueba. Schlittler ya no tiene que esforzarse por meterse en la conversación. Las últimas medidas a nivel nacional ya lo han situado al frente, mientras que el mal viernes de Cease ha hecho que la carrera sea aún más dura.
El sábado en Arizona le da al as de los Yankees otra oportunidad de ampliar aún más esa ventaja.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Payton Tolle's immaculate start might actually encourage Yankees before Red Sox Wild Card matchup
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski

item.content:encoded:
With the New York Yankees likely to face off against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, they will look to find any advantage they can to come out on top. That includes trying to gameplan against pitcher Payton Tolle, who will most likely be one of the Red Sox starters in the three-game set.
There's no question that Tolle is one the league's best and brightest young pitchers. Not only can he dominate a game, but he's so dang likeable that it's almost impossible to hate him. But that doesn't mean he's perfect.
Okay, he can be close to perfect sometimes, though. That's part of the problem. The Red Sox pitcher dazzled in the first inning in his Sept. 13 start against the Kansas City Royals. He threw the most smile-filled immaculate inning you’ll probably ever see, mainly utilizing his elite four-seam fastball. As his strongest pitch, he is using the four-seamer 45% of the time throughout his starts in 2026. And batters are hitting just .190 off of his heater on the season.
However, as the game against the Royals wore on, so did Tolle. His fastball velocity showed signs of dropping later in his start. While that's not too surprising for a starting pitcher, it could also be something for the Yankees to monitor. If they can work counts and force Tolle to throw a lot of pitches as he approaches a new and uncertain innings threshold, they may be able to sap his effectiveness early. The Royals start, as brilliant as it began, actually provided the Yankees with a blueprint.
The Yankees did not have luck against Tolle earlier this season
The Yankees are 1-1 against the Red Sox in games started by Tolle this season. However, he faced little resistance against the lineup in his two starts. On April 23, Tolle allowed just one run on three hits in six innings while striking out 11 batters. The Yankees scored three runs once Tolle left the game and picked up the win in Boston.
Two months later, Tolle pitched a seven-inning gem on June 26, once again at Fenway Park. He surrendered just one hit and two walks, striking out seven en route to a 6-1 Red Sox win. Nearly three months later, the Yankees will look to reverse their fortunes against the lefty. After a long season, the result could look a little differently for Tolle.
The 23-year-old has never thrown as many innings in a collegiate or professional season as he has in 2026. In fact, at 143 innings this season, he has pitched more than 50 innings over his previous career high. Now, you could look over at Cam Schlittler and say the thing, and you'd be correct. However, Schlittler’s velo hasn't trended downwards in a game as much as Tolle’s did on September 13.
To start the game, Tolle was consistently hitting 97 MPH with his four-seamer, a modest increase from his season average of 96.1 MPH. But by the sixth inning, his four-seam fastball was clocked as low as 92.7 MPH. Tolle still remained very effective, getting through the game without allowing a run and striking out seven. It's hard to say for certain if the wear and tear of a long MLB season is taking its toll on Tolle, but it could benefit a Yankees' lineup that has had mixed results against the fastball all season.
With an .845 slugging percentage against the heater, Ben Rice is by far the team's best batter when facing the cheese. He will look to set the tone early and jump on Tolle’s four-seamer. Luis García Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt have also raked against the fastball all season, though García Jr. has not hit as well against lefties. With Aaron Judge returning from injury and slowly returning to form, the team will have a decent advantage against any and all Red Sox fastballs, even Tolle's.
However, hitters like Cody Bellinger and Austin Wells will remain massive wild cards for the Yankees in the postseason. Each player has struggled to find success against the fastball in 2026. And if Jazz Chisholm Jr. is healthy enough to return to the lineup, his .338 slugging percentage will be the lowest of any starting position player. It'll be interesting to see which of these trends continues against Tolle’s fastball.
To add a hint of intrigue to the series, New York could also be facing off against another one of Boston's strong LHP. The Red Sox will gingerly work Garrett Crochet back into the mix, though he will also likely be on a pitch limit. It's not certain how the team will utilize Crochet, but he could certainly be a dangerous weapon for them, especially if paired with Tolle.
With Tolle already off to a great start in his career against the Yankees, he could continue his success this postseason. But with arm fatigue as a potential issue moving forward, his elite four-seam fastball may become just a little less overpowering. That's something that the Yankees could jump on.

item.content:encoded:
Sep 19, 2026, 11:07 AM ET
Boston Red Sox left-handed closer Aroldis Chapman (lat) felt some tightness in his lat while working out before Tuesday's game against the Texas Rangers and has not pitched since. Chapman said that he will not pitch this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays, but he expects to return during the final homestand of the regular season, which starts on Tuesday, according to Ian Browne of MLB.com. The veteran southpaw downplayed the injury on Friday, saying that the Red Sox are being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the series opener against the Rays, but the team told him not to. "I'm not worried at all," Chapman said. "From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time." Fantasy managers will be without Chapman this weekend, but for championship matchups next week, he will hopefully be ready to return to ninth-inning duties. The 38-year-old has been excellent in 2026 in his second year in Boston, posting a 1.95 ERA with a 1.14 WHIP, 34 saves, and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings pitched. Right-hander Garrett Whitlock should handle a save situation this weekend if it arises in Tampa.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Ian Browne
More Recent News
Justin Verlander Throws Live Batting Practice


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 10:03 AM ET
Detroit Tigers starting pitcher Justin Verlander (hamstring/hip) threw a one-inning, 20-pitch live batting practice session on Friday. The 43-year-old said that he felt great after this successful outing. This was yet another step in the right direction, as it was his first time throwing against live batters. What lies ahead in his progress remains to be seen, as the plan is for him to pitch one final time in his illustrious career on Saturday, September 26, against the Pittsburgh Pirates. Whether or not he is able to throw one inning or more remains questionable, but with him retiring after this season, chances are he will be healthy enough to make that appearance and cap off one of baseball's greatest careers. With 266 wins and 3,554 strikeouts over 21 seasons, the surefire Hall of Famer will be looking to finish his career where it started: in Detroit.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Chris McCosky
Trent Grisham Could Return This Season

Sep 19, 2026, 9:56 AM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Trent Grisham (hamstring) is pretty far into his recovery, two weeks after being placed on the 10-Day Injured List with a Grade 2 hamstring strain. Manager Aaron Boone reiterated that a return for him "could be in play" for the latter part of the season. It was also mentioned that when he does return, the Yankees would need to decide between him and Spencer Jones to play center field. This could complicate things for both players, as there could be some sort of platoon involving the two, diminishing their fantasy value down the stretch. Either way, the Yankees will be looking to solidify their lineup for the playoffs, and Grisham's fantasy value is very limited down the stretch, with or without a return before the playoffs.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller

Chicago White Sox outfielder Tristan Peters (rib/shoulder) crashed into the wall during Friday's game while trying to catch a fly ball in the outfield. He exited the game with contusions to both his ribs and shoulders, and Braden Montgomery took his place in the outfield. The good news is that he is listed as day-to-day and has no head injury, which was the initial concern at the time of impact. It's unclear if he will miss any time before returning, but with the White Sox in the middle of a divisional race, they may need his help sooner rather than later. The 26-year-old is hitting .272 on the season with 12 home runs and eight stolen bases, and is worth rostering in deep leagues.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Chicago White Sox
Justin Steele Completes Two-Inning Rehab Outing


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:30 AM ET
Chicago Cubs pitcher Justin Steele (elbow) threw a 33-pitch, two-inning rehab outing on Friday for the Triple-A Iowa Cubs. This was his fifth appearance since beginning his rehab assignment and the fourth that has been two innings in length. Arguably his most impressive outing yet, Steele walked the first batter of the game before striking out the side. He would finish with five strikeouts in total while not allowing a hit. While the velocity on his fastball sat at 90.2 miles per hour, it was his slider that impressed the most, generating four whiffs. It's unclear what lies ahead for him, as the Cubs are in the middle of a race for the Wild Card. While they have a comfortable lead on the teams chasing them, they do need to prepare for the postseason, and Steele returning to the Cubs may not be in the cards. What's clear is that he is feeling much better than he has in quite some time, and any return to the Cubs would likely be for a peace-of-mind appearance to allow him to enter the postseason on a healthy note, giving him the opportunity to work on coming back even stronger next spring. Fantasy managers should not expect much from him down the stretch, but those in dynasty leagues should take note and add him while they can.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Jason Kempf

Fairbanks landed on the Injured List on Tuesday with nerve irritation in his right hand. Now, the right-hander will undergo surgery to treat the injury. Cade Cavalli Agrees to Four-Year Extension With Nationals


Keith Hernandez




Sep 18, 2026, 4:50 PM ET
The Washington Nationals announced on Friday that they agreed to a four-year contract extension with right-hander Cade Cavalli through the 2030 season that includes a club option for the 2031 season. The deal is worth $47 million guaranteed and $70 million if the options are picked up, according to Spencer Nusbaum of The Athletic. The 28-year-old secures his future in D.C. after a breakout 2026 campaign. The former 22nd overall pick from the University of Oklahoma in 2020 has gone 12-5 this year with a 3.12 ERA (3.33 FIP), 1.17 WHIP, and 194:48 K:BB in 164 2/3 innings pitched across his 31 starts in his first full season in the big leagues. Cavalli only made one start in his debut season in 2022 with the Nats, did not pitch at all in 2023 due to Tommy John surgery, and made only 10 starts in Washington last year. He has posted a career-high 28.2% strikeout rate and maintained the command that he showed in a small sample size in 2025 by walking 7.0% of the batters he has faced. With a longer leash in 2027, Cavalli could be even better if he stays healthy.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Washington Nationals
Willson Contreras Held Out of Friday's Lineup


Keith Hernandez




Sep 18, 2026, 3:39 PM ET
Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (hand) is not in the team's starting lineup for Friday's series opener against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays, according to MLB.com. Nick Sogard will man first base for the BoSox and bat second against Rays left-hander Ian Seymour. It should not be a huge surprise that Contreras is not starting on Friday after he was pulled from Thursday's win over the Texas Rangers after being hit on the right hand by a pitch late in the game. Thankfully, X-rays came back negative, and Contreras was diagnosed with a bruised hand. Fantasy managers should consider him day-to-day and check back on him to see if he is playing in Game 2 of the series in Tampa on Saturday. The 34-year-old veteran and former catcher has battled through some injuries this year but has still been one of Boston's best bats in 2026, as he is currently hitting .276/.387/.518 with a .905 OPS, 27 home runs, 81 RBI, 68 runs scored, and three steals in his 446 at-bats in his first year in Beantown. However, he did hit just .217 (18-for-83) with three homers, 12 RBI, 11 walks, and 26 strikeouts in 23 games in August, and he has played in only four games so far in September.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com

Leer También: MLB: ´El Abusador´ Ronald Acuña jr. clave en la clasificación de los Bravos de Atlanta Su compatriota Wilyer Abreu negoció un boleto para iniciar el episodio antes de que Co
item.content:encoded:
Quedó a un pelotazo de igualar el récord para venezolanos en una temporada.
El carabobeño Willson Contreras, de los Medias Rojas de Boston, se vio obligado a salir del encuentro del jueves contra los Rangers de Texas debido a un bolazo en la mano derecha, durante el octavo inning, en la victoria de su club 4-3.
Leer También: MLB: ´El Abusador´ Ronald Acuña jr. clave en la clasificación de los Bravos de Atlanta
Su compatriota Wilyer Abreu negoció un boleto para iniciar el episodio antes de que Contreras fuera golpeado por un sinker de 92.3 millas por hora (mph) de Jakob Junis.
El toletero de 34 años de edad, quien disputa su undécima campaña en las Grandes Ligas, cayó al suelo del dolor antes de pararse otra vez y dirigirse a la primera base, donde Abreu lo atendió brevemente. El mánager interino de los patirrojos, Chad Tracy, y los preparadores físicos entraron al terreno, y Willson Contreras salió del encuentro poco después.
Esta campaña el ahora inicialista lleva 24 pelotazos para igualar su tope personal del certamen de 2022.
El récord de número pelotazos para venezolanos en una temporada es de 25. Lo comparten el caraqueño Andrés Galarraga (1998) y el larense Andrés Giménez (2022).
Andrés Galarraga es el líder en pelotazos recibidos en la historia entre los criollos tras ser golpeado 178 veces en 19 temporadas y 2.257 partidos. A Willson Contreras le han pegado 153 pelotazos en 1.207 juegos.
Contreras ha alcanzado marcas personales en jonrones (27), impulsadas (81) y OPS+ (155) en su primera temporada con los Medias Rojas. Lleva 199 cuadrangulares por vida en MLB.
Las radiografías realizadas el jueves a la mano lesionada del carabobeño descartaron cualquier fractura.
Willson Contreras batea para promedio este año de .276 en 129 careos. El nativo de Puerto Cabello marcha líder jonronero e impulsor de Boston.
Hender «Vivo» González
Con información de Líder

item.dc:creator: Scott Roche

item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox lost Roman Anthony to an injury in early May, little did anyone know what was about to happen. He would miss the next four months. However, while he was out, the Red Sox went on multiple winning streaks and are now closing in on a postseason berth.
Since coming back, Anthony has been slotted back into the top of the lineup by interim manager Chad Tracy. On Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, Anthony showed what he means to the top of the lineup.
Roman Anthony Leads Boston Red Sox To Win Over Tampa Bay Rays
Coming off a 4-3 win over the Texas Rangers, Anthony led off the game with a solo home run. In the second inning, he had a two-run single for a 3-1 lead in what turned into a 4-2 Boston victory. The win moved the Red Sox on the cusp of a postseason berth. They can clinch it as early as Saturday night.
After Anthony’s 2-for-5 night with three of Boston’s four RBIs, Tracy didn’t beat around the bush about what his young outfielder means to his club. Despite his struggles, Tracy has not moved Anthony lower in the lineup.
“You see what he can do,” Tracy said, per Peter Abraham of the Boston Globe. “It’s the game of baseball. There are ebbs and flows . . . When he’s going well, you can see the impact he makes.”
Anthony returned in late August, but his September has been a struggle. He is slashing .214/.335/.374 with four home runs and nine runs driven in this month. For Anthony, it’s all about getting ready for postseason baseball. That’s what Friday night’s game felt like.
“Obviously that’s a great team over there,” Anthony said, per Abraham. “It kind of felt like a playoff game and getting into that mode.”
Roman Anthony Credits Hitting Coach for Turning Things Around
After missing four months, it’s not easy to come back and hit MLB pitching. It doesn’t matter how many rehab assignments someone makes in the minors. Anthony has stayed the course and kept working with hitting coach John Soteropulos.
“He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, really, all throughout the Minor Leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk, nobody knows me better than John,” said Anthony, per Ian Browne of MLB.com. “I give so much credit to him in helping me out and getting into the video room and the cage and making sure everything is where we want it to be.”
Over their last 10 games, Boston is 5-5 thanks to wins over the Rangers and Rays. In 10 days, they will begin the American League wild-card series on the road, most likely in the Bronx against the New York Yankees. If Tampa Bay falters over the next week, New York could sneak up and win the division, which would send Boston to Tampa Bay for the wild-card series.
Regardless of who the Red Sox play, Roman Anthony is heating up, and that could be good news for the Red Sox and bad news for the rest of the playoff field.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Bill Madden: The 20-something stars are taking over MLB’s award races this season
item.dc:creator: Bill Madden
item.description: In the absence of Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge, the mysterious power outages of Vlad Guerrero Jr. and Cal Raleigh, and the injuries to Tarik Skubal and Garrett Crochet, baseball’s postseason awards are coming into focus by ushering in a new wave of 20-something superstars. Going into the weekend the teams with the best records in each league were the small market Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, both of which with leading candidates for baseball’s postseason hardware who are still years aw
item.content:encoded:
In the absence of Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge, the mysterious power outages of Vlad Guerrero Jr. and Cal Raleigh, and the injuries to Tarik Skubal and Garrett Crochet, baseball’s postseason awards are coming into focus by ushering in a new wave of 20-something superstars.
Going into the weekend the teams with the best records in each league were the small market Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, both of which with leading candidates for baseball’s postseason hardware who are still years away from their prime.
For the Brewers, 24-year-old Jacob Misiorowski is the runaway leader for the NL Cy Young Award, at 15-5 and leading the majors in ERA (1.89), strikeouts (243), WHIP (0.812) and strikeouts per nine innings (13.1) — while the Rays, in their bid to salt away the AL East, have gotten a late boost from their 23-year old third baseman Junior Caminero, who took over the AL home run lead last week and was neck and neck with Houston’s Yordan Alvarez in RBI and total bases.
On the surface, Alvarez, who leads the NL in OPS and batting (.311), would appear to have the overall statistical edge on Caminero for the MVP. But the fact that Alvarez is a DH and Caminero, who’s missed only one game while adding superior defense at third base for a team that is likely to win the division also bodes well for him. This is one race that figures to go down to the last day, with the deciding factor possibly being whether the Astros win the AL West.
As for the AL Cy Young Award, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees’ 25-year-old sophomore, has zoomed ahead of the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease with a season for the ages, including a major league-leading 1.95 ERA and 0.904 WHIP and the most starts in Yankee history allowing one or fewer runs (21). His 1.14 ERA for 16 road starts is also the lowest in American League history.
Over in the National League, with Ohtani shackled with knee and bicep injuries that have prevented him from pitching since July 3, effectively ending his chances for a fourth straight MVP, the Cubs’ 24-year-old Pete Crow-Armstrong has stepped up with a phenomenal breakthrough season. Going into the weekend, Crow-Armstrong, who’s played every game, was leading the majors in slugging, OPS and total bases and was second behind Kyle Schwarber in the NL in homers with 44 and third in RBI with 105. On Aug. 29 he hit three homers in a game and with his 44th homer on Sept. 17 surpassed Hall of Famer Billy Williams as the most by a left-handed hitter in Cubs history.
Sorry, but we’re again unable to refrain from reminding that Crow-Armstrong was the Mets’ 2020 first round draft pick who, the next season, they traded to the Cubs for two months of rental free agent Javy Baez.
When it comes to the Rookies of the Year, I realize in this lost season for the Mets there’s been a lot of buzz for Nolan McLean and Carson Benge, but neither are going to win the NL award. That would have to be Cincinnati’s unsung Sal Stewart, who even if nobody probably had him on their Rookie of the Year bingo card at the start of the season, happens to be leading all NL rookies in homers (32) and RBI (110) and has played every day. An equally strong favorite for the AL Rookie of the Year is Cleveland lefty Parker Messick, a second round draft pick out of Florida State three years ago, who leads all AL rookies in wins (12), ERA (2.57), strikeouts (186) and WHIP (1.04).
IT’S A MADD, MADD WORLD
You have to wonder if the window has already closed on Aaron Judge leading the Yankees to a World Series title. The 34-year-old Yankee captain has missed 317 games (and counting) and had only four full seasons since 2018 and the fact remains he’s 280 pounds — and every time he has to make a diving catch or crash into a wall at his age now that’s 280 pounds of impact on his body. No surprise the rib injury that’s sidelined him most of this season. … For nine decades, Juan Vene was a fixture in the press boxes of Yankee Stadium and Shea Stadium and even though his name may not be familiar to most New York baseball fans, he was a legend, especially in his native Venezuela, but really all over Latin America. Word came last week that Vene passed away Sept. 15 in Miami at age 97. A long-time member of the Baseball Writers Association and a regular Hall of Fame voter, Vene was a friend to all of us. Anyone needing an interview with a Latin player in the offseason could count on Vene to help set it up. RIP. … If the White Sox are somehow able to hold on and win the AL Central it will be a remarkable achievement given the year-long state of their starting pitching. According to the Elias Bureau, White Sox starters have logged by far the fewest innings (639) in the majors to the runner-up Nationals’ 671 1/3, and as they stagger to the finish line they have been employing “openers” 2-3 times a week.

item.content:encoded:
The former Miami-area mansion of ex-MLB star David Ortiz is back in the luxury real estate spotlight. The Boston Red Sox legend’s custom-built Pinecrest estate is back on the market with an asking price of $11.5 million, adding another high-profile chapter to the property after its multimillion-dollar sale in 2023.
In 2016, Ortiz bought the empty lot in Pinecrest for $1.5 million and finished building the contemporary home in 2019. Later in 2023, he listed the property for $12.5 million, selling it in June of that year for around $10.55 million, which was said to be a Pinecrest residential sales record at the time.
MLB legend David Ortiz’s former Miami mansion returns with $11.5 million asking price
Ex-MLB star David Ortiz's old Miami mansion hits market with $11.5M asking price
The estate is in North Pinecrest, Fla., and sits on approximately 10,178 square feet of space and more than an acre of landscaped grounds. The five-bedroom, eight-bathroom home offers open living spaces, dramatic architecture and ample entertaining spaces.
| Property detail | Information |
| Former owner | David Ortiz |
| Location | Pinecrest, Florida |
| Size | Approximately 10,178 sq. ft. |
| Lot | More than 1 acre |
| Bedrooms | 5 |
| Bathrooms | 8 |
| Current asking price | $11.5 million |
| 2023 sale price | Approximately $10.55 million |
David Ortiz built a luxury Pinecrest estate
The contemporary home has floor-to-ceiling glass that bathes the interiors in natural light and frames views of the tropical landscaping. The entry is dramatically designed with water and fire elements to create an atmosphere to match the modern design of the property.
The centerpiece is an Italian Officine Gullo kitchen with a walk-in pantry within.
The residence also features multiple private suites, including a primary suite with a boutique-style closet and a spa-inspired bathroom featuring a floating bathtub and oversized shower.
David Ortiz’s mansion features sports-inspired amenities
The former MLB star’s home was built for entertaining, too. A custom sports lounge with a nine-screen television wall and wet bar is dedicated to watching major games. A high-tech home theater with reclining seating adds yet another entertainment feature.
The outdoor spaces keep up the resort feel. Along with a swimming pool and spa, the property offers a summer kitchen, gazebo, covered terraces and three fire pits for ample outdoor entertaining space.
Thus, Ortiz's former Pinecrest mansion has notable real estate history and the lifestyle amenities that come with a high-end South Florida estate. After a record-setting sale in 2023, the property is entering a new era, with an asking price of $11.5 million for 2026.
Former MLB star David Ortiz’s ex-Pinecrest, Florida mansion is back on the market for $11.5M in 2026. The custom-built estate measures approximately 10,178 square feet and features luxury interiors, a sports lounge, a home theater, a pool, a spa and outdoor entertainment spaces. Ortiz sold the property in 2023 for $10.55 million.

item.title: [nytimes.com] Roman Anthony heating up ahead of the playoffs will be key for Red Sox offense
item.dc:creator: Jen McCaffrey

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — When Roman Anthony returned to the Boston Red Sox three weeks ago after nearly four months on the injury list with a torn right finger ligament, it initially looked as if he had barely missed any time.
Through his first five games after he was activated Aug. 30 in New York, Anthony recorded four games with multiple hits, going 10-for-22 with two homers, two doubles and a triple. His methodical rehab, missing 101 games, paid dividends with a bat that was ready to perform.
Advertisement
But then, as so often happens in baseball, he fell out of rhythm at the plate, collecting just seven hits, including just one extra-base hit, in his next 56 plate appearances.
That’s why he found himself in an early batting practice session Friday afternoon with hitting coach John Soteropulos, tinkering in the cage with a few mechanical adjustments.
The work clicked.
Oh baby, Roman! pic.twitter.com/aP7bBEgZX0
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 18, 2026
Three pitches into the game, Anthony clubbed a solo homer for a lead, and in the second inning, he smacked a bases-loaded single to drive in two more runs as the Red Sox beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-2, snapping the Rays’ six-game win streak. The win inched the Red Sox closer to clinching a playoff berth. A Red Sox win Saturday, coupled with a Texas Rangers loss, would punch Boston’s ticket to the playoffs.
“We came out and looked really good offensively in the first part of that game, and there was a lot of energy in the dugout,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “I think guys feel it. We’re not done yet, but I definitely think they sniff it, and we’re wanting to get there for sure.”
With eight games left in the regular season, getting Anthony’s bat hot again, particularly as Willson Contreras remains day to day with a deeply bruised right hand, will be imperative for the Red Sox lineup in the postseason.
“He will,” Tracy said confidently about Anthony’s bat regaining momentum. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows. He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.”
Before Soteropulos was elevated to lead hitting coach this season after an overhaul of the coaching staff, he was the minor-league hitting coordinator and worked closely with Anthony. That relationship has helped.
Advertisement
“Me and John have been working on some things, really since I have been back,” Anthony said. “He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, all throughout the minor leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk and when to tinker. Nobody knows me better than John.
“It’s such a constant game of adjustments and looking over a span of my last few at-bats, it obviously was not where I wanted to be. I was hitting the ball on the ground, to the right side, so I was trying to get away from that. Hitting early on the field with John and with Trevor (Story) definitely helped.”
Anthony’s first-inning homer came off the bat at an estimated 107.7 mph with an estimated distance of 438 feet, marking the longest homer of his career.
But to him, the two-run single was just as important. In a rough series in Texas, the Red Sox had gone just 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position. His goal was to alleviate some pressure on the offense by simply making contact.
“That’s my job, to do everything I can to put the ball in play and find ways on base,” he said. “That’s how I have had a lot of success in the past as a leadoff hitter. So over these last games, just keep putting an emphasis on being the best leadoff hitter I can be. See as many pitches I can and try and get on base. It was a huge way to start the game. This game is all about momentum, so any time you can get something like that going, it’s huge.”
The two-run single gave the Red Sox the lead back after the Rays tied the score off Ranger Suarez in the bottom of the first. Jahmai Jones made it 4-1 in the third with his sixth homer of the year.
The insurance gave the Red Sox a cushion as Suarez was uncharacteristically spotty with command, walking a career-high five batters.
Advertisement
Still, he navigated traffic in each of the first four innings and allowed just the one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings. Reliever Wyatt Olds wiggled out of a jam in the sixth after Suarez exited, walking two batters to load the bases, then falling behind pinch hitter Jake Fraley 3-1. Olds came back to strike out Fraley.
The Red Sox faced more trouble in the ninth, with reliever Erik Miller still searching for his command. Closer Aroldis Chapman remains day to day with lat tightness, and Tracy turned to Miller for the ninth with Garrett Whitlock having a heavy load of late.
Miller allowed a run in the ninth on an infield single, a wild pitch, a walk and a groundout. He loaded the bases after a strikeout got away on a wild pitch, but escaped the jam with a groundout to close it out.
Clinching their postseason spot with a week left in the regular season would allow the Red Sox to breathe and reset some players before the postseason. But they’re not there yet. Saturday awaits.
“It just kind of felt like a playoff game,” Anthony said. “Getting into that mode is huge from an at-bat standpoint and from a big-game standpoint of constantly being the next man up.”

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox pitcher Payton Tolle drew all the attention during the team's annual rookie dress-up day after Thursday's series finale against the Rangers. Boston won the tie 4-3, avoiding a series sweep on the road.
While Willson Contreras gave a postgame interview in the clubhouse, Tolle reportedly tried to squeeze into his orange Lorax costume and yelled, "There's going to be ripping." The incident prompted numerous fan reactions.
Here is a picture of Tolle in the Lorax costume, shared on X:
Fans reacted hilariously to the photo. Here are some of them:
"I need video of this more than anything in my life," one fan commented.
"Tolle single-handedly saving baseball this season," another fan commented.
Tolle is having a remarkable rookie season with the Red Sox. He is 9-6 with a 3.02 ERA, 166 strikeouts, and a 1.07 WHIP through 25 starts. The 23-year-old is scheduled to make two more starts for the rest of the season.
The Red Sox opened the crucial three-game intra-divisional series against Tampa Bay with a win on Friday night. Leadoff hitter Roman Anthony was the offensive star, with a couple of hits and three RBIs.
On the mound, Ranger Suarez allowed just one run, walked five, and struck out five over 5.2 IP, as Boston won the game 4-2.
The Red Sox Are All But Certain to Face the Yankees in The AL Wild Card Series
The Yankees are currently second in the AL East, just four games behind the Rays, with the Red Sox at 5.5 games back. The Bombers are projected to secure the fourth seed, and Boston the fifth, in the postseason.
The three-game Wild Card series is scheduled to begin on Sept. 29 at Yankee Stadium, based on the current seedings. The only way the matchups could be altered is if New York overcomes a four-game deficit to Tampa Bay with just nine games left in the regular season.
The Red Sox face the Rays on Saturday in Game 2 at Tropicana Field.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Red Sox look to stay hot vs. Rays behind surging Payton Tolle
item.dc:creator: FLM

But you could always pick up more stuff." In Friday's series opener,
item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy knows his team has figured out the Tampa Bay Rays pretty well this season.
That said, the Red Sox (84-70) still can learn more about the Rays (93-60) when the teams meet Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
"At this point with (the Rays), we've played them enough already," Tracy said. "We have a pretty good understanding of them, (and) they have a pretty good understanding of us. But you could always pick up more stuff."
In Friday's series opener, the Red Sox scored four runs over the first three innings and won 4-2 to snap Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak and improve to 6-5 this season vs. the Rays.
Boston currently holds the second wild-card position in the American League but is dealing with several injuries.
"We have guys beat up that aren't here, and the hope is we get people healthy, and the roster could look even different a week from now than it does right now," Tracy said.
Boston's Willson Contreras is day-to-day after getting hit on the hand, while closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) has been unavailable the past two contests.
Right-hander Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery in 2025) and lefty Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) have advanced in their rehab assignments.
Boston left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) is expected to make his 26th start on Saturday and will try to record his sixth consecutive win.
Tolle is 1-0 with an 0.75 ERA over 12 innings in his last two starts, allowing one run on eight hits while striking out 19 with a walk. He is 0-2 with a 4.50 ERA in two starts and one relief outing against Tampa Bay, which already has clinched a playoff berth.
Whatever Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the rest of the staff have done with trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta certainly has been a success.
Acquired by the club from the New York Mets for three prospects on Aug. 2, Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) -- a right-hander who will start for the Rays on Saturday -- arrived from the Big Apple as a lesser version of what he was during his two All-Star seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers.
He was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA with the Mets, but the work was immediately put in by the Rays to adjust Peralta to where he was when he was a 17-game winner with a sub-3.00 ERA last season.
"For some reason, when I got here, when I sat here with Kyle and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and (manager Kevin Cash), they told me, like, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it,'" Peralta said.
"And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments. We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."
With the Rays, Peralta is 4-2 with a 3.86 ERA in eight starts, but his past four outings have been gems. He has pitched 23 innings and has allowed just two runs on 10 hits, with 17 strikeouts, four walks and an 0.78 ERA in that span.
"Fastball Freddy," who is using his changeup much more with the Rays, is 0-2 with a 5.40 ERA in three career starts against Boston.
Peralta allowed two runs on three hits in 4 1/3 innings in a 4-0 loss at Boston on July 11 while with the Mets.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Trevor Story is delivering an emphatic counterpoint to his doubters amid Red Sox offensive surge
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: Trevor Story has drawn the ire of Boston Red Sox fans multiple times in his Red Sox tenure, especially over the last two seasons. Between injuries and extended slumps, fans have turned against Story many times, but each time he has come back and proved them wrong. In 2025, Story, finally healthy, started the season ice cold. On June 6th, 2025, Story was hitting .214 with a .582 OPS. Many in Red Sox Nation were calling for Story's head, wanting the club to designate him for assignment. Then, he f
item.content:encoded:
Trevor Story has drawn the ire of Boston Red Sox fans multiple times in his Red Sox tenure, especially over the last two seasons. Between injuries and extended slumps, fans have turned against Story many times, but each time he has come back and proved them wrong.
In 2025, Story, finally healthy, started the season ice cold. On June 6th, 2025, Story was hitting .214 with a .582 OPS. Many in Red Sox Nation were calling for Story's head, wanting the club to designate him for assignment.
Then, he figured it out. From June 7 until the end of the season, the righty hit .297 with an .834 OPS. He had 43 extra-base hits and 70 RBI in 96 games.
Even with extended success, fans were still calling for him to be benched during a small slump in August, but he again rebounded in September, hitting over .300 in the final month. Story then was one of the few hitters to show up in the playoffs, leading the team in hits and RBIs, and having the Sox's only homer of the Wild Card Series.
Red Sox Nation should have known how 2026 would go for Trevor Story after what happened in 2025
Even with how well he played in the second half of the season and his success in the playoffs, fans were still unsure about him during the offseason. He did nothing to help himself in the first half of the 2026 season. Before Story was officially shut down with his sports hernia, he was hitting .206 with a .547 OPS. He had just ten extra-base hits and eight walks in 41 games.
Once again, injuries and prolonged slumps had fans turning against Story. He became almost out-of-sight out-of-mind during the Red Sox turnaround, but eventually reports about him getting healthy and going on rehab assignments had some in Red Sox Nation once again pushing against his return. Many fans didn't want to force the shortstop back into the lineup after his performance, but once again he's proved them wrong.
In 16 games since his return from the IL, Story is hitting .349 with an .867 OPS. He came back and immediately went on a seven-game hit streak. He's hit seven doubles, and his first home run since his return was a three-run shot that gave the Sox a 4-3 lead against the Rangers. After being worth -0.3 fWAR in his first 41 games, Story has accumulated 0.6 fWAR since coming back.
Story put everything together at the right time again. With the playoffs less than two weeks away, nobody is questioning whether the 33-year-old should be playing every day or on the playoff roster.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox Lose Speedster for 2026, Enter Braiden Ward?
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The biggest story of the 2026 Major League Baseball trade deadline was the Boston Red Sox's addition of Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles. While this is the case, he wasn't Boston's only impactful addition. Boston went out and acquired speedy outfielder Eli White from the Atlanta Braves in exchange for right-handed pitcher Tyler Uberstine. The deal for White was certainly quieter than the Rutschman deal, to say the least. White is a 32-year-old speedster who gets on base, can steal base
item.content:encoded:
The biggest story of the 2026 Major League Baseball trade deadline was the Boston Red Sox's addition of Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles. While this is the case, he wasn't Boston's only impactful addition.
Boston went out and acquired speedy outfielder Eli White from the Atlanta Braves in exchange for right-handed pitcher Tyler Uberstine. The deal for White was certainly quieter than the Rutschman deal, to say the least. White is a 32-year-old speedster who gets on base, can steal bases and plays good defense. He's a good guy to have on a playoff roster, but unfortunately he is "likely" done for the season now with a torn ligament in his foot in his foot, per WEEI's Rob Bradford.
"No news on Contreras. No new scans. See how grip strength improves. Also, Eli White has a tear in the ligament in his foot and is likely out for the season. Crochet will throw another side session tomorrow with up-downs," Bradford wrote.
With White now likely done for the season, this only adds fuel to the idea that someone like Braiden Ward should be considered for a promotion to the big league club before all is said and done on the 2026 season.
The Red Sox A Decision To Make
White may not be a big-name player, but this news isn't great for Boston. White played in 27 games in Boston after the trade and slashed .276/.300/.379 with a .679 OPS, one home run, 12 RBIs, three doubles and 10 runs scored. Overall, White was a 1.4-WAR player this season, the highest mark of his career, in 96 total games with Boston and Atlanta.
Ward was a Spring Training standout for Boston and stole 19 bases. He was sent down to Triple-A Worcester when the regular season kicked off and he has spent the entire season there. Ward has played in 108 games and is slashing .251/.364/.372 with a .736 OPS, six home runs, 33 RBIs and most importantly, 61 stolen bases.
We made the case for Boston to give Ward a look back on Sep. 13. On Sep. 16, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about Ward and insinuated that the idea to promote the speedster would at least be considered. With the bad news for White, now should be the time to give Ward a look. He has game-changing speed and could be used simply as a pinch runner in the playoffs. White likely would've been in a similar role if he didn't get hurt. Now, the Red Sox should turn to Ward.

item.title: [Boston.com] Red Sox’ Willson Contreras has ominous comments after latest HBP
item.dc:creator: Kaley Brown
item.description: The ever-fiery Willson Contreras had some on-brand quotes after his latest hit-by-pitch. The Red Sox first baseman got drilled on the right hand by a pitch from Texas Rangers right-handed pitcher Jakob Junis in the eighth inning on Thursday night. He was in visible pain and immediately exited the game. After the game, he said he thought his hand was fractured upon being struck, but he appears to have avoided serious injury. His X-rays came back negative. Also postgame, Contreras expressed immens
item.content:encoded:
The ever-fiery Willson Contreras had some on-brand quotes after his latest hit-by-pitch.
The Red Sox first baseman got drilled on the right hand by a pitch from Texas Rangers right-handed pitcher Jakob Junis in the eighth inning on Thursday night. He was in visible pain and immediately exited the game.
After the game, he said he thought his hand was fractured upon being struck, but he appears to have avoided serious injury. His X-rays came back negative.
Also postgame, Contreras expressed immense discontent with the fact that he’s been hit by pitches on 24 separate occasions this season. The total ties a career high (2022 with the Chicago Cubs) and continues a trend he’s experienced his entire MLB career. Only two players have been hit more this year (Cardinals’ Ivan Herrera, 29; White Sox’ Sam Antonacci, 27).
“I feel like … ” Contreras said, pausing for seven seconds, “I want to say something I can’t say. Let’s leave it at that (via The Boston Globe’s Tim Healey).”
Contreras, attempting to elaborate without getting into specifics, added:
“If nobody does anything about it, I’m going to keep getting hit. That’s the way I see it. That’s it.”
The 34-year-old, who has been Boston’s best hitter during its memorable season, came off the injured list last weekend after recovering from a hamstring strain. He expressed frustration about not knowing when he’ll return to the diamond again.
“It’s really frustrating because I just came back from the IL, and this might take days,” Contreras said. “I mean, sore bones in the hands — might take two days, might take a week, might take 10 days.”
Contreras is known as a right-handed batter who crowds the plate, which leads to more HBPs. He pushed back on that notion, though, saying other hitters do the same thing but get drilled less often.
“A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate, but I’m seeing a lot of players hit on top of the plate. They don’t get hit like me,” Contreras said.
The Venezuelan has been hit 146 times since 2018, which leads MLB.
Interim manager Chad Tracy offered an injury update on Contreras before Friday’s game against the Rays in Tampa.
“(He’s) sore. Obviously sore with some swelling,” Tracy told reporters. “Nothing new other than just, over the next couple of days, they’ll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out. See if he can get grip strength back, and then we’ll go from there. Just day to day.”
Tracy didn’t write off Contreras returning to the lineup this weekend.
“Never want to rule it out,” he said. “You get the swelling out of there and he could turn a corner really quickly. Just hard to say.”

item.title: [yardbarker.com] 'Get Hit and Cry': Red Sox’s Willson Contreras Faces Brutal MLB Analyst Criticism After Injury Scare
item.dc:creator: Sourav Kumar Ghatak
item.description: Willson Contreras was left furious after a 92.3 mph sinker drilled his right hand and forced him out of Thursday’s game. Just four days removed from a 10-day IL stint, Boston’s hitting leader was back screaming in pain at the plate, leaving Red Sox fans fearing the worst. But while Boston held its breath over another injury scare, former MLB catcher Erik Kratz had little sympathy. “This picture right here with a line on the inside of the plate, this is why he’s getting hit. There are plenty of d
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras was left furious after a 92.3 mph sinker drilled his right hand and forced him out of Thursday’s game. Just four days removed from a 10-day IL stint, Boston’s hitting leader was back screaming in pain at the plate, leaving Red Sox fans fearing the worst. But while Boston held its breath over another injury scare, former MLB catcher Erik Kratz had little sympathy.
“This picture right here with a line on the inside of the plate, this is why he’s getting hit. There are plenty of dudes that get hit. There are plenty of dudes that stand close to the plate that get hit and cry less than Willson,” Kratz said via Foul Territory.
“Starling Marte is up there. Freddie Freeman is up there. When and how many times do we hear those guys complaining about it? Anthony Rizzo was this guy. Rarely was there like, ‘Ooh, we gotta have retaliation.’ When you’re close to the plate, you’re gonna get hit. That’s the reality of it, but he’s taking exception to it. It’s also kind of a ploy. Get that ball out over the plate where I can do some damage.”
The only relief for Contreras was that X-rays came back negative. But with only eight regular-season games left, even a short absence from Boston’s best hitter is bad timing.
Thursday’s plunk was already his 24th of 2026, and Kratz is not buying the idea that this is simply bad luck.
Contreras crowds the plate. That is the point.
“If he’s concerned about getting hit in the hand, he can’t sit out over the plate looking for breaking balls and then all of a sudden the heater that doesn’t break catches him on the hand,” Kratz said.
He did not dismiss the danger, either. Kratz admitted the pitch could have been an “absolute death play” if it had broken Contreras’ hand. But his larger point was that Contreras knowingly puts himself in that position.
Contreras pushed back on that explanation.
“A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate. But I’m seeing a lot of players hit on top of the plate. They don’t get hit like me,” he said.
Kratz pointed to Freddie Freeman, Starling Marte, and Anthony Rizzo as the counterargument.
“Freddie Freeman is up there. How many times do we hear those guys complaining about it? Anthony Rizzo was this guy. Rarely was there like, ‘Oh, we gotta have retaliation.’”
Jose Altuve offers the opposite comparison. He stands farther off the plate and has been hit just three times this season and 83 times in 16 years. Contreras, meanwhile, is already at 24 HBPs in 2026 after recording 13 in 2023 and 12 in 2024.
Kratz boiled his criticism down even further.
“When you’re close to the plate, you’re going to get hit. That’s the reality of it.”
He also suggested there is another layer to Contreras’ setup.
“It’s also kind of a ploy. Get that ball out over the plate where I can do some damage.”
That is why Kratz sees this less as a Red Sox pitching problem and more as a trade-off Contreras accepts every time he steps into the box. The stance gives him access to pitches away, but it also leaves almost no room when pitchers challenge him inside.
And retaliation would not change that. Boston could answer by hitting someone back, but Contreras would still return to the same spot in the box.
For Kratz, this is not something the Red Sox pitching staff can solve for him. Contreras chose the setup, and the bruises come with it.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Ranger Suarez may not have been at his best, but the Red Sox lefthander still showed he had enough fight - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tara Sullivan
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter. This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week fro
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony Powers Red Sox Past Rays, Closer To Playoff Berth originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox spent much of Friday night walking a tightrope. Roman Anthony made sure they had enough of a cushion to survive. Anthony homered and drove in three runs, Ranger Suárez battled through 5 2/3 innings and the Red Sox held on for a 4-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field.
Boston improved to 84-70 with its second consecutive victory and snapped Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak. The Red Sox entered the series opener with a magic number of three to clinch an American League wild-card berth and could secure their postseason spot as early as Saturday.
It was not a comfortable victory.
Red Sox pitchers issued nine walks, including four over the final four innings. The Rays loaded the bases in both the sixth and ninth but went 0-for-13 with runners in scoring position and stranded 12 runners. Erik Miller finally ended the ninth-inning adventure by getting Chandler Simpson to ground out with the bases loaded.
Here are three takeaways from Boston's important victory.
Roman Anthony Sets Tone Immediately
Anthony did not wait long to make his presence felt. The Red Sox rookie crushed Ian Seymour's third pitch of the game 438 feet to center field, giving Boston a 1-0 lead before most of the announced crowd of 23,342 had settled into its seats.
It was Anthony's fifth home run of the season and the third leadoff homer of his young career. The Rays answered in the bottom of the first when Junior Caminero drove in Yandy Díaz with a groundout, but Anthony struck again one inning later.
Trevor Story singled and Caleb Durbin followed with another base hit. After Nate Eaton walked to load the bases, Anthony delivered a two-out single to right that scored Story and Durbin. Anthony finished 2-for-5 with three RBIs, accounting for nearly all of Boston's offense on one of the biggest nights of its season.
Jahmai Jones supplied the other run by launching a 414-foot solo homer to left in the third inning. Jones' sixth home run gave Boston a 4-1 advantage that held until the ninth.
Ranger Suárez Bends Without Breaking
Suárez rarely had a clean inning, but the left-hander consistently found his way out of trouble. The Boston starter allowed only three hits and one run while striking out five. He also issued five walks and needed 98 pitches to record 17 outs.
His best defensive moment came in the fourth inning.
Taylor Walls hit a 100-mph line drive directly back at Suárez, who made the catch before throwing to first base to double off Nick Fortes. The play erased a scoring opportunity and helped Suárez navigate another stressful inning. The left-hander improved to 8-4 and lowered his ERA to 3.27.
Wyatt Olds entered with two outs in the sixth and immediately made matters worse by issuing two walks. He recovered to strike out Jake Fraley with the bases loaded, preserving Boston's three-run advantage.
Greg Weissert provided the calmest portion of the night, allowing one hit over two scoreless innings.
Erik Miller Survives Chaotic Ninth Inning
The Red Sox carried a 4-1 lead into the ninth, but Miller turned the final three outs into a full-blown ordeal. The left-hander issued two walks and threw three wild pitches during a 32-pitch inning. Jonathan Aranda drove in one run with a fielder's choice, cutting Boston's lead to 4-2.
Tampa Bay eventually loaded the bases with two outs, bringing Simpson to the plate as the potential winning run. Miller induced a ground ball to third baseman Durbin, who completed the force play at second to end the game. Miller earned his fifth save despite allowing one run, one hit and two walks.
Boston will take the victory, especially at this stage of the season, but the nine walks gave the club another issue to clean up before October. The Red Sox will attempt to clinch their postseason berth Saturday when they continue the three-game series in Tampa Bay. The Rays are scheduled to start right-hander Freddy Peralta, while Boston has yet to announce it's starter.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox’ Ranger Suarez sets a career high in walks, but navigates tightrope in win
item.dc:creator: Sean McAdam
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all.
There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings.
But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough.
"I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today and that was part of it."
Suarez had difficulty explaining how the walks piled up on him. It wasn't mechanical, and it wasn't the result of nibbling around the strike zone.
"I think it was one of those nights when I didn't have the command," he said. "But I was able to get outs when I needed."
The latter has always been his calling card. In an era when most starters unleash fastballs at 95 mph or better, Suarez thrives by mixing pitches, keeping hitters off balance and inducing soft contact.
On nights when he can't locate with precision, the margin for error slips further. But again, knowing how to get out of trouble is a mound skill in and of itself.
Suarez has used that talent particularly well in the postseason before, which is part of what motivated the Red Sox to offer him $130 million over five years last winter. Suarez isn't about to come unglued in Yankee Stadium in two weeks — or any other time he gets the ball in the postseason. His career ERA of 1.48 in the playoffs virtually guarantees that.
"He was very competitive with men on base," said interim manager Chad Tracy. "He lost some counts, was behind more counts today, but he wa able to really good pitches with people on base."
Even as he labored, Suarez was adding to a September resumé which has him 3-0 with 0.92 ERA in his last three outings while limiting opposing hitters to a .186 batting average.
No one knows exactly how or when Suarez will fit into Boston's postseason rotation. The assumption is that Sonny Gray will pitch Game 1, with either Payton Tolle or Suarez slotted for Game 2, and the remaining choice available for a winner-take-all Game 3.
Of course, the risk there is that a team may never get to its third starter if it doesn't win at least one of the first two games. That's part of the difficult decision the Red Sox will have to make before their wild card round gets underway.
Even with his history of success in October, Suarez isn't thinking too much about the postseason — not yet anyway.
"No, no,'' he said with a chuckle. "When we clinch, I'll be able to do that. But mathematically, we're not there yet, so I'm not thinking about that."
Suarez has one more start in the regular season, which he can treat as both a tuneup for himself and an audition for Game 2 in the best-of-three wild card round.,
"He's a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he's going to find his way through it. He does that at times this year, so that's never a concern with him."

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Red Sox beat Rays to close in on playoff spot
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

The Red Sox, who entered Friday with a magic number of three, could secure a wild-card spot as early as Saturday. Junior Caminero and Jonathan Aranda drove in runs for the post-season-bound Rays. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Roman Anthony homered and drove in three runs and the Boston Red Sox took a big step toward clinching an American League playoff spot with a 4-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday night.
The Red Sox, who entered Friday with a magic number of three, could secure a wild-card spot as early as Saturday.
Junior Caminero and Jonathan Aranda drove in runs for the post-season-bound Rays. They had won six in a row.
Anthony hit the game’s third pitch from Ian Seymour (9-7) into the right-field seats for his third career leadoff homer. Then, in the second inning, Anthony broke a 1-1 tie and drove in two more runs with a two-out single.
Jahmai Jones gave Boston a 4-1 advantage with his own solo homer to lead off the third. Caleb Durbin added two hits for the Red Sox, who own the American League’s third-best record (84-70), behind the Rays and Yankees.
Red Sox starter Ranger Suarez (8-4) threw 5 2/3 innings, allowing three hits and one run with five walks and five strikeouts. He also snared Taylor Walls’ 100-mph liner in the fourth, before completing an inning-ending double play.
Tampa Bay couldn’t capitalize on multiple opportunities, including nine Red Sox walks. The Rays left the bases loaded in the sixth and ninth, when Erik Miller retired Chandler Simpson on a game-ending grounder. Tampa Bay was 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position.
Boston left-hander Erik Miller had his fifth save despite a shaky ninth inning, including three wild pitches and two walks.
Up next
Tampa Bay RHP Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) was set to start Saturday. Boston had yet to announce a starter.
